abstract: A new class of neural network aimed at early visual processing is described; we call it a Neural Analog Diffusion-Enhancement Layer or "NADEL." The network consists of two levels which are coupled through feedfoward and shunted feedback connections. The lower level is a two-dimensional diffusion map which accepts visual features as input, and spreads activity over larger scales as a function of time. The upper layer is periodically fed the activity from the diffusion layer and locates local maxima in it (an extreme form of contrast enhancement) using a network of local comparators. These local maxima are fed back to the diffusion layer using an on-center/off-surround shunting anatomy. The maxima are also available as output of the network. The network dynamics serves to cluster features on multiple scales as a function of time, and can be used in a variety of early visual processing tasks such as: extraction of comers and high curvature points along edge contours, line end detection, gap filling in contours, generation of fixation points, perceptual grouping on multiple scales, correspondence and path impletion in long-range apparent motion, and building 2-D shape representations that are invariant to location, orientation, scale, and small deformation on the visual field.

paragraphs: NADEL is a two-level neural network for early visual processing. Its lower level receives visual features on a two-dimensional map and spreads their activity over progressively larger spatial scales as time passes. This diffusion makes elapsed time part of how the network organizes visual information.

The upper level periodically receives the diffusion map's activity and uses local comparisons to find activity peaks. These peaks provide the network's output and are also fed back through connections that enhance the center and suppress the surrounding region. The interaction between spreading activity and selective enhancement produces feature clusters at multiple scales.

The authors describe uses ranging from finding corners, sharp bends, and line endings to filling contour gaps and choosing fixation points. They also identify multiscale perceptual grouping, long-range apparent-motion correspondence, and two-dimensional shape representation as applications. The common mechanism is the changing organization of local features over space and time. The proposed shape representations can tolerate changes in position, orientation, scale, and small deformations.
summary.tldr: NADEL combines spatial diffusion with feedback from local activity peaks to group visual features across scales over time.

title: Neural Analog Diffusion-Enhancement Layer and Spatio-Temporal Grouping in Early Vision

abstract: Several parallel analogue algorithms, based upon mean field theory (MFT) approximations to an underlying statistical mechanics formulation, and re(cid:173) quiring an externally prescribed annealing schedule, now exist for finding approximate solutions to difficult combinatorial optimisation problems. They have been applied to the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP), as well as to various issues in computational vision and cluster analysis. I show here that any given MFT algorithm can be combined in a natural way with notions from the areas of constrained optimisation and adaptive simulated annealing to yield a single homogenous and efficient parallel re(cid:173) laxation technique, for which an externally prescribed annealing schedule is no longer required. The results of numerical simulations on 50-city and 100-city TSP problems are presented, which show that the ensuing algo(cid:173) rithms are typically an order of magnitude faster than the MFT algorithms alone, and which also show, on occasion, superior solutions as well.

paragraphs: The paper improves a family of parallel analog methods for finding approximate solutions to difficult combinatorial problems. These methods use mean-field approximations derived from statistical mechanics and normally require an externally chosen annealing schedule. That schedule controls how the optimization process changes as it progresses toward a solution.

The proposed approach combines a given mean-field algorithm with ideas from constrained optimization and adaptive simulated annealing. The combination produces a unified parallel relaxation procedure that no longer needs an externally prescribed schedule. This integrates the management of the annealing process into the optimization method itself, addressing a practical requirement of the earlier algorithms.

Numerical simulations on traveling-salesman problems with 50 and 100 cities show that the combined algorithms are typically about ten times faster than the mean-field algorithms alone. They also sometimes produce better solutions. The findings concern approximate optimization: the main reported advantage is a large speed improvement, accompanied in some cases by an improvement in solution quality.
summary.tldr: Combining constrained optimization with adaptive annealing removes an external schedule and typically speeds tested TSP solvers by about tenfold.

title: Merging Constrained Optimisation with Deterministic Annealing to "Solve" Combinatorially Hard Problems

paragraphs: This paper derives training criteria for turning adaptive classifiers into unsupervised data analyzers. The starting point is a classifier that outputs a probability vector over possible classes. Instead of relying on supplied classification labels, the proposed criteria guide how the network organizes its interpretations of the input data.

The first criterion converts a simple Gaussian classifier into a Gaussian-mixture analyzer. The second applies more broadly and uses mutual information. It reduces to a difference between two entropy terms: one encourages decisive interpretations, while the other encourages fairness among the available alternatives. The objective brings these two pressures together rather than rewarding confidence alone.

The general criterion can be applied to any network with probability-like outputs, creating a bridge from supervised classifier architectures to unsupervised analysis. However, the authors explicitly note that it does not necessarily produce useful behavior. Its broad applicability therefore concerns where the objective can be used; it does not guarantee that the resulting classifications will reveal a useful organization of the data.
summary.tldr: Mutual-information criteria turn probabilistic classifiers toward unsupervised learning by balancing decisive assignments with fair use of alternative classes.

title: Unsupervised Classifiers, Mutual Information and 'Phantom Targets

abstract: In many optimization problems, the structure of solutions reflects complex relationships between the different input parameters. For example, experience may tell us that certain parameters are closely related and should not be explored independently. Similarly, ex(cid:173) perience may establish that a subset of parameters must take on particular values. Any search of the cost landscape should take advantage of these relationships. We present MIMIC, a framework in which we analyze the global structure of the optimization land(cid:173) scape. A novel and efficient algorithm for the estimation of this structure is derived. We use knowledge of this structure to guide a randomized search through the solution space and, in turn, to re(cid:173) fine our estimate ofthe structure. Our technique obtains significant speed gains over other randomized optimization procedures.

For example, experience may tell us that certain parameters are closely related and should not be explored independently. Similarly, ex(cid:173) perience may establish that a subset of parameters must take on particular values. Any search of the cost landscape should take advantage of these relationships. We present MIMIC, a framework in which we analyze the global structure of the optimization land(cid:173) scape. A novel and efficient algorithm for the estimation of this structure is derived. We use knowledge of this structure to guide a randomized search through the solution space and, in turn, to re(cid:173) fine our estimate ofthe structure. Our technique obtains significant speed gains over other randomized optimization procedures.

paragraphs: Optimization becomes difficult when useful settings of different parameters depend on one another. Searching each parameter independently can overlook these relationships. MIMIC approaches optimization by estimating structure in the solution space, including dependencies between parameters and restrictions on which combinations of values are useful.

The framework uses an efficient estimation algorithm to characterize the global structure of the optimization landscape. That estimated structure guides randomized exploration of candidate solutions. The candidates found during exploration then help refine the structural estimate, creating a cycle in which the search and its model inform each other.

The paper reports significant speed gains over other randomized optimization procedures. The stated mechanism gives those gains a clear interpretation: the search uses learned relationships among parameters to direct its exploration. The broader contribution is to treat probability-density estimation as part of optimization itself, so that information gathered during a search changes how later candidate solutions are explored.
summary.tldr: MIMIC accelerates randomized optimization by learning parameter relationships and using them to guide further search.

title: MIMIC: Finding Optima by Estimating Probability Densities

abstract: Perceptron Decision Trees (also known as Linear Machine DTs, etc.) are analysed in order that data-dependent Structural Risk Minimisation can be applied. Data-dependent analysis is performed which indicates that choosing the maximal margin hyperplanes at the decision nodes will improve the generalization. The analysis uses a novel technique to bound the generalization error in terms of the margins at individual nodes. Experiments performed on real data sets confirm the validity of the approach.
originalAbstract: Perceptron Decision Trees (also known as Linear Machine DTs, etc.) are analysed in order that data-dependent Structural Risk Minimisation can be applied. Data-dependent analysis is performed which indicates that choosing the maximal margin hyperplanes at the decision nodes will improve the generalization. The analysis uses a novel technique to bound the generalization error in terms of the margins at individual nodes. Experiments performed on real data sets confirm the validity of the approach.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes decision trees whose internal decisions use perceptrons, or linear separating boundaries. Its concern is generalization: how choices made while fitting the training data affect predictions on new examples. The authors develop an analysis that depends on the observed data so that structural risk minimization can be applied to these trees.

The key quantity is the margin at each decision node, expressing separation around that node's decision boundary. A new bounding technique connects these individual margins to the tree's generalization error. This provides a mathematical reason to examine the quality of the boundaries within the tree, rather than considering the tree only as a completed classifier.

The analysis indicates that choosing maximum-margin hyperplanes at decision nodes should improve generalization. Experiments on real datasets support the approach. The contribution links a local design choice, how to place each separating boundary, to a bound on the predictive behavior of the whole tree, giving the margin criterion a role in principled model selection.
summary.tldr: Bounds based on individual node margins support using maximum-margin splits to improve perceptron decision-tree generalization.

title: Data-Dependent Structural Risk Minimization for Perceptron Decision Trees

abstract: Invariance to topographic transformations such as translation and shearing in an image has been successfully incorporated into feed(cid:173) forward mechanisms, e.g., "convolutional neural networks", "tan(cid:173) gent propagation". We describe a way to add transformation invari(cid:173) ance to a generative density model by approximating the nonlinear transformation manifold by a discrete set of transformations. An EM algorithm for the original model can be extended to the new model by computing expectations over the set of transformations. We show how to add a discrete transformation variable to Gaussian mixture modeling, factor analysis and mixtures of factor analysis. We give results on filtering microscopy images, face and facial pose clustering, and handwritten digit modeling and recognition.
originalAbstract: Invariance to topographic transformations such as translation and shearing in an image has been successfully incorporated into feed(cid:173) forward mechanisms, e.g., "convolutional neural networks", "tan(cid:173) gent propagation". We describe a way to add transformation invari(cid:173) ance to a generative density model by approximating the nonlinear transformation manifold by a discrete set of transformations. An EM algorithm for the original model can be extended to the new model by computing expectations over the set of transformations. We show how to add a discrete transformation variable to Gaussian mixture modeling, factor analysis and mixtures of factor analysis. We give results on filtering microscopy images, face and facial pose clustering, and handwritten digit modeling and recognition.

paragraphs: This paper adds invariance to image transformations, such as translation and shearing, to generative density models. Such transformations can change an image's appearance without changing the underlying content being modeled. The approach represents transformation as a hidden variable, allowing the probabilistic model to account for multiple transformed versions of an observation.

The key approximation replaces a nonlinear transformation manifold with a discrete collection of transformations. An existing expectation-maximization algorithm can then be extended by taking expectations over that collection. This supplies a concrete mechanism for incorporating transformation uncertainty into learning. The authors show how to apply it to Gaussian mixtures, factor analysis, and mixtures of factor analysers.

Reported applications include filtering microscopy images, clustering faces and facial poses, and modeling and recognizing handwritten digits. These examples demonstrate the range of tasks to which the transformation variable is applied. The methodological contribution is a reusable extension of generative models: transformation handling becomes part of the probabilistic representation and its inference procedure.
summary.tldr: A discrete hidden transformation variable lets generative image models account for changes such as translation and shearing through extended EM inference.

title: Topographic Transformation as a Discrete Latent Variable

abstract: This paper describes a clustering algorithm for vector quantizers using a “stochastic association model”. It offers a new simple and powerful soft- max adaptation rule. The adaptation process is the same as the on-line K-means clustering method except for adding random ﬂuctuation in the distortion error evaluation process. Simulation results demonstrate that the new algorithm can achieve efﬁcient adaptation as high as the “neural gas” algorithm, which is reported as one of the most efﬁcient clustering methods. It is a key to add uncorrelated random ﬂuctuation in the simi- larity evaluation process for each reference vector. For hardware imple- mentation of this process, we propose a nanostructure, whose operation is described by a single-electron circuit. It positively uses ﬂuctuation in quantum mechanical tunneling processes.

The adaptation process is the same as the on-line K-means clustering method except for adding random ﬂuctuation in the distortion error evaluation process. Simulation results demonstrate that the new algorithm can achieve efﬁcient adaptation as high as the “neural gas” algorithm, which is reported as one of the most efﬁcient clustering methods. It is a key to add uncorrelated random ﬂuctuation in the simi- larity evaluation process for each reference vector. It positively uses ﬂuctuation in quantum mechanical tunneling processes.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a clustering algorithm for vector quantization, where reference vectors represent groups of input observations. The method uses a stochastic association model to obtain a simple softmax adaptation rule. Its update process closely follows online K-means, making the source of its different behavior particularly specific.

The change is to introduce random fluctuations when evaluating distortion, or how well a reference vector matches an input. The authors emphasize that these fluctuations must be uncorrelated across reference vectors. Randomness therefore enters the comparison process that guides adaptation, rather than being presented merely as an incidental disturbance to otherwise deterministic computation.

Simulations show adaptation efficiency comparable to neural gas, the strong clustering method identified in the abstract. The paper also proposes a nanostructure implementation described through a single-electron circuit. That proposal uses fluctuations arising from quantum tunneling as part of the computation itself. Together, the algorithm and hardware proposal connect a useful stochastic learning rule with a physical process capable of supplying its randomness.
summary.tldr: Adding independent random fluctuations to online clustering comparisons yields efficient adaptation and motivates a single-electron hardware implementation.

title: An Efficient Clustering Algorithm Using Stochastic Association Model and Its Implementation Using Nanostructures

abstract: Inner-product operators, often referred to as kernels in statistical learning, de- ﬁne a mapping from some input space into a feature space. The focus of this paper is the construction of biologically-motivated kernels for cortical ac- tivities. The kernels we derive, termed Spikernels, map spike count sequences into an abstract vector space in which we can perform various prediction tasks. We discuss in detail the derivation of Spikernels and describe an efﬁcient al- gorithm for computing their value on any two sequences of neural population spike counts. We demonstrate the merits of our modeling approach using the Spikernel and various standard kernels for the task of predicting hand move- ment velocities from cortical recordings. In all of our experiments all the ker- nels we tested outperform the standard scalar product used in regression with the Spikernel consistently achieving the best performance.

The focus of this paper is the construction of biologically-motivated kernels for cortical ac- tivities. The kernels we derive, termed Spikernels, map spike count sequences into an abstract vector space in which we can perform various prediction tasks. We discuss in detail the derivation of Spikernels and describe an efﬁcient al- gorithm for computing their value on any two sequences of neural population spike counts. We demonstrate the merits of our modeling approach using the Spikernel and various standard kernels for the task of predicting hand move- ment velocities from cortical recordings. In all of our experiments all the ker- nels we tested outperform the standard scalar product used in regression with the Spikernel consistently achieving the best performance.

paragraphs: Predicting behavior from cortical activity requires a useful way to compare neural recordings. This paper constructs biologically motivated kernels called Spikernels for sequences of neural population spike counts. A kernel supplies an inner-product comparison associated with an abstract feature space, allowing the recordings to be used in prediction tasks through that representation.

The authors explain how to derive these kernels and provide an efficient algorithm for evaluating a Spikernel on two sequences. The method therefore addresses both the definition of a neural-activity comparison and its computation. Its input is a sequence of spike counts, preserving a sequential representation of the recorded population activity.

The evaluation predicts hand movement velocities from cortical recordings and compares Spikernels with several standard kernels. In every reported experiment, all tested kernels outperform the ordinary scalar product used in regression, and the Spikernel performs best. These results support the value of the proposed representation for this decoding task, with the consistent advantage referring to the experiments reported in the paper.
summary.tldr: Biologically motivated Spikernels compare neural spike-count sequences and perform best among the tested kernels for predicting hand velocity.

title: Spikernels: Embedding Spiking Neurons in Inner-Product Spaces

abstract: We study a new, model-free form of approximate policy iteration which uses Sarsa updates with linear state-action value function approximation for policy evaluation, and a “policy improvement operator” to generate a new policy based on the learned state-action values. We prove that if the policy improvement operator produces -soft policies and is Lipschitz continuous in the action values, with a constant that is not too large, then the approximate policy iteration algorithm converges to a unique solu- tion from any initial policy. To our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst conver- gence result for any form of approximate policy iteration under similar computational-resource assumptions.
originalAbstract: We study a new, model-free form of approximate policy iteration which uses Sarsa updates with linear state-action value function approximation for policy evaluation, and a “policy improvement operator” to generate a new policy based on the learned state-action values. We prove that if the policy improvement operator produces -soft policies and is Lipschitz continuous in the action values, with a constant that is not too large, then the approximate policy iteration algorithm converges to a unique solu- tion from any initial policy. To our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst conver- gence result for any form of approximate policy iteration under similar computational-resource assumptions.

paragraphs: Policy iteration alternates between estimating how well a decision rule performs and constructing a new rule from those estimates. This paper studies a model-free version in which policy evaluation uses Sarsa updates and a linear approximation to state-action values. A separate policy improvement operator turns the learned values into the next policy.

The main result is a conditional convergence guarantee. The improvement operator must produce soft policies, retaining some probability of alternative actions. It must also be Lipschitz continuous in the action values, with a sufficiently small constant. In plain language, changes in estimated values must not cause excessively large changes in the resulting policy.

Under those conditions, the algorithm converges to a unique solution from any starting policy. The guarantee therefore links stable learning to controlled policy updates, even when values are approximated. It establishes convergence to a unique solution under the stated assumptions; it does not identify that solution as an optimal policy.
summary.tldr: Approximate policy iteration converges to a unique solution when its policy updates remain sufficiently smooth and exploratory.

title: A Convergent Form of Approximate Policy Iteration

abstract: People routinely make sophisticated causal inferences unconsciously, ef- fortlessly, and from very little data – often from just one or a few ob- servations. We argue that these inferences can be explained as Bayesian computations over a hypothesis space of causal graphical models, shaped by strong top-down prior knowledge in the form of intuitive theories. We present two case studies of our approach, including quantitative mod- els of human causal judgments and brief comparisons with traditional bottom-up models of inference.
originalAbstract: People routinely make sophisticated causal inferences unconsciously, ef- fortlessly, and from very little data – often from just one or a few ob- servations. We argue that these inferences can be explained as Bayesian computations over a hypothesis space of causal graphical models, shaped by strong top-down prior knowledge in the form of intuitive theories. We present two case studies of our approach, including quantitative mod- els of human causal judgments and brief comparisons with traditional bottom-up models of inference.

paragraphs: The paper asks how people can draw sophisticated causal conclusions from only one or a few observations. Its proposed explanation is that people bring substantial prior knowledge to the task. Intuitive theories shape which causal accounts they consider, helping explain how limited evidence can support judgments that would be difficult to derive from observations alone.

The authors formalize this idea as Bayesian reasoning over causal graphical models. Different graphs represent possible causal explanations, while prior knowledge shapes the space of hypotheses. Evidence is interpreted within that structured space, making the interaction between observations and existing beliefs central to the account of causal judgment.

Two case studies develop the approach, including quantitative models of human judgments and brief comparisons with traditional bottom-up inference models. These cases illustrate how theory-guided probabilistic reasoning can be used to explain human causal inference. The paper argues for this explanation rather than establishing that every causal judgment follows the same mechanism. Its main contribution is an explicit connection between intuitive theories, structured causal hypotheses, and learning from very little data.
summary.tldr: The paper models human causal judgments as Bayesian inference over causal graphs shaped by prior intuitive theories.

title: Theory-Based Causal Inference

abstract: We propose in this paper a probabilistic approach for adaptive inference of generalized nonlinear classiﬁcation that combines the computational advantage of a parametric solution with the ﬂexibility of sequential sam- pling techniques. We regard the parameters of the classiﬁer as latent states in a ﬁrst order Markov process and propose an algorithm which can be regarded as variational generalization of standard Kalman ﬁlter- ing. The variational Kalman ﬁlter is based on two novel lower bounds that enable us to use a non-degenerate distribution over the adaptation rate. An extensive empirical evaluation demonstrates that the proposed method is capable of infering competitive classiﬁers both in stationary and non-stationary environments. Although we focus on classiﬁcation, the algorithm is easily extended to other generalized nonlinear models.
originalAbstract: We propose in this paper a probabilistic approach for adaptive inference of generalized nonlinear classiﬁcation that combines the computational advantage of a parametric solution with the ﬂexibility of sequential sam- pling techniques. We regard the parameters of the classiﬁer as latent states in a ﬁrst order Markov process and propose an algorithm which can be regarded as variational generalization of standard Kalman ﬁlter- ing. The variational Kalman ﬁlter is based on two novel lower bounds that enable us to use a non-degenerate distribution over the adaptation rate. An extensive empirical evaluation demonstrates that the proposed method is capable of infering competitive classiﬁers both in stationary and non-stationary environments. Although we focus on classiﬁcation, the algorithm is easily extended to other generalized nonlinear models.

paragraphs: This paper treats classification as an inference problem that may need to adapt as observations arrive. Instead of viewing a classifier's parameters as permanently fixed, it models them as hidden states in a first-order Markov process. The current parameter state is therefore linked to the preceding state, providing a probabilistic description of how the classifier evolves.

The resulting algorithm is a variational extension of Kalman filtering for generalized nonlinear classification. It aims to combine the computational benefits of a parametric representation with flexibility associated with sequential sampling. Two new lower bounds make it possible to retain a non-degenerate distribution over the adaptation rate, representing uncertainty about adaptation instead of collapsing it to one fixed value.

The empirical evaluation reports competitive classifiers in both stationary environments and environments that change over time. This supports the method's use across those two settings without implying that adaptation always improves performance. Although classification is the focus, the authors also state that the algorithm extends easily to other generalized nonlinear models, making the inference construction broader than the particular task studied.
summary.tldr: A variational Kalman filter adapts nonlinear classifiers by treating their parameters and adaptation rate probabilistically.

title: Adaptive Classification by Variational Kalman Filtering

abstract: We describe a pattern acquisition algorithm that learns, in an unsuper- vised fashion, a streamlined representation of linguistic structures from a plain natural-language corpus. This paper addresses the issues of learn- ing structured knowledge from a large-scale natural language data set, and of generalization to unseen text. The implemented algorithm repre- sents sentences as paths on a graph whose vertices are words (or parts of words). Signiﬁcant patterns, determined by recursive context-sensitive statistical inference, form new vertices. Linguistic constructions are rep- resented by trees composed of signiﬁcant patterns and their associated equivalence classes. An input module allows the algorithm to be sub- jected to a standard test of English as a Second Language (ESL) proﬁ- ciency. The results are encouraging: the model attains a level of per- formance considered to be “intermediate” for 9th-grade students, de- spite having been trained on a corpus (CHILDES) containing transcribed speech of parents directed to small children.

This paper addresses the issues of learn- ing structured knowledge from a large-scale natural language data set, and of generalization to unseen text. Signiﬁcant patterns, determined by recursive context-sensitive statistical inference, form new vertices. Linguistic constructions are rep- resented by trees composed of signiﬁcant patterns and their associated equivalence classes. An input module allows the algorithm to be sub- jected to a standard test of English as a Second Language (ESL) proﬁ- ciency. The results are encouraging: the model attains a level of per- formance considered to be “intermediate” for 9th-grade students, de- spite having been trained on a corpus (CHILDES) containing transcribed speech of parents directed to small children.

paragraphs: The paper presents an unsupervised algorithm for learning linguistic structure from a plain natural-language corpus. It addresses both the acquisition of structured knowledge from substantial text collections and generalization to unseen text. The aim is a compact representation built from patterns discovered in the language data.

Sentences are represented as paths through a graph whose vertices initially correspond to words or word parts. Recursive statistical inference uses context to identify significant patterns, which become new vertices. Linguistic constructions are then represented as trees composed of these patterns and their associated equivalence classes. This allows discovered structure to become part of the representation used for further learning.

An input module lets the system take a standard English-as-a-Second-Language proficiency test. Its performance reaches a level described as intermediate for ninth-grade students, despite training on CHILDES transcripts of parents speaking to young children. This is an encouraging test result for generalization from that corpus. It describes performance on the proficiency assessment, rather than establishing equivalence to a student’s overall language abilities.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised graph-based language learner discovers contextual patterns and achieves an intermediate ninth-grade ESL test level after training on child-directed speech.

title: Unsupervised Context Sensitive Language Acquisition from a Large Corpus

abstract: We introduce a class of nonstationary covariance functions for Gaussian process (GP) regression. Nonstationary covariance functions allow the model to adapt to functions whose smoothness varies with the inputs. The class includes a nonstationary version of the Matérn stationary co- variance, in which the differentiability of the regression function is con- trolled by a parameter, freeing one from ﬁxing the differentiability in advance. In experiments, the nonstationary GP regression model per- forms well when the input space is two or three dimensions, outperform- ing a neural network model and Bayesian free-knot spline models, and competitive with a Bayesian neural network, but is outperformed in one dimension by a state-of-the-art Bayesian free-knot spline model. The model readily generalizes to non-Gaussian data. Use of computational methods for speeding GP ﬁtting may allow for implementation of the method on larger datasets.
originalAbstract: We introduce a class of nonstationary covariance functions for Gaussian process (GP) regression. Nonstationary covariance functions allow the model to adapt to functions whose smoothness varies with the inputs. The class includes a nonstationary version of the Matérn stationary co- variance, in which the differentiability of the regression function is con- trolled by a parameter, freeing one from ﬁxing the differentiability in advance. In experiments, the nonstationary GP regression model per- forms well when the input space is two or three dimensions, outperform- ing a neural network model and Bayesian free-knot spline models, and competitive with a Bayesian neural network, but is outperformed in one dimension by a state-of-the-art Bayesian free-knot spline model. The model readily generalizes to non-Gaussian data. Use of computational methods for speeding GP ﬁtting may allow for implementation of the method on larger datasets.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression uses a covariance function to express relationships between function values. This paper introduces covariance functions that can vary with location in the input space. Such nonstationary models can adapt when the function being learned is smoother in some regions than in others.

The proposed class includes a nonstationary form of the Matérn covariance. A parameter controls differentiability, allowing that property to be represented within the model rather than fixed in advance. This combines adaptation across inputs with control over how smoothly the regression function behaves. The authors also state that the model readily extends to non-Gaussian data.

Experiments show strong performance in two and three input dimensions: the model outperforms a neural network and Bayesian free-knot spline models while remaining competitive with a Bayesian neural network. In one dimension, a state-of-the-art Bayesian free-knot spline model performs better. The authors suggest that methods for accelerating GP fitting may enable larger datasets, so that scalability extension is presented as a possibility rather than a demonstrated result.
summary.tldr: Nonstationary Gaussian process covariances adapt to changing smoothness and show favorable, dimension-dependent regression results.

title: Nonstationary Covariance Functions for Gaussian Process Regression

abstract: This paper devises a novel kernel function for structured natural language data. In the ﬁeld of Natural Language Processing, feature extraction consists of the following two steps: (1) syntactically and semantically analyzing raw data, i.e., character strings, then representing the results as discrete structures, such as parse trees and dependency graphs with part-of-speech tags; (2) creating (possibly high-dimensional) numerical feature vectors from the discrete structures. The new kernels, called Hier- archical Directed Acyclic Graph (HDAG) kernels, directly accept DAGs whose nodes can contain DAGs. HDAG data structures are needed to fully reﬂect the syntactic and semantic structures that natural language data inherently have. In this paper, we deﬁne the kernel function and show how it permits efﬁcient calculation. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed kernels are superior to existing kernel functions, e.g., se- quence kernels, tree kernels, and bag-of-words kernels.

These structures may include parse trees, dependency graphs, and part-of-speech information. This paper develops a kernel that can work directly with a richer structured representation, preserving the syntactic and semantic organization that motivates those intermediate analyses.

The proposed Hierarchical Directed Acyclic Graph kernels accept directed acyclic graphs whose nodes can themselves contain further graphs. This nesting allows the representation to express structure at multiple levels. The authors define a kernel for these objects and show how to calculate it efficiently, making the structured representation usable for kernel-based learning.

Experiments report better performance than existing sequence, tree, and bag-of-words kernels. The result supports the usefulness of the richer representation in the experiments presented. The central contribution joins representational expressiveness with computation: the method can compare nested graph structures directly while providing an efficient calculation procedure for the resulting kernel.
summary.tldr: HDAG kernels efficiently compare nested graph representations of language and outperform several existing kernels in the reported experiments.

title: Kernels for Structured Natural Language Data

abstract: This paper explores the use of a Maximal Average Margin (MAM) optimality principle for the design of learning algorithms. It is shown that the application of this risk minimization principle results in a class of (computationally) simple learning machines similar to the classical Parzen window classifier. A direct relation with the Rademacher complexities is established, as such facilitating analysis and providing a notion of certainty of prediction. This analysis is related to Support Vector Machines by means of a margin transformation. The power of the MAM principle is illustrated further by application to ordinal regression tasks, resulting in an $O(n)$ algorithm able to process large datasets in reasonable time.

paragraphs: This paper studies a learning objective called Maximal Average Margin, or MAM. The objective uses the average margin as an optimality principle for designing learning algorithms. Applying it produces computationally simple learning machines resembling the classical Parzen window classifier, connecting a margin-based design principle with an established form of classification.

The authors establish a direct relationship between this principle and Rademacher complexities, mathematical quantities used to analyze learning methods. That relationship supports theoretical analysis and provides a notion of certainty for predictions. They also connect the analysis to support vector machines through a transformation of the margin, relating the proposed approach to another margin-based learning framework.

The paper further applies MAM to ordinal regression, where the prediction task concerns ordered outcomes. This produces an O(n) algorithm, giving linear computational scaling in n and allowing large datasets to be processed in reasonable time. The broader contribution is a design principle that yields simple algorithms while retaining connections to learning theory and prediction certainty.
summary.tldr: Maximizing average margin yields simple Parzen-like learning methods, theoretical measures of prediction certainty, and a linear-time ordinal regression algorithm.

title: A Risk Minimization Principle for a Class of Parzen Estimators

abstract: Many existing approaches to collaborative ﬁltering can neither handle very large datasets nor easily deal with users who have very few ratings. In this paper we present the Probabilistic Matrix Factorization (PMF) model which scales linearly with the number of observations and, more importantly, performs well on the large, sparse, and very imbalanced Netﬂix dataset. We further extend the PMF model to include an adaptive prior on the model parameters and show how the model capacity can be controlled automatically. Finally, we introduce a con- strained version of the PMF model that is based on the assumption that users who have rated similar sets of movies are likely to have similar preferences. The result- ing model is able to generalize considerably better for users with very few ratings. When the predictions of multiple PMF models are linearly combined with the predictions of Restricted Boltzmann Machines models, we achieve an error rate of 0.8861, that is nearly 7% better than the score of Netﬂix’s own system.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering must often learn from a large collection of ratings in which many entries are missing and some users contribute very little. This paper presents Probabilistic Matrix Factorization, or PMF, with computational scaling linear in the number of observed ratings. It reports strong performance on the large, sparse, and highly imbalanced Netflix dataset.

The authors extend PMF with an adaptive prior over model parameters, allowing model capacity to be controlled automatically. A constrained version adds the assumption that users who rated similar sets of movies are likely to share preferences. This uses the pattern of which movies were rated as information about users, and considerably improves generalization for users with very few ratings.

The strongest numerical result belongs to a combination of models. Linearly combining predictions from multiple PMF models and Restricted Boltzmann Machine models produces an error rate of 0.8861, nearly seven percent better than Netflix’s own system. That result supports the combined predictor, while the separate PMF contributions address computational scale, automatic capacity control, and sparse user histories.
summary.tldr: PMF scales with observed ratings and improves sparse-user predictions, while an ensemble combining PMF and RBMs beats Netflix’s reported system score.

title: Probabilistic Matrix Factorization

abstract: The standard assumption of identically distributed training and test data can be violated when an adversary can exercise some control over the generation of the test data. In a prediction game, a learner produces a predictive model while an adversary may alter the distribution of input data. We study single-shot prediction games in which the cost functions of learner and adversary are not necessarily antagonistic. We identify conditions under which the prediction game has a unique Nash equilibrium, and derive algorithms that will find the equilibrial prediction models. In a case study, we explore properties of Nash-equilibrial prediction models for email spam filtering empirically.

In a prediction game, a learner produces a predictive model while an adversary may alter the distribution of input data. We study single-shot prediction games in which the cost functions of learner and adversary are not necessarily antagonistic. We identify conditions under which the prediction game has a unique Nash equilibrium, and derive algorithms that will find the equilibrial prediction models. In a case study, we explore properties of Nash-equilibrial prediction models for email spam filtering empirically.

paragraphs: Prediction often assumes that training and test examples come from the same distribution. This paper studies a setting where an adversary can influence the test inputs, breaking that assumption. The learner's model and the adversary's changes are treated as decisions in a prediction game, so the data distribution becomes part of a strategic interaction.

The authors consider single-shot games whose participants need not have exactly opposing costs. This allows the learner's objective and the adversary's objective to differ without requiring every gain for one to be an equal loss for the other. They identify conditions that ensure a unique Nash equilibrium and derive algorithms for finding the corresponding prediction models.

An equilibrium describes mutually compatible choices: neither participant improves its own objective by changing its decision alone while the other stays fixed. This makes equilibrium analysis relevant to prediction under strategically altered inputs. An empirical email spam-filtering case study explores properties of the resulting models, complementing the conditional theoretical results on existence of a unique equilibrium and its computation.
summary.tldr: The paper gives conditions and algorithms for unique Nash-equilibrium prediction models when an adversary can alter test-input distributions.

title: Nash Equilibria of Static Prediction Games

abstract: The commute distance between two vertices in a graph is the expected time it takes a random walk to travel from the first to the second vertex and back. We study the behavior of the commute distance as the size of the underlying graph increases. We prove that the commute distance converges to an expression that does not take into account the structure of the graph at all and that is completely meaningless as a distance function on the graph. Consequently, the use of the raw commute distance for machine learning purposes is strongly discouraged for large graphs and in high dimensions. As an alternative we introduce the amplified commute distance that corrects for the undesired large sample effects.

paragraphs: Commute distance measures the expected time for a random walk to travel between two graph vertices and return. Because the walk follows the graph's connections, this quantity appears naturally suited to describing relationships between vertices. The paper investigates whether that interpretation remains useful as the graph becomes larger.

The authors prove that, in their large-sample analysis, commute distance approaches an expression that no longer captures graph structure. This is a problem for using it as a meaningful distance: a quantity derived from movement through the graph can lose the structural information that motivated its use. The finding concerns the limiting behavior of the measure, rather than merely a computational difficulty in calculating it.

On this basis, the paper strongly discourages using raw commute distance for machine learning on large graphs and in high dimensions. It introduces amplified commute distance to correct the unwanted large-sample effects. The contribution combines a warning grounded in theoretical analysis with an alternative designed to address the identified failure.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that raw commute distance loses structural meaning in its large-sample limit and proposes an amplified correction.

title: Getting lost in space: Large sample analysis of the resistance distance

abstract: We consider the problem of discovering links of an evolving undirected graph given a series of past snapshots of that graph. The graph is observed through the time sequence of its adjacency matrix and only the presence of edges is observed. The absence of an edge on a certain snapshot cannot be distinguished from a missing entry in the adjacency matrix. Additional information can be provided by examining the dynamics of the graph through a set of topological features, such as the degrees of the vertices. We develop a novel methodology by building on both static matrix completion methods and the estimation of the future state of relevant graph features. Our procedure relies on the formulation of an optimization problem which can be approximately solved by a fast alternating linearized algorithm whose properties are examined. We show experiments with both simulated and real data which reveal the interest of our methodology.

paragraphs: The paper investigates link discovery in an evolving undirected graph observed through past snapshots. The observations reveal edges that are present, but an unrecorded edge is ambiguous: it might truly be absent or simply missing from the data. Consequently, each snapshot gives incomplete information about the graph's actual connectivity.

The authors combine static matrix completion with predictions of how relevant graph features will evolve. Features such as vertex degrees summarize aspects of network topology, and their dynamics provide information beyond the observed entries of the adjacency matrices. The method brings these two sources of information together in an optimization problem for discovering links.

A fast alternating linearized algorithm approximately solves that problem, and the paper examines its properties. Experiments on simulated and real data illustrate the usefulness of the methodology. The central contribution is to make graph evolution informative through tracked structural features, supplementing completion methods that would otherwise rely on static connectivity information. This directly addresses the ambiguity created when missing observations cannot be distinguished from absent edges.
summary.tldr: The method combines matrix completion with forecasts of graph features to discover links from incomplete snapshots of an evolving network.

title: Link Discovery using Graph Feature Tracking

abstract: We propose a discriminative model for recognizing group activities. Our model jointly captures the group activity, the individual person actions, and the interactions among them. Two new types of contextual information, group-person interaction and person-person interaction, are explored in a latent variable framework. Different from most of the previous latent structured models which assume a predefined structure for the hidden layer, e.g. a tree structure, we treat the structure of the hidden layer as a latent variable and implicitly infer it during learning and inference. Our experimental results demonstrate that by inferring this contextual information together with adaptive structures, the proposed model can significantly improve activity recognition performance.

Different from most of the previous latent structured models which assume a predefined structure for the hidden layer, e.g. a tree structure, we treat the structure of the hidden layer as a latent variable and implicitly infer it during learning and inference. Our experimental results demonstrate that by inferring this contextual information together with adaptive structures, the proposed model can significantly improve activity recognition performance.

paragraphs: Recognizing a group activity involves understanding both what individuals are doing and how their actions relate to the group. This paper proposes a discriminative model that handles those elements jointly. Its representation connects the overall activity, each person's action, and the interactions that provide context for interpreting them.

The model includes two kinds of context: interactions between a group and a person, and interactions between people. It represents these within a latent-variable framework, where relevant hidden information is inferred. The structure connecting the hidden variables is itself treated as unknown. Rather than requiring a predefined arrangement such as a tree, the method implicitly infers that arrangement during learning and prediction.

The experiments show that jointly inferring contextual information and adapting the hidden structure can significantly improve activity recognition. The result supports the usefulness of allowing the model to determine how contextual relationships should be organized. The contribution therefore concerns both the information used for recognition and the flexibility of the structure through which that information influences predictions.
summary.tldr: A group-activity recognition model jointly infers individual actions, contextual interactions, and their hidden structure, improving recognition in experiments.

title: Beyond Actions: Discriminative Models for Contextual Group Activities

abstract: This manuscript considers the convergence rate of boosting under a large class of losses, including the exponential and logistic losses, where the best previous rate of convergence was O(exp(1/ε²)). First, it is established that the setting of weak learnability aids the entire class, granting a rate O(ln(1/ε)). Next, the (disjoint) conditions under which the infimal empirical risk is attainable are characterized in terms of the sample and weak learning class, and a new proof is given for the known rate O(ln(1/ε)). Finally, it is established that any instance can be decomposed into two smaller instances resembling the two preceding special cases, yielding a rate O(1/ε), with a matching lower bound for the logistic loss. The principal technical hurdle throughout this work is the potential unattainability of the infimal empirical risk; the technique for overcoming this barrier may be of general interest.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes how quickly boosting approaches the lowest possible empirical risk for a broad class of losses, including exponential and logistic losses. A central difficulty is that the risk's infimum may not be attained by any available solution. The analysis explicitly addresses this obstacle rather than assuming a minimizer exists.

Under weak learnability, the authors establish a convergence rate of order ln(1/ε) for the whole loss class. They also characterize a separate set of conditions, based on the sample and weak learning class, under which the infimum is attainable. For that setting, they provide a new proof of the known logarithmic rate.

The authors then show that any instance can be decomposed into two smaller instances resembling those special cases. This yields a general rate of order 1/ε, improving the previously available order exp(1/ε²) rate. A matching lower bound for logistic loss shows that the general rate cannot be improved in order for that loss. The work therefore explains both favorable special cases and a sharper general convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: A decomposition of boosting problems yields a general O(1/ε) convergence rate, with faster special cases and a matching logistic-loss lower bound.

title: The Fast Convergence of Boosting

abstract: We develop collaborative topic Poisson factorization (CTPF), a generative model of articles and reader preferences. CTPF can be used to build recommender systems by learning from reader histories and content to recommend personalized articles of interest. In detail, CTPF models both reader behavior and article texts with Poisson distributions, connecting the latent topics that represent the texts with the latent preferences that represent the readers. This provides better recommendations than competing methods and gives an interpretable latent space for understanding patterns of readership. Further, we exploit stochastic variational inference to model massive real-world datasets. For example, we can fit CPTF to the full arXiv usage dataset, which contains over 43 million ratings and 42 million word counts, within a day. We demonstrate empirically that our model outperforms several baselines, including the previous state-of-the-art approach.

This paper develops collaborative topic Poisson factorization, or CTPF, to connect those sources in a generative model. It learns representations of articles and reader preferences together, using them to recommend articles suited to individual readers.

CTPF uses Poisson distributions to model reader behavior and article text. Latent topics describing the text are connected to latent preferences describing readers. This shared representation supports personalized prediction and offers an interpretable view of readership patterns. The model's internal space therefore serves both recommendation and analysis of how reading preferences relate to content.

They report fitting the full arXiv usage dataset, with more than 43 million ratings and 42 million word counts, within a day. Their empirical comparisons show better recommendations than several baselines, including the previous state-of-the-art approach, alongside evidence that the model can operate at substantial scale.
summary.tldr: CTPF connects article topics with reader preferences in a scalable Poisson model that improves recommendations in the reported comparisons.

title: Content-based recommendations with Poisson factorization

abstract: The dynamics of simple decisions are well understood and modeled as a class of random walk models (e.g. Laming, 1968; Ratcliff, 1978; Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993; Usher and McClelland, 2001; Bogacz et al., 2006). However, most real-life decisions include a rich and dynamically-changing influence of additional information we call context. In this work, we describe a computational theory of decision making under dynamically shifting context. We show how the model generalizes the dominant existing model of fixed-context decision making (Ratcliff, 1978) and can be built up from a weighted combination of fixed-context decisions evolving simultaneously. We also show how the model generalizes re- cent work on the control of attention in the Flanker task (Yu et al., 2009). Finally, we show how the model recovers qualitative data patterns in another task of longstanding psychological interest, the AX Continuous Performance Test (Servan-Schreiber et al., 1996), using the same model parameters.

paragraphs: The paper studies decisions made while relevant background information changes. Existing random-walk models describe simple decisions well, but everyday choices also depend on context that can shift during deliberation. The authors develop a computational theory that brings these changing influences into the decision process, extending the treatment beyond situations with a fixed context.

The central construction combines multiple fixed-context decision processes that evolve simultaneously, assigning weights to their contributions. This gives the new theory a direct connection to established models: it generalizes a dominant fixed-context account rather than introducing an unrelated mechanism. It also extends an existing model of attention control in the Flanker task.

The authors further show that the model reproduces qualitative patterns in the AX Continuous Performance Test using the same parameters. This matters because the proposed framework connects behavior across different tasks without requiring a new parameter setting for that demonstration. The stated result concerns the qualitative patterns it recovers, supporting a shared computational account of decisions influenced by changing context.
summary.tldr: A model built from simultaneous, weighted decision processes explains how changing context can shape choices across psychological tasks.

title: A Theory of Decision Making Under Dynamic Context

abstract: Spectral embedding based on the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) is a widely used preprocessing step in many learning tasks, typically leading to dimensionality reduction by projecting onto a number of dominant singular vectors and rescaling the coordinate axes (by a predefined function of the singular value). However, the number of such vectors required to capture problem structure grows with problem size, and even partial SVD computation becomes a bottleneck. In this paper, we propose a low-complexity it compressive spectral embedding algorithm, which employs random projections and finite order polynomial expansions to compute approximations to SVD-based embedding. For an m times n matrix with T non-zeros, its time complexity is O((T+m+n)log(m+n)), and the embedding dimension is O(log(m+n)), both of which are independent of the number of singular vectors whose effect we wish to capture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to circumvent this dependence on the number of singular vectors for general SVD-based embeddings. The key to sidestepping the SVD is the observation that, for downstream inference tasks such as clustering and classification, we are only interested in using the resulting embedding to evaluate pairwise similarity metrics derived from the euclidean norm, rather than capturing the effect of the underlying matrix on arbitrary vectors as a partial SVD tries to do. Our numerical results on network datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, and motivate further exploration of its application to large-scale inference tasks.

paragraphs: Spectral embeddings often reduce dimensionality by projecting data onto dominant singular vectors and rescaling the resulting coordinates. As datasets grow, capturing their structure may require more vectors, making even a partial singular value decomposition expensive. This paper proposes an approximate embedding that avoids a computational dependence on how many singular vectors contribute.

The method combines random projections with finite-order polynomial expansions. Its central observation is that downstream tasks such as clustering and classification often need pairwise similarities based on Euclidean distance. Preserving those quantities is a narrower objective than representing how the original matrix acts on arbitrary vectors, which is what a partial decomposition attempts to capture.

For an m-by-n matrix with T nonzero entries, the stated running time is O((T+m+n)log(m+n)), with embedding dimension O(log(m+n)). Both are independent of the number of singular vectors whose effects are represented. Numerical results on network datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness and motivate further large-scale applications. The contribution is an efficient approximation directed at the similarities downstream inference actually uses.
summary.tldr: Random projections and polynomial approximations produce compact spectral embeddings without explicitly computing the contributing singular vectors.

title: Compressive spectral embedding: sidestepping the SVD

abstract: Kernel-based quadrature rules are becoming important in machine learning and statistics, as they achieve super-$¥sqrt{n}$ convergence rates in numerical integration, and thus provide alternatives to Monte Carlo integration in challenging settings where integrands are expensive to evaluate or where integrands are high dimensional. These rules are based on the assumption that the integrand has a certain degree of smoothness, which is expressed as that the integrand belongs to a certain reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). However, this assumption can be violated in practice (e.g., when the integrand is a black box function), and no general theory has been established for the convergence of kernel quadratures in such misspecified settings. Our contribution is in proving that kernel quadratures can be consistent even when the integrand does not belong to the assumed RKHS, i.e., when the integrand is less smooth than assumed. Specifically, we derive convergence rates that depend on the (unknown) lesser smoothness of the integrand, where the degree of smoothness is expressed via powers of RKHSs or via Sobolev spaces.

Kernel-based quadrature can converge faster than the usual Monte Carlo rate, but its analysis typically assumes a particular degree of smoothness. That assumption is represented by membership in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS.

The paper asks what happens when the function is less smooth than the chosen kernel assumes. This mismatch is plausible for a black-box function whose regularity is unknown. The authors prove that kernel quadrature can still be consistent even when the function lies outside the assumed RKHS, so misspecification need not prevent convergence.

Their convergence rates depend on the function's actual, potentially unknown, lower smoothness. They express that smoothness using powers of RKHSs or Sobolev spaces. The result extends the theoretical basis for kernel integration beyond correctly specified smoothness assumptions: useful convergence remains possible, while the rate reflects the rougher function being integrated.
summary.tldr: Kernel quadrature can remain consistent when functions are less smooth than assumed, with convergence rates reflecting their actual smoothness.

title: Convergence guarantees for kernel-based quadrature rules in misspecified settings

abstract: Sensing is the process of deriving signals from the environment that allows artificial systems to interact with the physical world. The Shannon theorem specifies the maximum rate at which information can be acquired. However, this upper bound is hard to achieve in many man-made systems. The biological visual systems, on the other hand, have highly efficient signal representation and processing mechanisms that allow precise sensing. In this work, we argue that redundancy is one of the critical characteristics for such superior performance. We show architectural advantages by utilizing redundant sensing, including correction of mismatch error and significant precision enhancement. For a proof-of-concept demonstration, we have designed a heuristic-based analog-to-digital converter - a zero-dimensional quantizer. Through Monte Carlo simulation with the error probabilistic distribution as a priori, the performance approaching the Shannon limit is feasible. In actual measurements without knowing the error distribution, we observe at least 2-bit extra precision. The results may also help explain biological processes including the dominance of binocular vision, the functional roles of the fixational eye movements, and the structural mechanisms allowing hyperacuity.

abstract: We study an online decision making problem where on each round a learner chooses a list of items based on some side information, receives a scalar feedback value for each individual item, and a reward that is linearly related to this feedback. These problems, known as contextual semibandits, arise in crowdsourcing, recommendation, and many other domains. This paper reduces contextual semibandits to supervised learning, allowing us to leverage powerful supervised learning methods in this partial-feedback setting. Our first reduction applies when the mapping from feedback to reward is known and leads to a computationally efficient algorithm with near-optimal regret. We show that this algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on real-world learning-to-rank datasets, demonstrating the advantage of oracle-based algorithms. Our second reduction applies to the previously unstudied setting when the linear mapping from feedback to reward is unknown. Our regret guarantees are superior to prior techniques that ignore the feedback.

paragraphs: A contextual semibandit chooses a list of items using side information and then receives feedback for each selected item. Its overall reward is a linear combination of that feedback. This creates a learning problem with more information than a single overall reward, while still providing only partial feedback about the available choices. Recommendation and crowdsourcing are motivating applications.

The paper reduces this problem to supervised learning, allowing supervised learning methods to serve as computational building blocks for sequential decisions. Its first reduction assumes that the linear relationship between item feedback and reward is known. Under that setup, the resulting algorithm is computationally efficient and has near-optimal regret.

On real-world learning-to-rank datasets, the first algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches used in the experiments. A second reduction addresses the case where the linear feedback-to-reward relationship is unknown. Its regret guarantees improve on prior techniques that ignore item feedback, demonstrating the theoretical value of using the additional observations even when their relationship to reward must be learned.
summary.tldr: Reductions to supervised learning enable efficient contextual semibandit algorithms that exploit item-level feedback with known or unknown reward mappings.

title: Contextual semibandits via supervised learning oracles

abstract: Recent work on deriving $O(\log T)$ anytime regret bounds for stochastic dueling bandit problems has considered mostly Condorcet winners, which do not always exist, and more recently, winners defined by the Copeland set, which do always exist. In this work, we consider a broad notion of winners defined by tournament solutions in social choice theory, which include the Copeland set as a special case but also include several other notions of winners such as the top cycle, uncovered set, and Banks set, and which, like the Copeland set, always exist. We develop a family of UCB-style dueling bandit algorithms for such general tournament solutions, and show $O(\log T)$ anytime regret bounds for them. Experiments confirm the ability of our algorithms to achieve low regret relative to the target winning set of interest.

A central issue is deciding what counts as a winner when preferences do not identify one alternative that defeats every other. Such an alternative, called a Condorcet winner, need not exist, making algorithms built around its existence restrictive.

This paper considers winner sets defined by tournament solutions from social choice theory. These include the Copeland set as well as the top cycle, uncovered set, and Banks set. The stated solutions always provide a winning set, allowing learning objectives to remain meaningful even when no Condorcet winner exists. Different solutions provide different targets for the comparison process.

The authors develop a family of algorithms based on upper confidence bounds for these broader objectives. They prove anytime regret bounds that grow logarithmically with the number of rounds. Experiments also show low regret relative to the particular winning set being targeted. The contribution is a broader framework for efficient comparison-based learning: the algorithm can pursue several well-defined notions of success instead of depending on one potentially nonexistent winner.
summary.tldr: The paper develops dueling-bandit algorithms with logarithmic anytime regret for several winner definitions that always yield a winning set.

title: Dueling Bandits: Beyond Condorcet Winners to General Tournament Solutions

abstract: We study consistency properties of machine learning methods based on minimizing convex surrogates. We extend the recent framework of Osokin et al. (2017) for the quantitative analysis of consistency properties to the case of inconsistent surrogates. Our key technical contribution consists in a new lower bound on the calibration function for the quadratic surrogate, which is non-trivial (not always zero) for inconsistent cases. The new bound allows to quantify the level of inconsistency of the setting and shows how learning with inconsistent surrogates can have guarantees on sample complexity and optimization difficulty. We apply our theory to two concrete cases: multi-class classification with the tree-structured loss and ranking with the mean average precision loss. The results show the approximation-computation trade-offs caused by inconsistent surrogates and their potential benefits.

paragraphs: Machine learning often optimizes a convenient surrogate loss in place of the task's original loss. A convex surrogate can simplify optimization, but an inconsistent surrogate does not fully align its optimum with the desired task objective. This paper asks how useful learning guarantees can still be established when that mismatch is present.

The authors extend a quantitative consistency framework to inconsistent surrogates. Their main technical result is a lower bound on the calibration function for the quadratic surrogate that can remain informative in inconsistent cases, instead of always collapsing to zero. The bound quantifies the degree of inconsistency and supports guarantees concerning sample complexity and optimization difficulty.

The theory is applied to multiclass classification with a tree-structured loss and ranking with mean average precision loss. These examples expose a tradeoff between approximation quality and computational considerations. The findings show why inconsistency alone need not make a surrogate useless: its mismatch can be measured, and useful guarantees can remain available. The potential benefits depend on the resulting approximation-computation tradeoff.
summary.tldr: A new calibration bound quantifies how inconsistent quadratic surrogates can still offer learning guarantees and useful approximation-computation tradeoffs.

title: Quantifying Learning Guarantees for Convex but Inconsistent Surrogates

abstract: Groups of humans are often able to find ways to cooperate with one another in complex, temporally extended social dilemmas. Models based on behavioral economics are only able to explain this phenomenon for unrealistic stateless matrix games. Recently, multi-agent reinforcement learning has been applied to generalize social dilemma problems to temporally and spatially extended Markov games. However, this has not yet generated an agent that learns to cooperate in social dilemmas as humans do. A key insight is that many, but not all, human individuals have inequity averse social preferences. This promotes a particular resolution of the matrix game social dilemma wherein inequity-averse individuals are personally pro-social and punish defectors. Here we extend this idea to Markov games and show that it promotes cooperation in several types of sequential social dilemma, via a profitable interaction with policy learnability. In particular, we find that inequity aversion improves temporal credit assignment for the important class of intertemporal social dilemmas. These results help explain how large-scale cooperation may emerge and persist.

Such settings are more complex than a single matrix game because actions influence later situations and rewards. The authors focus on inequity aversion: a preference against unequal outcomes that is present in many, though not all, people.

The work extends this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning in Markov games. In simpler social-dilemma models, inequity-averse individuals can support cooperation through prosocial behavior and punishment of defectors. Here, the authors investigate how the same kind of preference interacts with the process by which agents learn policies in sequential environments.

They find that inequity aversion promotes cooperation in several types of sequential social dilemma through its interaction with policy learnability. These findings offer a possible explanation for how cooperation can emerge and persist at larger scales, grounded in both social preferences and learning dynamics.
summary.tldr: Inequity-averse preferences promote cooperation in several sequential social dilemmas, partly by improving temporal credit assignment.

title: Inequity aversion improves cooperation in intertemporal social dilemmas

abstract: In this work, we consider the distributed optimization of non-smooth convex functions using a network of computing units. We investigate this problem under two regularity assumptions: (1) the Lipschitz continuity of the global objective function, and (2) the Lipschitz continuity of local individual functions. Under the local regularity assumption, we provide the first optimal first-order decentralized algorithm called multi-step primal-dual (MSPD) and its corresponding optimal convergence rate. A notable aspect of this result is that, for non-smooth functions, while the dominant term of the error is in $O(1/\sqrt{t})$, the structure of the communication network only impacts a second-order term in $O(1/t)$, where $t$ is time. In other words, the error due to limits in communication resources decreases at a fast rate even in the case of non-strongly-convex objective functions. Under the global regularity assumption, we provide a simple yet efficient algorithm called distributed randomized smoothing (DRS) based on a local smoothing of the objective function, and show that DRS is within a $d^{1/4}$ multiplicative factor of the optimal convergence rate, where $d$ is the underlying dimension.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a network of computing units can jointly minimize a nonsmooth convex objective. It separates two assumptions: Lipschitz continuity of the overall objective, and Lipschitz continuity of each local function. These conditions control how quickly function values can change, but they provide different information to a distributed algorithm.

Under the local assumption, the authors introduce multi-step primal-dual, an optimal first-order decentralized algorithm. Its error has a dominant term of order 1/sqrt(t), while communication-network structure affects a secondary term of order 1/t. Consequently, the contribution associated with limited communication decays faster than the dominant error term, even without strong convexity.

Under the global assumption, the paper proposes distributed randomized smoothing, which locally smooths the objective to support optimization. Its convergence rate is within a multiplicative factor of d^(1/4) of optimal, where d is the problem dimension. The two results clarify how available regularity assumptions shape achievable performance: one supports an optimal decentralized method, while the other yields a simple method with an explicit dimension-dependent gap.
summary.tldr: The paper gives an optimal decentralized algorithm under local Lipschitz assumptions and a dimension-qualified near-optimal method under global regularity.

title: Optimal Algorithms for Non-Smooth Distributed Optimization in Networks

abstract: Persistence diagrams (PDs) are now routinely used to summarize the underlying topology of complex data. Despite several appealing properties, incorporating PDs in learning pipelines can be challenging because their natural geometry is not Hilbertian. Indeed, this was recently exemplified in a string of papers which show that the simple task of averaging a few PDs can be computationally prohibitive. We propose in this article a tractable framework to carry out standard tasks on PDs at scale, notably evaluating distances, estimating barycenters and performing clustering. This framework builds upon a reformulation of PD metrics as optimal transport (OT) problems. Doing so, we can exploit recent computational advances: the OT problem on a planar grid, when regularized with entropy, is convex can be solved in linear time using the Sinkhorn algorithm and convolutions. This results in scalable computations that can stream on GPUs. We demonstrate the efficiency of our approach by carrying out clustering with diagrams metrics on several thousands of PDs, a scale never seen before in the literature.
