In particular, computing an average diagram can be costly because these objects do not have the geometry of an ordinary inner-product space. This paper develops a tractable framework for distances, barycenters, and clustering directly with persistence diagrams.

The key step is to express diagram metrics as optimal transport problems. This opens access to computational methods developed for transport. On a planar grid, adding entropy regularization yields a convex problem that can be solved in linear time using the Sinkhorn algorithm and convolutions. The resulting computations can also stream on GPUs, supporting larger collections of diagrams.

The contribution matters because it makes basic statistical operations more practical while retaining a connection to diagram geometry. Its computational route specifically relies on the grid-based, entropy-regularized transport formulation described in the abstract.
summary.tldr: An entropy-regularized optimal transport framework scales persistence-diagram distances, averages, and clustering to thousands of diagrams.

title: Large Scale computation of Means and Clusters for Persistence Diagrams using Optimal Transport

abstract:
Population risk is always of primary interest in machine learning; however, learning algorithms only have access to the empirical risk. Even for applications with nonconvex non-smooth losses (such as modern deep networks), the population risk is generally significantly more well behaved from an optimization point of view than the empirical risk. In particular, sampling can create many spurious local minima. We consider a general framework which aims to optimize a smooth nonconvex function $F$ (population risk) given only access to an approximation $f$ (empirical risk) that is pointwise close to $F$ (i.e., $
orm{F-f}_{\infty} \le 
u$). Our objective is to find the $\epsilon$-approximate local minima of the underlying function $F$ while avoiding the shallow local minima---arising because of the tolerance $
u$---which exist only in $f$. We propose a simple algorithm based on stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a smoothed version of $f$ that is guaranteed to achieve our goal as long as $
u \le O(\epsilon^{1.5}/d)$. We also provide an almost matching lower bound showing that our algorithm achieves optimal error tolerance $
u$ among all algorithms making a polynomial number of queries of $f$. As a concrete example, we show that our results can be directly used to give sample complexities for learning a ReLU unit.

Sampling can introduce shallow local minima that belong only to the empirical objective. This paper asks how an algorithm can avoid those misleading minima and find approximate local minima of the underlying population objective.

The analysis assumes a smooth, nonconvex population function F and access only to an approximation f whose error is uniformly at most ν. The proposed algorithm runs stochastic gradient descent on a smoothed version of f. It is guaranteed to find an ε-approximate local minimum of F when ν is at most O(ε^1.5/d), linking the allowable approximation error to accuracy and dimension.

summary.tldr: SGD on a smoothed empirical objective can find population-risk local minima under an essentially optimal uniform approximation-error condition.

title: On the Local Minima of the Empirical Risk

abstract: Despite the recent progress in hyperparameter optimization (HPO), available benchmarks that resemble real-world scenarios consist of a few and very large problem instances that are expensive to solve. This blocks researchers and practitioners no only from systematically running large-scale comparisons that are needed to draw statistically significant results but also from reproducing experiments that were conducted before. This work proposes a method to alleviate these issues by means of a meta-surrogate model for HPO tasks trained on off-line generated data. The model combines a probabilistic encoder with a multi-task model such that it can generate inexpensive and realistic tasks of the class of problems of interest. We demonstrate that benchmarking HPO methods on samples of the generative model allows us to draw more coherent and statistically significant conclusions that can be reached orders of magnitude faster than using the original tasks. We provide evidence of our findings for various HPO methods on a wide class of problems.

Realistic benchmark tasks can be so expensive that researchers can afford only a few instances or limited repetition. This paper addresses the resulting difficulty of drawing statistically meaningful comparisons and reproducing previous experiments.

The authors train a meta-surrogate model using data generated offline. It combines a probabilistic encoder with a multi-task model to generate inexpensive tasks resembling the problem class of interest. Instead of repeatedly solving only the original costly tasks, researchers can benchmark optimization methods on samples from this learned task generator.

The paper demonstrates that these generated benchmarks support more coherent and statistically significant conclusions, reached orders of magnitude faster than with the original tasks. Evidence covers multiple hyperparameter optimization methods and a broad class of problems. The practical contribution is a way to expand the scale of comparative evaluation while retaining a learned connection to the kinds of optimization tasks researchers actually want to study.
summary.tldr: A learned task generator enables faster, more statistically informative benchmarking of hyperparameter optimization methods.

title: Meta-Surrogate Benchmarking for Hyperparameter Optimization

abstract: We show that Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) learn representations that preserve the topology of the input space and prove that this implies the existence of functions Neural ODEs cannot represent. To address these limitations, we introduce Augmented Neural ODEs which, in addition to being more expressive models, are empirically more stable, generalize better and have a lower computational cost than Neural ODEs.

To address these limitations, we introduce Augmented Neural ODEs which, in addition to being more expressive models, are empirically more stable, generalize better and have a lower computational cost than Neural ODEs.

paragraphs: This paper examines a representational restriction of Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, or Neural ODEs. The authors show that the representations these models learn preserve the topology of the input space. Topology concerns structural relationships in a space, so preserving it places constraints on the transformations a model can express.

The authors prove that this restriction means some functions cannot be represented by Neural ODEs. This is an expressiveness result: the issue concerns which functions belong to the model’s repertoire, beyond how successfully a particular training procedure fits data. The paper introduces Augmented Neural ODEs to address these representational limitations and establishes that they are more expressive.

The reported experiments also favor the augmented models on stability, generalization, and computational cost relative to Neural ODEs. Those practical advantages are empirical findings, whereas the original representational restriction is proved. Together, the results connect a mathematical constraint on a model family with an architectural response that also performs better in the authors’ empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: Augmented Neural ODEs address proven expressiveness limits of Neural ODEs and empirically improve stability, generalization, and computational cost.

title: Augmented Neural ODEs

abstract: The ability to combine known skills to create new ones may be crucial in the solution of complex reinforcement learning problems that unfold over extended periods. We argue that a robust way of combining skills is to define and manipulate them in the space of pseudo-rewards (or "cumulants"). Based on this premise, we propose a framework for combining skills using the formalism of options. We show that every deterministic option can be unambiguously represented as a cumulant defined in an extended domain. Building on this insight and on previous results on transfer learning, we show how to approximate options whose cumulants are linear combinations of the cumulants of known options. This means that, once we have learned options associated with a set of cumulants, we can instantaneously synthesise options induced by any linear combination of them, without any learning involved. We describe how this framework provides a hierarchical interface to the environment whose abstract actions correspond to combinations of basic skills. We demonstrate the practical benefits of our approach in a resource management problem and a navigation task involving a quadrupedal simulated robot.

This paper proposes composing skills through their pseudo-rewards, called cumulants. It uses the formalism of options to connect these descriptions of what a skill pursues with the behavior that carries it out.

This separates learning the available skills from choosing how to combine their objectives for subsequent behavior. Demonstrations in resource management and simulated quadrupedal navigation show practical benefits. The synthesis guarantee concerns approximating the options induced by linear cumulant combinations, preserving the distinction between composing objectives and exactly recovering every desired behavior.
summary.tldr: The Option Keyboard combines learned skills through linear combinations of their pseudo-rewards, synthesizing approximate new options without further learning.

title: The Option Keyboard: Combining Skills in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The landscape of empirical risk has been widely studied in a series of machine learning problems, including low-rank matrix factorization, matrix sensing, matrix completion, and phase retrieval. In this work, we focus on the situation where the corresponding population risk is a degenerate non-convex loss function, namely, the Hessian of the population risk can have zero eigenvalues. Instead of analyzing the non-convex empirical risk directly, we first study the landscape of the corresponding population risk, which is usually easier to characterize, and then build a connection between the landscape of the empirical risk and its population risk. In particular, we establish a correspondence between the critical points of the empirical risk and its population risk without the strongly Morse assumption, which is required in existing literature but not satisfied in degenerate scenarios. We also apply the theory to matrix sensing and phase retrieval to demonstrate how to infer the landscape of empirical risk from that of the corresponding population risk.
originalAbstract: The landscape of empirical risk has been widely studied in a series of machine learning problems, including low-rank matrix factorization, matrix sensing, matrix completion, and phase retrieval. In this work, we focus on the situation where the corresponding population risk is a degenerate non-convex loss function, namely, the Hessian of the population risk can have zero eigenvalues. Instead of analyzing the non-convex empirical risk directly, we first study the landscape of the corresponding population risk, which is usually easier to characterize, and then build a connection between the landscape of the empirical risk and its population risk. In particular, we establish a correspondence between the critical points of the empirical risk and its population risk without the strongly Morse assumption, which is required in existing literature but not satisfied in degenerate scenarios. We also apply the theory to matrix sensing and phase retrieval to demonstrate how to infer the landscape of empirical risk from that of the corresponding population risk.

paragraphs: An empirical risk is the loss computed from observed data, while population risk describes the corresponding average over the underlying distribution. The population landscape can be easier to characterize. This paper asks how to use that simpler landscape to understand a nonconvex empirical loss when the population loss is degenerate, meaning its Hessian can have zero eigenvalues.

The authors first analyze the population risk and then establish a connection to the empirical risk. Their central result gives a correspondence between critical points of the two landscapes without requiring the strongly Morse assumption used in earlier work. Removing that requirement matters because it is not satisfied in the degenerate situations considered here.

The theory is applied to matrix sensing and phase retrieval to demonstrate how population-level analysis can inform the landscape of a loss built from data. The contribution is a way to transfer structural information between these two objectives when flat curvature directions obstruct the earlier assumptions. It supports landscape analysis without requiring a direct characterization of the empirical objective from the outset.
summary.tldr: The paper connects empirical and population critical points in degenerate nonconvex problems without the strongly Morse assumption.

title: The Landscape of Non-convex Empirical Risk with Degenerate Population Risk

abstract: When optimizing over-parameterized models, such as deep neural networks, a large set of parameters can achieve zero training error. In such cases, the choice of the optimization algorithm and its respective hyper-parameters introduces biases that will lead to convergence to specific minimizers of the objective. Consequently, this choice can be considered as an implicit regularization for the training of over-parametrized models. In this work, we push this idea further by studying the discrete gradient dynamics of the training of a two-layer linear network with the least-squares loss. Using a time rescaling, we show that, with a vanishing initialization and a small enough step size, this dynamics sequentially learns the solutions of a reduced-rank regression with a gradually increasing rank.

paragraphs: An over-parameterized model can have many parameter settings that fit the training data perfectly. The optimization algorithm and its hyperparameters can influence which solution training reaches. This paper studies that influence as implicit regularization: a preference introduced by the training procedure even without an explicit penalty in the objective.

The analysis concerns discrete gradient updates for a two-layer linear network trained with least-squares loss. Using a rescaling of time, the authors show that training sequentially learns reduced-rank regression solutions whose rank gradually increases. In this description, the training trajectory moves through solutions of increasing rank rather than treating every possible solution equally.

The result requires initialization that vanishes and a sufficiently small step size. Those conditions are central to the stated characterization. Within that setting, the work makes optimization's bias concrete: the dynamics organize learning according to rank. This provides a precise example of how training choices can shape the solutions learned by an over-parameterized model.
summary.tldr: Under vanishing initialization and small steps, a two-layer linear network learns reduced-rank regression solutions in increasing rank order.

title: Implicit Regularization of Discrete Gradient Dynamics in Linear Neural Networks

abstract: Statistical analysis of a graph often starts with embedding, the process of representing its nodes as points in space. How to choose the embedding dimension is a nuanced decision in practice, but in theory a notion of true dimension is often available. In spectral embedding, this dimension may be very high. However, this paper shows that existing random graph models, including graphon and other latent position models, predict the data should live near a much lower-dimensional set. One may therefore circumvent the curse of dimensionality by employing methods which exploit hidden manifold structure.

paragraphs: Graph embedding represents nodes as points in a space so that statistical methods can analyze them. Choosing the number of dimensions is consequential: a representation may require many coordinates according to its theoretical definition, especially with spectral embedding. This paper examines whether that high dimension reflects the full geometric complexity of the embedded data.

The authors show that existing random graph models, including graphon models and other latent-position models, predict that embedded points should lie near a much lower-dimensional set. The distinction is between the dimension of the surrounding representation space and the dimension of the structure the points actually occupy. A high-dimensional embedding can therefore contain substantial lower-dimensional organization.

This result suggests a way to address the curse of dimensionality: use statistical methods that exploit the hidden manifold structure. The implication is conditional on the structure predicted by the models under study. Rather than treating every embedding coordinate as an independent source of complexity, analysis may benefit from the more compact geometry underlying the node representations.
summary.tldr: Common random graph models predict low-dimensional manifold structure inside potentially high-dimensional spectral embeddings.

title: Manifold structure in graph embeddings

abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have shown to be effective in handling unordered data like point clouds and meshes. In this work we propose novel approaches for graph convolution, pooling and unpooling, inspired from finite differences and algebraic multigrid frameworks. We form a parameterized convolution kernel based on discretized differential operators, leveraging the graph mass, gradient and Laplacian. This way, the parameterization does not depend on the graph structure, only on the meaning of the network convolutions as differential operators. To allow hierarchical representations of the input, we propose pooling and unpooling operations that are based on algebraic multigrid methods, which are mainly used to solve partial differential equations on unstructured grids. To motivate and explain our method, we compare it to standard convolutional neural networks, and show their similarities and relations in the case of a regular grid. Our proposed method is demonstrated in various experiments like classification and part-segmentation, achieving on par or better than state of the art results. We also analyze the computational cost of our method compared to other GCNs.

Consequently, its parameterization follows the meaning of those operators rather than depending on a particular graph structure. Pooling and unpooling draw on algebraic multigrid methods, which are used to solve partial differential equations on unstructured grids, to support representations at multiple levels.

The authors explain the construction by relating it to standard convolutional networks on regular grids. Experiments including classification and part segmentation achieve results comparable to or better than the state of the art, and the paper analyzes computational costs relative to other graph networks. These findings support differential operators and multigrid ideas as useful foundations for learning on irregular data.
summary.tldr: DiffGCN builds graph convolutions from differential operators and hierarchical pooling from algebraic multigrid, achieving competitive classification and segmentation results.

title: DiffGCN: Graph Convolutional Networks via Differential Operators and Algebraic Multigrid Pooling

abstract: We study deep neural networks (DNNs) trained on natural image data with entirely random labels. Despite its popularity in the literature, where it is often used to study memorization, generalization, and other phenomena, little is known about what DNNs learn in this setting. In this paper, we show analytically for convolutional and fully connected networks that an alignment between the principal components of network parameters and data takes place when training with random labels. We study this alignment effect by investigating neural networks pre-trained on randomly labelled image data and subsequently fine-tuned on disjoint datasets with random or real labels. We show how this alignment produces a positive transfer: networks pre-trained with random labels train faster downstream compared to training from scratch even after accounting for simple effects, such as weight scaling. We analyze how competing effects, such as specialization at later layers, may hide the positive transfer. These effects are studied in several network architectures, including VGG16 and ResNet18, on CIFAR10 and ImageNet.

paragraphs: Training a neural network on randomly labeled images is often used to study memorization, but the images still contain structure. This paper investigates what networks learn from that structure despite the meaningless labels. For convolutional and fully connected networks, the authors analytically show alignment between principal components of the network parameters and those of the data.

They examine the effect by first training networks on randomly labeled images and then fine-tuning them on disjoint datasets with either random or real labels. The alignment produces positive transfer: the pretrained networks learn downstream tasks faster than networks trained from scratch. This benefit persists after accounting for simple explanations such as weight scaling.

Other effects can obscure the benefit, including specialization in later network layers. The authors investigate these competing influences across several architectures, including VGG16 and ResNet18, using CIFAR10 and ImageNet. The findings show that random-label training can leave useful structure in network parameters, even when its downstream benefit is not immediately visible in every part of the network.
summary.tldr: Networks trained with random labels can learn data-aligned parameter structure that speeds subsequent learning, although competing effects may hide this transfer.

title: What Do Neural Networks Learn When Trained With Random Labels?

abstract: We consider the problem of discovering $K$ related Gaussian directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where the involved graph structures share a consistent causal order and sparse unions of supports. Under the multi-task learning setting, we propose a $l_1/l_2$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for learning $K$ linear structural equation models. We theoretically show that the joint estimator, by leveraging data across related tasks, can achieve a better sample complexity for recovering the causal order (or topological order) than separate estimations. Moreover, the joint estimator is able to recover non-identifiable DAGs, by estimating them together with some identifiable DAGs. Lastly, our analysis also shows the consistency of union support recovery of the structures. To allow practical implementation, we design a continuous optimization problem whose optimizer is the same as the joint estimator and can be approximated efficiently by an iterative algorithm. We validate the theoretical analysis and the effectiveness of the joint estimator in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning several related causal graphs together. The graphs describe Gaussian linear structural equation models and are assumed to share a consistent causal ordering, with a sparse union of their edge supports. Those assumptions provide a basis for sharing information across tasks while allowing their graph structures to differ.

The authors propose a joint maximum likelihood estimator with an l1/l2 regularizer. They prove that joint estimation can require fewer samples to recover the causal ordering than learning each graph separately. They also show that a graph that is not identifiable on its own can become recoverable when estimated together with some identifiable graphs under the studied setting.

The analysis additionally establishes consistency for recovering the union of graph supports. To make the estimator implementable, the authors formulate a continuous optimization problem with the same optimizer and develop an iterative algorithm to approximate it efficiently. Experiments support the theory and effectiveness of joint estimation. The result explains how shared ordering and structural sparsity can turn related tasks into useful evidence for causal discovery.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning related Gaussian causal graphs can improve sample complexity and recover otherwise non-identifiable graphs under shared-order and sparsity assumptions.

title: Multi-task Learning of Order-Consistent Causal Graphs

abstract: We introduce a new kind of linear transform named Deformable Butterfly (DeBut) that generalizes the conventional butterfly matrices and can be adapted to various input-output dimensions. It inherits the fine-to-coarse-grained learnable hierarchy of traditional butterflies and when deployed to neural networks, the prominent structures and sparsity in a DeBut layer constitutes a new way for network compression. We apply DeBut as a drop-in replacement of standard fully connected and convolutional layers, and demonstrate its superiority in homogenizing a neural network and rendering it favorable properties such as light weight and low inference complexity, without compromising accuracy. The natural complexity-accuracy tradeoff arising from the myriad deformations of a DeBut layer also opens up new rooms for analytical and practical research. The codes and Appendix are publicly available at: https://github.com/ruilin0212/DeBut.

paragraphs: Neural network compression can change the structure of the transformations performed inside a model. This paper introduces Deformable Butterfly, or DeBut, a sparse linear transform that generalizes conventional butterfly matrices. A key feature is its ability to accommodate different input and output dimensions, making the structure adaptable to a range of neural network layers.

DeBut retains a learnable hierarchy that progresses from fine-scale to coarse-scale interactions. Its structured sparsity supplies the basis for compression, and the authors use it as a drop-in replacement for standard fully connected and convolutional layers. Using the same family of transforms for these different layer types also gives the network a more uniform internal structure.

The paper reports lightweight models and low inference complexity without sacrificing accuracy in its demonstrations. Different deformations of a DeBut layer provide different choices along a complexity–accuracy tradeoff. The contribution is therefore both a specific compressed layer design and a flexible family of structured transforms through which computational demands and predictive performance can be studied together.
summary.tldr: DeBut generalizes sparse butterfly transforms into adaptable replacements for neural network layers, demonstrating reduced inference complexity without accuracy loss.

title: Deformable Butterfly: A Highly Structured and Sparse Linear Transform

abstract: Neural SDEs combine many of the best qualities of both RNNs and SDEs, and as such are a natural choice for modelling many types of temporal dynamics. They offer memory efficiency, high-capacity function approximation, and strong priors on model space. Neural SDEs may be trained as VAEs or as GANs; in either case it is necessary to backpropagate through the SDE solve. In particular this may be done by constructing a backwards-in-time SDE whose solution is the desired parameter gradients. However, this has previously suffered from severe speed and accuracy issues, due to high computational complexity, numerical errors in the SDE solve, and the cost of reconstructing Brownian motion. Here, we make several technical innovations to overcome these issues. First, we introduce the \textit{reversible Heun method}: a new SDE solver that is algebraically reversible -- which reduces numerical gradient errors to almost zero, improving several test metrics by substantial margins over state-of-the-art. Moreover it requires half as many function evaluations as comparable solvers, giving up to a $1.98\times$ speedup. Next, we introduce the \textit{Brownian interval}. This is a new and computationally efficient way of exactly sampling \textit{and reconstructing} Brownian motion; this is in contrast to previous reconstruction techniques that are both approximate and relatively slow. This gives up to a $10.6\times$ speed improvement over previous techniques. After that, when specifically training Neural SDEs as GANs (Kidger et al. 2021), we demonstrate how SDE-GANs may be trained through careful weight clipping and choice of activation function. This reduces computational cost (giving up to a $1.87\times$ speedup), and removes the truncation errors of the double adjoint required for gradient penalty, substantially improving several test metrics. Altogether these techniques offer substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art, with respect to both training speed and with respect to classification, prediction, and MMD test metrics. We have contributed implementations of all of our techniques to the \texttt{torchsde} library to help facilitate their adoption.

paragraphs: Neural stochastic differential equations model temporal dynamics using learned functions and random variation. Training requires gradients through the numerical solution. Backward-in-time gradient calculations can be slow and inaccurate because of numerical errors, computational complexity, and the work needed to reconstruct the Brownian motion driving the process.

The paper introduces reversible Heun, an algebraically reversible solver that reduces numerical gradient errors to almost zero. It uses half as many function evaluations as comparable solvers and gives speedups of up to 1.98 times. This removes truncation errors associated with the double adjoint needed for gradient penalties and gives up to a 1.87-fold speedup. Together, the techniques improve training speed and several classification, prediction, and MMD test metrics. Implementations were contributed to torchsde.
summary.tldr: Reversible numerical solving, exact Brownian reconstruction, and revised GAN training improve neural SDE gradient accuracy and training speed.

title: Efficient and Accurate Gradients for Neural SDEs

abstract: Bayesian deep learning seeks to equip deep neural networks with the ability to precisely quantify their predictive uncertainty, and has promised to make deep learning more reliable for safety-critical real-world applications. Yet, existing Bayesian deep learning methods fall short of this promise; new methods continue to be evaluated on unrealistic test beds that do not reflect the complexities of downstream real-world tasks that would benefit most from reliable uncertainty quantification. We propose the RETINA Benchmark, a set of real-world tasks that accurately reflect such complexities and are designed to assess the reliability of predictive models in safety-critical scenarios. Specifically, we curate two publicly available datasets of high-resolution human retina images exhibiting varying degrees of diabetic retinopathy, a medical condition that can lead to blindness, and use them to design a suite of automated diagnosis tasks that require reliable predictive uncertainty quantification. We use these tasks to benchmark well-established and state-of-the-art Bayesian deep learning methods on task-specific evaluation metrics. We provide an easy-to-use codebase for fast and easy benchmarking following reproducibility and software design principles. We provide implementations of all methods included in the benchmark as well as results computed over 100 TPU days, 20 GPU days, 400 hyperparameter configurations, and evaluation on at least 6 random seeds each.

paragraphs: Bayesian deep learning aims to make neural networks express how uncertain their predictions are. This matters for safety-critical applications, where confidence needs to be reliable as well as predictions accurate. The paper argues that commonly used experimental settings do not adequately reflect the complexities of the real applications that most need trustworthy uncertainty estimates.

The RETINA Benchmark addresses this mismatch using two publicly available collections of high-resolution retinal images showing different degrees of diabetic retinopathy. The authors turn these data into automated diagnosis tasks designed to require reliable uncertainty quantification. They assess established and newer Bayesian methods using evaluation measures tailored to the tasks.

The contribution includes implementations, reproducible benchmarking software, and a substantial experimental reference: 400 hyperparameter configurations, evaluation with at least six random seeds each, and computation spanning 100 TPU days and 20 GPU days. This provides a concrete setting for comparing how methods handle uncertainty in medically relevant prediction tasks. The abstract establishes the benchmark and experimental scope without identifying a method that resolves the reliability problem.
summary.tldr: RETINA benchmarks Bayesian deep learning on retinal-image diagnosis tasks designed to test predictive uncertainty under realistic complexities.

title: Benchmarking Bayesian Deep Learning on Diabetic Retinopathy Detection Tasks

abstract: Bilevel optimization have gained growing interests, with numerous applications found in meta learning, minimax games, reinforcement learning, and nested composition optimization. This paper studies the problem of decentralized distributed bilevel optimization over a network where agents can only communicate with neighbors, and gives examples from multi-task, multi-agent learning and federated learning.In this paper, we propose a gossip-based distributed bilevel learning algorithm that allows networked agents to solve both the inner and outer optimization problems in a single timescale and share information through network propagation. We show that our algorithm enjoys the $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{K \epsilon^2})$ per-agent sample complexity for general nonconvex bilevel optimization and $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{K \epsilon})$ for Polyak-Łojasiewicz objective, achieving a speedup that scales linearly with the network size $K$. The sample complexities are optimal in both $\epsilon$ and $K$.We test our algorithm on the examples of hyperparameter tuning and decentralized reinforcement learning. Simulated experiments confirmed that our algorithm achieves the state-of-the-art training efficiency and test accuracy.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization contains an outer learning problem that depends on an inner optimization problem. This paper studies how a network of agents can solve such problems when each agent communicates only with its neighbors. That restriction makes the spread of information through the network part of the optimization challenge.

The proposed algorithm uses gossip-based communication and updates both optimization levels on a single timescale. Agents share information locally, allowing it to propagate through the network. For K agents and accuracy parameter epsilon, the paper proves per-agent sample complexity of order 1/(K epsilon²) for general nonconvex bilevel problems and 1/(K epsilon) for objectives satisfying the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition.

These bounds give a linear improvement with network size in the stated sample complexity, and the paper establishes optimal dependence on both K and epsilon. Simulated experiments in hyperparameter tuning and decentralized reinforcement learning report state-of-the-art training efficiency and test accuracy. Together, the results show how local communication can support statistically efficient cooperation on nested optimization problems.
summary.tldr: A gossip-based bilevel optimizer achieves optimal per-agent sample complexity with linear scaling benefits from the number of networked agents.

title: Decentralized Gossip-Based Stochastic Bilevel Optimization over Communication Networks

abstract: We consider the task of training machine learning models with data-dependent constraints. Such constraints often arise as empirical versions of expected value constraints that enforce fairness or stability goals. We reformulate data-dependent constraints so that they are calibrated: enforcing the reformulated constraints guarantees that their expected value counterparts are satisfied with a user-prescribed probability. The resulting optimization problem is amendable to standard stochastic optimization algorithms, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our method on a fairness-sensitive classification task where we wish to guarantee the classifier's fairness (at test time).
originalAbstract: We consider the task of training machine learning models with data-dependent constraints. Such constraints often arise as empirical versions of expected value constraints that enforce fairness or stability goals. We reformulate data-dependent constraints so that they are calibrated: enforcing the reformulated constraints guarantees that their expected value counterparts are satisfied with a user-prescribed probability. The resulting optimization problem is amendable to standard stochastic optimization algorithms, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our method on a fairness-sensitive classification task where we wish to guarantee the classifier's fairness (at test time).

paragraphs: Machine learning models may need to meet requirements beyond predictive performance, such as fairness or stability. These requirements often concern expected behavior, but training only has access to data-based estimates. A constraint that holds on the observed sample therefore raises a further question: how can enforcing it provide a guarantee about its expected-value counterpart?

The paper addresses this gap by reformulating the constraints through calibration. Enforcing the reformulated version guarantees satisfaction of the expected-value constraint with a probability chosen by the user. The probability qualification is central: the result connects empirical enforcement to a specified level of confidence in the underlying requirement, rather than claiming unconditional satisfaction in every instance.

The resulting training problem can be handled with standard stochastic optimization algorithms. This makes calibration part of the optimization formulation, rather than only a check performed after training. The authors demonstrate the method on a classification task with a fairness requirement at test time. The demonstration shows how a desired probabilistic guarantee can be connected to constraints that a training algorithm actually enforces.
summary.tldr: Calibrated training constraints guarantee satisfaction of their expected-value counterparts with a user-chosen probability.

title: Calibrated Data-Dependent Constraints with Exact Satisfaction Guarantees

abstract: Neural networks are powerful surrogates for numerous forward processes.The inversion of such surrogates is extremely valuable in science and engineering. The most important property of a successful neural inverse method is the performance of its solutions when deployed in the real world, i.e., on the native forward process (and not only the learned surrogate). We propose Autoinverse, a highly automated approach for inverting neural network surrogates. Our main insight is to seek inverse solutions in the vicinity of reliable data which have been sampled form the forward process and used for training the surrogate model. Autoinverse finds such solutions by taking into account the predictive uncertainty of the surrogate and minimizing it during the inversion. Apart from high accuracy, Autoinverse enforces the feasibility of solutions, comes with embedded regularization, and is initialization free. We verify our proposed method through addressing a set of real-world problems in control, fabrication, and design.

paragraphs: A neural network can approximate a forward process, making it useful for searching backward from a desired result to a suitable input. The difficulty is that a solution must work in the original process, not merely in its learned approximation. Autoinverse addresses this distinction when inverting neural network surrogates for science and engineering.

Its central idea is to seek solutions near reliable examples sampled from the forward process and used to train the surrogate. During inversion, Autoinverse accounts for predictive uncertainty and minimizes it. This makes the surrogate's reliability part of the search itself, directing attention toward solutions supported by the data behind the approximation.

The authors describe the method as highly automated, initialization free, and equipped with embedded regularization and feasibility enforcement. They verify it on real-world problems in control, fabrication, and design. The stated contribution combines accurate inversion with explicit attention to whether proposed solutions remain useful when evaluated through the native forward process.
summary.tldr: Autoinverse minimizes surrogate uncertainty during neural network inversion to seek feasible solutions near reliable training data.

title: Autoinverse: Uncertainty Aware Inversion of Neural Networks

abstract: In the future, powerful AI systems may be deployed in high-stakes settings, where a single failure could be catastrophic. One technique for improving AI safety in high-stakes settings is adversarial training, which uses an adversary to generate examples to train on in order to achieve better worst-case performance.In this work, we used a safe language generation task (``avoid injuries'') as a testbed for achieving high reliability through adversarial training. We created a series of adversarial training techniques---including a tool that assists human adversaries---to find and eliminate failures in a classifier that filters text completions suggested by a generator. In our task, we determined that we can set very conservative classifier thresholds without significantly impacting the quality of the filtered outputs. We found that adversarial training significantly increased robustness to the adversarial attacks that we trained on--- tripling the time to find adversarial examples without tools and doubling the time with our tool (from 13 to 26 minutes)---without affecting in-distribution performance. We hope to see further work in the high-stakes reliability setting, including more powerful tools for enhancing human adversaries and better ways to measure high levels of reliability, until we can confidently rule out the possibility of catastrophic deployment-time failures of powerful models.

paragraphs: The paper studies adversarial training in a setting where reliability matters more than average performance. Its testbed is a language generation task that aims to avoid descriptions involving injuries. A generator proposes text completions, and a classifier filters them. The researchers develop several ways to find failures in that classifier, including a tool that helps human adversaries search.

The approach turns discovered failures into training material. In this task, the researchers also find that very conservative filtering thresholds can be used without significantly reducing output quality. This matters because stricter filtering would be less useful if it removed too many acceptable completions.

Adversarial training makes attacks of the kinds used during training harder to find, while preserving performance on ordinary inputs. Human search takes three times longer without tools; with the assistance tool, it increases from 13 to 26 minutes. These results demonstrate increased resistance to the tested attacks, rather than establishing that catastrophic failures are impossible. The authors identify stronger attack tools and better measurements of high reliability as directions for further work.
summary.tldr: Adversarial training makes failures harder to find in a text-filtering testbed without reducing ordinary-task performance.

title: Adversarial training for high-stakes reliability

abstract: This paper introduces Honor of Kings Arena, a reinforcement learning (RL) environment based on the Honor of Kings, one of the world’s most popular games at present. Compared to other environments studied in most previous work, ours presents new generalization challenges for competitive reinforcement learning. It is a multi-agent problem with one agent competing against its opponent; and it requires the generalization ability as it has diverse targets to control and diverse opponents to compete with. We describe the observation, action, and reward specifications for the Honor of Kings domain and provide an open-source Python-based interface for communicating with the game engine. We provide twenty target heroes with a variety of tasks in Honor of Kings Arena and present initial baseline results for RL-based methods with feasible computing resources. Finally, we showcase the generalization challenges imposed by Honor of Kings Arena and possible remedies to the challenges. All of the software, including the environment-class, are publicly available.

paragraphs: Competitive reinforcement learning must account for both the character an agent controls and the opponent it faces. Honor of Kings Arena introduces an environment built around these sources of variation. It uses a game setting in which one agent competes against an opponent, with diverse controllable targets and opposing characters creating generalization challenges.

The paper specifies the observations available to an agent, the actions it can take, and the rewards used for learning. It also provides an open-source Python interface to the game engine. Twenty target heroes and a variety of tasks give researchers multiple settings in which to examine whether learned behavior carries over across different competitive situations.

The authors present initial reinforcement-learning baselines using feasible computing resources and demonstrate the environment’s generalization challenges. They also discuss possible remedies for those challenges. The contribution is an accessible experimental environment and starting point for studying transfer across characters and opponents. Publicly available software, including the environment class, supports further work on these questions.
summary.tldr: Honor of Kings Arena provides an open environment for studying how competitive reinforcement-learning agents generalize across heroes and opponents.

title: Honor of Kings Arena: an Environment for Generalization in Competitive Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Trajectory inference aims at recovering the dynamics of a population from snapshots of its temporal marginals. To solve this task, a min-entropy estimator relative to the Wiener measure in path space was introduced in [Lavenant et al., 2021], and shown to consistently recover the dynamics of a large class of drift-diffusion processes from the solution of an infinite dimensional convex optimization problem. In this paper, we introduce a grid-free algorithm to compute this estimator. Our method consists in a family of point clouds (one per snapshot) coupled via Schrödinger bridges which evolve with noisy gradient descent. We study the mean-field limit of the dynamics and prove its global convergence to the desired estimator. Overall, this leads to an inference method with end-to-end theoretical guarantees that solves an interpretable model for trajectory inference. We also present how to adapt the method to deal with mass variations, a useful extension when dealing with single cell RNA-sequencing data where cells can branch and die.

paragraphs: Trajectory inference tries to recover how a population evolves from snapshots of its distribution at different times. Earlier work formulated an estimator through minimum entropy relative to Wiener measure over paths and established consistency for a broad class of drift-diffusion processes. This paper contributes an algorithm for computing that estimator without a spatial grid.

The algorithm represents each snapshot with a cloud of points. Schrödinger bridges couple these clouds, and noisy gradient descent evolves them toward the desired solution. This provides a computational representation of a problem originally expressed as infinite-dimensional convex optimization over trajectories, while retaining the connection to the underlying statistical model.

The authors analyze the mean-field limit of the resulting dynamics and prove global convergence to the estimator. Combined with the estimator's existing properties, this supports end-to-end theoretical guarantees. They also explain an adaptation for populations whose mass changes over time. That extension is relevant to single-cell RNA-sequencing settings, where cells can branch and die rather than form a population of constant size.
summary.tldr: A grid-free method uses coupled point clouds and noisy gradient descent to compute a trajectory estimator with mean-field convergence guarantees.

title: Trajectory Inference via Mean-field Langevin in Path Space

abstract: The industry practice has been moving to embedding based retrieval (EBR). For example, in many applications, the embedding vectors are trained by some form of two-tower models. During serving phase, candidates (embedding vectors) are retrieved according to the rankings of cosine similarities either exhaustively or by approximate near neighbor (ANN) search algorithms. For those applications, it is natural to apply ``sign random projections'' (SignRP) or variants, on the trained embedding vectors to facilitate efficient data storage and cosine distance computations. SignRP is also one of the standard indexing schemes for conducting approximate near neighbor search. In the literature, SignRP has been popular and, to an extent, becomes the default method for ``locality sensitive hashing'' (LSH). In this paper, we propose ``sign random Fourier features'' (SignRFF) as an alternative to SignRP. The original method of random Fourier features (RFF) is a standard technique for approximating the Gaussian kernel (as opposed to the linear cosine kernel), in the literature of large-scale machine learning. Basically, RFF applies a simple nonlinear transformation on the samples generated by random projections (RP). Thus, in the pipeline of EBR, it is straightforward to replace SignRP by SignRFF. This paper explains, in a principled manner, why it makes sense to do so. In this paper, a new analytical measure called \textbf{Ranking Efficiency (RE)} is developed, which in retrospect is closely related to the ``two-sample mean'' $t$-test statistic for binomial variables. RE provides a systematic and unified framework for comparing different LSH methods. We compare our proposed SignRP with SignRP, KLSH (kernel LSH), as well SQ-RFF (which is another 1-bit coding scheme for RFF). According to the RE expression, SignRFF consistently outperforms KLSH (for Gaussian kernel) and SQ-RFF. SignRFF also outperforms SignRP in the relatively high similarity region. The theoretical comparison results are consistent with our empirical findings. In addition, experiments are conducted to compare SignRFF with a wide range of data-dependent and deep learning based hashing methods and show the advantage of SignRFF with a sufficient number of hash bits.

These qualifications matter: the reported comparisons depend on similarity region, comparator, and, for the broader experiments, sufficient code length.
summary.tldr: SignRFF offers a nonlinear binary hashing alternative with favorable ranking analysis and empirical gains under stated similarity and code-length conditions.

title: SignRFF: Sign Random Fourier Features

abstract: Recently, several attempts have demonstrated that 3D deep learning models are as vulnerable to adversarial example attacks as 2D models. However, these methods are still far from stealthy and suffer from severe performance degradation in the physical world. Although 3D data is highly structured, it is difficult to bound the perturbations with simple metrics in the Euclidean space. In this paper, we propose a novel $\epsilon$-isometric ($\epsilon$-ISO) attack method to generate natural and robust 3D adversarial examples in the physical world by considering the geometric properties of 3D objects and the invariance to physical transformations. For naturalness, we constrain the adversarial example and the original one to be $\epsilon$-isometric by adopting the Gaussian curvature as the surrogate metric under a theoretical analysis. For robustness under physical transformations, we propose a maxima over transformation (MaxOT) method to actively search for the most difficult transformations rather than random ones to make the generated adversarial example more robust in the physical world. Extensive experiments on typical point cloud recognition models validate that our approach can improve the attack success rate and naturalness of the generated 3D adversarial examples than the state-of-the-art attack methods.

paragraphs: Adversarial changes to three-dimensional objects need to do more than fool a recognition model digitally: they should also look natural and remain effective under physical transformations. The paper argues that simple Euclidean measures poorly capture acceptable changes to highly structured 3D shapes. It introduces an attack that explicitly considers object geometry and transformation robustness.

For naturalness, the method constrains the original and modified shapes to be approximately isometric, using Gaussian curvature as a surrogate metric supported by theoretical analysis. This makes geometric properties part of the constraint on adversarial changes. For robustness, its MaxOT component actively searches for particularly difficult transformations instead of relying on randomly selected ones.

Experiments on typical point-cloud recognition models show improvements in attack success and the naturalness of generated examples compared with the state-of-the-art attacks evaluated. The findings support treating shape preservation and robustness to transformations as joint design concerns. The result is a method aimed at adversarial objects whose changes remain less conspicuous and whose attacks better survive the conditions encountered in the physical world.
summary.tldr: Geometry-aware shape constraints and difficult-transformation search improve the naturalness and physical robustness of evaluated 3D adversarial examples.

title: Isometric 3D Adversarial Examples in the Physical World

abstract: Real-world datasets exhibit imbalances of varying types and degrees. Several techniques based on re-weighting and margin adjustment of loss are often used to enhance the performance of neural networks, particularly on minority classes. In this work, we analyze the class-imbalanced learning problem by examining the loss landscape of neural networks trained with re-weighting and margin based techniques. Specifically, we examine the spectral density of Hessian of class-wise loss, through which we observe that the network weights converges to a saddle point in the loss landscapes of minority classes. Following this observation, we also find that optimization methods designed to escape from saddle points can be effectively used to improve generalization on minority classes. We further theoretically and empirically demonstrate that Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), a recent technique that encourages convergence to a flat minima, can be effectively used to escape saddle points for minority classes. Using SAM results in a 6.2\% increase in accuracy on the minority classes over the state-of-the-art Vector Scaling Loss, leading to an overall average increase of 4\% across imbalanced datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/val-iisc/Saddle-LongTail.

paragraphs: Class imbalance means some categories have much less training data than others. Common responses change how heavily examples count in the loss or adjust classification margins. This paper examines what happens to optimization under those methods by studying each class's loss landscape, giving particular attention to minority classes.

The authors analyze the spectrum of the Hessian, which describes curvature around the network's weights. They observe that training reaches saddle points in the minority-class loss landscapes. This suggests that minority-class performance can suffer from the geometry of the reached solution. They then investigate optimization methods designed to escape such points.

The paper provides theoretical and empirical support for using Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, to escape minority-class saddle points. Although SAM encourages flatter minima, it also helps address the saddle behavior identified here. The authors report a 6.2% increase in minority-class accuracy over Vector Scaling Loss and an overall average increase of 4% across imbalanced datasets. The findings connect improved generalization to the optimization landscape of underrepresented classes.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies minority-class saddle points during imbalanced learning and shows that SAM can escape them and improve generalization.

title: Escaping Saddle Points for Effective Generalization on Class-Imbalanced Data

abstract: Currently, Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) is proposed to seek the parameters that lie in a flat region to improve the generalization when training neural networks. In particular, a minimax optimization objective is defined to find the maximum loss value centered on the weight, out of the purpose of simultaneously minimizing loss value and loss sharpness. For the sake of simplicity, SAM applies one-step gradient ascent to approximate the solution of the inner maximization. However, one-step gradient ascent may not be sufficient and multi-step gradient ascents will cause additional training costs. Based on this observation, we propose a novel random smoothing based SAM (R-SAM) algorithm. To be specific, R-SAM essentially smooths the loss landscape, based on which we are able to apply the one-step gradient ascent on the smoothed weights to improve the approximation of the inner maximization. Further, we evaluate our proposed R-SAM on CIFAR and ImageNet datasets. The experimental results illustrate that R-SAM can consistently improve the performance on ResNet and Vision Transformer (ViT) training.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization aims to find network weights in relatively flat regions of the loss landscape. It does this through a minimax objective that considers the largest nearby loss as well as the loss at the current weights. In practice, the inner maximization is commonly approximated with one gradient-ascent step to keep training manageable.

The paper focuses on the quality of that approximation. One ascent step may be insufficient, while taking multiple steps increases training cost. The proposed Random Sharpness-Aware Minimization method uses random smoothing to smooth the loss landscape. It then applies a single ascent step on the smoothed weights to improve the approximation of the inner maximization.

The authors evaluate R-SAM on CIFAR and ImageNet with ResNets and Vision Transformers, reporting consistent performance improvements in those experiments. The approach therefore targets how the sharpness objective is approximated, using smoothing to improve the usefulness of a one-step update. The reported evidence supports the method across the tested datasets and architecture families, rather than establishing that smoothing improves every possible training setup.
summary.tldr: R-SAM smooths the loss landscape to improve SAM's one-step inner maximization and reports better ResNet and Vision Transformer performance.

title: Random Sharpness-Aware Minimization

abstract: Multi-head attention empowers the recent success of transformers, the state-of-the-art models that have achieved remarkable success in sequence modeling and beyond. These attention mechanisms compute the pairwise dot products between the queries and keys, which results from the use of unnormalized Gaussian kernels with the assumption that the queries follow a mixture of Gaussian distribution. There is no guarantee that this assumption is valid in practice. In response, we first interpret attention in transformers as a nonparametric kernel regression. We then propose the FourierFormer, a new class of transformers in which the dot-product kernels are replaced by the novel generalized Fourier integral kernels. Different from the dot-product kernels, where we need to choose a good covariance matrix to capture the dependency of the features of data, the generalized Fourier integral kernels can automatically capture such dependency and remove the need to tune the covariance matrix. We theoretically prove that our proposed Fourier integral kernels can efficiently approximate any key and query distributions. Compared to the conventional transformers with dot-product attention, FourierFormers attain better accuracy and reduce the redundancy between attention heads. We empirically corroborate the advantages of FourierFormers over the baseline transformers in a variety of practical applications including language modeling and image classification.

paragraphs: This paper examines transformer attention through the lens of nonparametric kernel regression. In the authors' account, conventional dot-product attention corresponds to unnormalized Gaussian kernels under a Gaussian-mixture assumption about queries. Because that assumption need not hold in practice, they investigate a different family of kernels for relating queries and keys.

FourierFormer replaces dot-product kernels with generalized Fourier integral kernels. These kernels can automatically capture dependencies between data features, removing the need to tune a covariance matrix for that purpose. The authors also prove that their proposed kernels can efficiently approximate arbitrary key and query distributions. This provides theoretical support for a more flexible treatment of the distributions involved in attention.

Empirical evaluations include language modeling and image classification. Compared with the baseline dot-product transformers, FourierFormers achieve better accuracy and less redundancy between attention heads. The results connect the kernel-level change to both prediction quality and how distinctly the heads behave, supporting the proposed attention mechanism in the applications evaluated.
summary.tldr: FourierFormer replaces dot-product attention kernels with generalized Fourier kernels, improving reported accuracy and reducing attention-head redundancy.

title: FourierFormer: Transformer Meets Generalized Fourier Integral Theorem

abstract: Despite the success of practical solvers in various NP-complete domains such as SAT and CSP as well as using deep reinforcement learning to tackle two-player games such as Go, certain classes of PSPACE-hard planning problems have remained out of reach. Even carefully designed domain-specialized solvers can fail quickly due to the exponential search space on hard instances. Recent works that combine traditional search methods, such as best-first search and Monte Carlo tree search, with Deep Neural Networks' (DNN) heuristics have shown promising progress and can solve a significant number of hard planning instances beyond specialized solvers. To better understand why these approaches work, we studied the interplay of the policy and value networks of DNN-based best-first search on Sokoban and show the surprising effectiveness of the policy network, further enhanced by the value network, as a guiding heuristic for the search. To further understand the phenomena, we studied the cost distribution of the search algorithms and found that Sokoban instances can have heavy-tailed runtime distributions, with tails both on the left and right-hand sides. In particular, for the first time, we show the existence of \textit{left heavy tails} and propose an abstract tree model that can empirically explain the appearance of these tails. The experiments show the critical role of the policy network as a powerful heuristic guiding the search, which can lead to left heavy tails with polynomial scaling by avoiding exploring exponentially sized subtrees. Our results also demonstrate the importance of random restarts, as are widely used in traditional combinatorial solvers, for DNN-based search methods to avoid left and right heavy tails.

paragraphs: Neural-network guidance has helped traditional search solve difficult planning instances, but understanding that success requires examining how the guidance affects exploration. This paper studies best-first search for Sokoban, focusing on the interaction between policy and value networks. It finds that the policy network is a surprisingly effective search heuristic, with further benefits from the value network.

The authors examine search-cost distributions and find that Sokoban instances can have heavy tails on both sides of their runtime distributions. They report the existence of left heavy tails and propose an abstract tree model that empirically explains their appearance. This connects the observed runtime behavior to the structure of the search.

That finding concerns the studied search behavior, rather than establishing polynomial complexity for Sokoban generally. The results also emphasize random restarts as an important tool for handling both left and right heavy tails in neural-network-guided search.
summary.tldr: Sokoban experiments link effective policy-network search guidance to heavy-tailed runtimes and highlight the value of random restarts.

title: Left Heavy Tails and the Effectiveness of the Policy and Value Networks in DNN-based best-first search for Sokoban Planning

abstract: As a longstanding learning paradigm, multi-task learning has been widely applied into a variety of machine learning applications. Nonetheless, identifying which tasks should be learned together is still a challenging fundamental problem because the possible task combinations grow exponentially with the number of tasks, and existing solutions heavily relying on heuristics may probably lead to ineffective groupings with severe performance degradation. To bridge this gap, we develop a systematic multi-task grouping framework with a new meta-learning problem on task combinations, which is to predict the per-task performance gains of multi-task learning over single-task learning for any combination. Our underlying assumption is that no matter how large the space of task combinations is, the relationships between task combinations and performance gains lie in some low-dimensional manifolds and thus can be learnable. Accordingly, we develop a neural meta learner, MTG-Net, to capture these relationships, and design an active learning strategy to progressively select meta-training samples. In this way, even with limited meta samples, MTG-Net holds the potential to produce reasonable gain estimations on arbitrary task combinations. Extensive experiments on diversified multi-task scenarios demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our method. Specifically, in a large-scale evaluation with $27$ tasks, which produce over one hundred million task combinations, our method almost doubles the performance obtained by the existing best solution given roughly the same computational cost. Data and code are available at https://github.com/ShawnKS/MTG-Net.
originalAbstract: As a longstanding learning paradigm, multi-task learning has been widely applied into a variety of machine learning applications. Nonetheless, identifying which tasks should be learned together is still a challenging fundamental problem because the possible task combinations grow exponentially with the number of tasks, and existing solutions heavily relying on heuristics may probably lead to ineffective groupings with severe performance degradation. To bridge this gap, we develop a systematic multi-task grouping framework with a new meta-learning problem on task combinations, which is to predict the per-task performance gains of multi-task learning over single-task learning for any combination. Our underlying assumption is that no matter how large the space of task combinations is, the relationships between task combinations and performance gains lie in some low-dimensional manifolds and thus can be learnable. Accordingly, we develop a neural meta learner, MTG-Net, to capture these relationships, and design an active learning strategy to progressively select meta-training samples. In this way, even with limited meta samples, MTG-Net holds the potential to produce reasonable gain estimations on arbitrary task combinations. Extensive experiments on diversified multi-task scenarios demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our method. Specifically, in a large-scale evaluation with $27$ tasks, which produce over one hundred million task combinations, our method almost doubles the performance obtained by the existing best solution given roughly the same computational cost. Data and code are available at https://github.com/ShawnKS/MTG-Net.

paragraphs: Learning several tasks together can help or hurt, so deciding which tasks should share training is consequential. Exhaustively testing groups becomes impractical because the number of combinations grows exponentially. This paper frames grouping as a prediction problem: estimate how much each task would gain from a proposed group compared with learning it alone.

The neural meta learner MTG-Net learns relationships between task combinations and their performance gains. The approach assumes that these relationships occupy low-dimensional manifolds despite the enormous combination space. An active learning strategy progressively chooses combinations for meta-training, aiming to obtain useful gain estimates from relatively few evaluated combinations.

Experiments across varied multi-task scenarios support the method's efficiency and effectiveness. In an evaluation with 27 tasks and more than one hundred million possible combinations, the method almost doubles the reported performance of the best existing solution at roughly the same computational cost. Its broader promise depends on whether the assumed learnable structure captures the relationships among task groups.
summary.tldr: MTG-Net learns to predict the benefits of task combinations, enabling effective multi-task grouping without evaluating every possible group.

title: Efficient and Effective Multi-task Grouping via Meta Learning on Task Combinations

abstract: The main challenge of offline reinforcement learning, where data is limited, arises from a sequence of counterfactual reasoning dilemmas within the realm of potential actions: What if we were to choose a different course of action? These circumstances frequently give rise to extrapolation errors, which tend to accumulate exponentially with the problem horizon. Hence, it becomes crucial to acknowledge that not all decision steps are equally important to the final outcome, and to budget the number of counterfactual decisions a policy make in order to control the extrapolation. Contrary to existing approaches that use regularization on either the policy or value function, we propose an approach to explicitly bound the amount of out-of-distribution actions during training. Specifically, our method utilizes dynamic programming to decide where to extrapolate and where not to, with an upper bound on the decisions different from behavior policy. It balances between the potential for improvement from taking out-of-distribution actions and the risk of making errors due to extrapolation. Theoretically, we justify our method by the constrained optimality of the fixed point solution to our $Q$ updating rules. Empirically, we show that the overall performance of our method is better than the state-of-the-art offline RL methods on tasks in the widely-used D4RL benchmarks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns decisions from a fixed dataset. When a policy considers actions unlike those represented in that data, it must estimate outcomes without direct support. These extrapolation errors can compound across a sequence of decisions. The paper starts from the observation that some departures from recorded behavior may matter more to the final outcome than others.

The proposed method places an explicit budget on decisions that differ from the behavior policy. Dynamic programming determines where to spend that budget: which steps warrant trying an unsupported action and which should remain closer to recorded behavior. This makes the tradeoff between potential improvement and extrapolation risk part of the sequential decision problem itself.

The theoretical result establishes constrained optimality of the fixed point of the proposed Q-value updates. That means optimality within the imposed budget, rather than unrestricted optimality. Experiments report better overall performance than state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning methods on evaluated D4RL tasks, supporting the value of allocating departures selectively.
summary.tldr: The method budgets departures from recorded behavior and uses dynamic programming to decide where those departures are most worthwhile.

title: Budgeting Counterfactual for Offline RL

abstract: Leveraging the compositional nature of our world to expedite learning and facilitate generalization is a hallmark of human perception. In machine learning, on the other hand, achieving compositional generalization has proven to be an elusive goal, even for models with explicit compositional priors. To get a better handle on compositional generalization, we here approach it from the bottom up: Inspired by identifiable representation learning, we investigate compositionality as a property of the data-generating process rather than the data itself. This reformulation enables us to derive mild conditions on only the support of the training distribution and the model architecture, which are sufficient for compositional generalization. We further demonstrate how our theoretical framework applies to real-world scenarios and validate our findings empirically. Our results set the stage for a principled theoretical study of compositional generalization.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization concerns learning reusable parts and applying them in combinations beyond those encountered during training. Although people routinely benefit from this ability, machine-learning models can struggle even when their designs explicitly encourage composition. This paper asks what conditions can actually support such generalization, approaching the question through the mechanism that produces observations.

The authors treat compositionality as a property of the data-generating process. Inspired by identifiable representation learning, this perspective shifts attention from whether examples appear compositional to whether the underlying process has a recoverable compositional structure. They derive sufficient conditions involving the support of the training distribution—the cases it can contain—and the model architecture.

The conditions are described as mild, and the authors demonstrate applications of the framework to real-world scenarios alongside empirical validation. Their result establishes circumstances under which compositional generalization is supported by theory. Because the conditions are sufficient, the claim does not imply that every successful model must satisfy them. The broader contribution is a foundation for reasoning about composition through explicit assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper derives sufficient conditions for compositional generalization by studying the structure of the data-generating process.

title: Compositional Generalization from First Principles

abstract: ReLU networks have remained the default choice for models in the area of image prediction despite their well-established spectral bias towards learning low frequencies faster, and consequently their difficulty of reproducing high frequency visual details. As an alternative, sin networks showed promising results in learning implicit representations of visual data. However training these networks in practically relevant settings proved to be difficult, requiring careful initialization, dealing with issues due to inconsistent gradients, and a degeneracy in local minima. In this work, we instead propose replacing a baseline network’s existing activations with a novel ensemble function with trainable parameters. The proposed MetaSin activation can be trained reliably without requiring intricate initialization schemes, and results in consistently lower test loss compared to alternatives. We demonstrate our method in the areas of Monte-Carlo denoising and image resampling where we set new state-of-the-art through a knowledge distillation based training procedure. We present ablations on hyper-parameter settings, comparisons with alternative activation function formulations, and discuss the use of our method in other domains, such as image classification.
