paragraphs: Image prediction networks using ReLU activations tend to learn low-frequency structure faster than high-frequency detail. Sine-based networks offer an alternative for representing visual data, but their training can require careful initialization and can encounter inconsistent gradients and problematic local minima. This paper proposes changing the activation function to address that practical tension.

MetaSin replaces a baseline network's existing activations with an ensemble function whose parameters are trainable. The authors report reliable training without intricate initialization schemes and consistently lower test loss than the alternatives they examine. The approach makes the activation itself adaptable, giving the network a learned component where a fixed nonlinearity would ordinarily sit.

The main demonstrations involve Monte-Carlo denoising and image resampling. With a knowledge-distillation-based training procedure, the method achieves reported state-of-the-art results in these areas. The paper also examines hyperparameter choices and alternative activation formulations, and discusses image classification as another domain. Its strongest stated performance findings concern the demonstrated image-processing tasks and their accompanying training procedure.
summary.tldr: MetaSin introduces trainable ensemble activations that improve reported image-prediction results while avoiding the intricate initialization required by sine networks.

title: Empowering Convolutional Neural Nets with MetaSin Activation

abstract: This paper presents Triangulation Residual loss (TR loss) for multiview 3D pose estimation in a data-efficient manner. Existing 3D supervised models usually require large-scale 3D annotated datasets, but the amount of existing data is still insufficient to train supervised models to achieve ideal performance, especially for animal pose estimation. To employ unlabeled multiview data for training, previous epipolar-based consistency provides a self-supervised loss that considers only the local consistency in pairwise views, resulting in limited performance and heavy calculations. In contrast, TR loss enables self-supervision with global multiview geometric consistency. Starting from initial 2D keypoint estimates, the TR loss can fine-tune the corresponding 2D detector without 3D supervision by simply minimizing the smallest singular value of the triangulation matrix in an end-to-end fashion. Our method achieves the state-of-the-art 25.8mm MPJPE and competitive 28.7mm MPJPE with only 5\% 2D labeled training data on the Human3.6M dataset. Experiments on animals such as mice demonstrate our TR loss's data-efficient training ability.

paragraphs: Estimating 3D pose from multiple views often requires large amounts of annotated training data. This is particularly difficult for animals. The paper introduces Triangulation Residual loss, or TR loss, to use unlabeled multiview observations for training by checking whether predicted keypoints agree geometrically across the available views.

Earlier epipolar consistency objectives compare pairs of views locally. TR loss instead enforces global multiview consistency. Starting with initial 2D keypoint estimates, it minimizes the smallest singular value of the triangulation matrix. This scalar training signal allows end-to-end fine-tuning of the 2D detector without requiring 3D supervision.

On Human3.6M, the method reports a state-of-the-art mean per-joint position error of 25.8 millimeters and a competitive 28.7 millimeters using only 5% of the 2D labeled training data. Experiments with animals, including mice, also demonstrate data-efficient training. The findings show how geometric agreement among views can supply useful supervision, reducing dependence on labeled poses while improving the detector that provides the initial 2D estimates.
summary.tldr: TR loss uses global multiview geometry to fine-tune pose detectors without 3D labels and with limited 2D annotation.

title: Triangulation Residual Loss for Data-efficient 3D Pose Estimation

abstract: To avoid failures on out-of-distribution data, recent works have sought to extract features that have an invariant or stable relationship with the label across domains, discarding "spurious" or unstable features whose relationship with the label changes across domains. However, unstable features often carry complementary information that could boost performance if used correctly in the test domain. In this work, we show how this can be done without test-domain labels. In particular, we prove that pseudo-labels based on stable features provide sufficient guidance for doing so, provided that stable and unstable features are conditionally independent given the label. Based on this theoretical insight, we propose Stable Feature Boosting (SFB), an algorithm for: (i) learning a predictor that separates stable and conditionally-independent unstable features; and (ii) using the stable-feature predictions to adapt the unstable-feature predictions in the test domain. Theoretically, we prove that SFB can learn an asymptotically-optimal predictor without test-domain labels. Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SFB on real and synthetic data.

paragraphs: Features whose relationship with a label changes across domains are often discarded to improve out-of-distribution reliability. This paper asks whether those unstable features can still contribute useful information in a new domain. Its focus is adapting their use without access to labels from that domain, using predictions from stable features as guidance.

The theoretical result requires stable and unstable features to be conditionally independent given the label. Under that assumption, pseudo-labels produced from stable features provide sufficient guidance for using unstable features. Stable Feature Boosting turns this insight into a procedure that learns separate stable and conditionally independent unstable features, then adapts unstable-feature predictions using stable-feature predictions at test time.

The authors prove that SFB can learn an asymptotically optimal predictor without test-domain labels and demonstrate effectiveness on real and synthetic data. The conditional-independence assumption is central to the stated theoretical justification. The broader implication is that unstable information can remain valuable when a stable predictor supplies an appropriate basis for adapting how that information is used in the target domain.
summary.tldr: Under a conditional-independence assumption, stable-feature predictions can guide useful adaptation of unstable features without test-domain labels.

title: Spuriosity Didn’t Kill the Classifier: Using Invariant Predictions to Harness Spurious Features

abstract: Recent works have shown that diffusion models can learn essentially any distribution provided one can perform score estimation.Yet it remains poorly understood under what settings score estimation is possible, let alone when practical gradient-based algorithms for this task can provably succeed. In this work, we give the first provably efficient results for one of the most fundamental distribution families, Gaussian mixture models.We prove that GD on the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) objective can efficiently recover the ground truth parameters of the mixture model in the following two settings:1. We show GD with random initialization learns mixtures of two spherical Gaussians in $d$ dimensions with $1/\text{poly}(d)$-separated centers.2. We show GD with a warm start learns mixtures of $K$ spherical Gaussians with $\Omega(\sqrt{\log(\min(K,d))})$-separated centers.A key ingredient in our proofs is a new connection between score-based methods and two other approaches to distribution learning, EM and spectral methods.

paragraphs: Diffusion models have broad distribution-learning capabilities if accurate score estimation is available. That premise leaves an important question unresolved: when can practical gradient-based training actually learn the required quantities? This paper studies that question for Gaussian mixture models and proves efficient recovery of their true parameters by gradient descent on the denoising diffusion probabilistic model objective.

The guarantees cover two specific settings. For a mixture of two spherical Gaussians in d dimensions, random initialization succeeds when the centers have inverse-polynomial separation in d. For a mixture of K spherical Gaussians, the result instead requires a warm start and center separation of order at least the square root of log(min(K, d)). Initialization and separation are therefore essential parts of the statements.

A central proof ingredient connects score-based learning with expectation-maximization and spectral methods, two other approaches to learning distributions. These connections help establish when the diffusion training objective can support efficient parameter recovery. The contribution makes progress from assuming score estimation is possible to proving that a concrete training algorithm succeeds for specified mixture families.
summary.tldr: Gradient descent on the DDPM objective provably recovers spherical Gaussian mixtures under specified initialization and separation conditions.

title: Learning Mixtures of Gaussians Using the DDPM Objective

abstract: Urban mobility analysis has been extensively studied in the past decade using a vast amount of GPS trajectory data, which reveals hidden patterns in movement and human activity within urban landscapes. Despite its significant value, the availability of such datasets often faces limitations due to privacy concerns, proprietary barriers, and quality inconsistencies. To address these challenges, this paper presents a synthetic trajectory dataset with high fidelity, offering a general solution to these data accessibility issues. Specifically, the proposed dataset adopts a diffusion model as its synthesizer, with the primary aim of accurately emulating the spatial-temporal behavior of the original trajectory data. These synthesized data can retain the geo-distribution and statistical properties characteristic of real-world datasets. Through rigorous analysis and case studies, we validate the high similarity and utility between the proposed synthetic trajectory dataset and real-world counterparts. Such validation underscores the practicality of synthetic datasets for urban mobility analysis and advocates for its wider acceptance within the research community. Finally, we publicly release the trajectory synthesizer and datasets, aiming to enhance the quality and availability of synthetic trajectory datasets and encourage continued contributions to this rapidly evolving field. The dataset is released for public online availability https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/SynMob.

paragraphs: GPS trajectories reveal how people move through cities, but useful datasets can be difficult to access because of privacy concerns, ownership restrictions, and inconsistent quality. SynMob addresses accessibility by creating synthetic trajectories intended to preserve important characteristics of real movement data. The contribution includes both a trajectory-generating system and publicly released datasets.

The synthesizer uses a diffusion model to emulate spatial and temporal behavior in the original trajectories. Its goal is for generated data to retain geographic distributions and statistical properties characteristic of real datasets. These properties matter because urban mobility analysis depends on patterns across locations and time, rather than simply on producing plausible-looking individual routes.

Analyses and case studies find high similarity and useful correspondence between the synthetic data and real-world counterparts. These results support using synthetic trajectories for urban mobility analysis in the settings examined. By releasing the synthesizer alongside the data, the authors also provide a basis for further synthetic dataset creation. The reported evidence concerns fidelity and analytical utility, rather than a formal privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: SynMob uses a diffusion model to generate publicly available synthetic GPS trajectories with demonstrated similarity and utility for urban mobility analysis.

title: SynMob: Creating High-Fidelity Synthetic GPS Trajectory Dataset for Urban Mobility Analysis

abstract: Irregularly sampled time series are increasingly prevalent, particularly in medical domains. While various specialized methods have been developed to handle these irregularities, effectively modeling their complex dynamics and pronounced sparsity remains a challenge. This paper introduces a novel perspective by converting irregularly sampled time series into line graph images, then utilizing powerful pre-trained vision transformers for time series classification in the same way as image classification. This method not only largely simplifies specialized algorithm designs but also presents the potential to serve as a universal framework for time series modeling. Remarkably, despite its simplicity, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art specialized algorithms on several popular healthcare and human activity datasets. Especially in the rigorous leave-sensors-out setting where a portion of variables is omitted during testing, our method exhibits strong robustness against varying degrees of missing observations, achieving an impressive improvement of 42.8% in absolute F1 score points over leading specialized baselines even with half the variables masked. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Leezekun/ViTST.

Specialized models try to handle these patterns directly, but their dynamics remain challenging. This paper takes a visual approach: it converts the measurements into line graph images and treats the resulting prediction problem as image classification.

The method applies pretrained vision transformers to those graphs. This reduces the need for specialized algorithm designs for irregular sampling and creates a way to use pretrained image models for time series classification. The authors suggest that this perspective could potentially support a universal time series modeling framework, while their demonstrated application focuses on classification.

Experiments on healthcare and human activity datasets outperform leading specialized methods. The approach is also robust in leave-sensors-out tests, where variables are absent at evaluation time. With half the variables masked, the paper reports an absolute improvement of 42.8 F1 score points over leading specialized baselines, demonstrating strong performance under that missing-observation setting.
summary.tldr: Turning irregular time series into graph images lets pretrained vision transformers deliver strong classification results, including when many variables are missing.

title: Time Series as Images: Vision Transformer for Irregularly Sampled Time Series

abstract: Chats emerge as an effective user-friendly approach for information retrieval, and are successfully employed in many domains, such as customer service, healthcare, and finance. However, existing image retrieval approaches typically address the case of a single query-to-image round, and the use of chats for image retrieval has been mostly overlooked. In this work, we introduce ChatIR: a chat-based image retrieval system that engages in a conversation with the user to elicit information, in addition to an initial query, in order to clarify the user's search intent. Motivated by the capabilities of today's foundation models, we leverage Large Language Models to generate follow-up questions to an initial image description. These questions form a dialog with the user in order to retrieve the desired image from a large corpus. In this study, we explore the capabilities of such a system tested on a large dataset and reveal that engaging in a dialog yields significant gains in image retrieval. We start by building an evaluation pipeline from an existing manually generated dataset and explore different modules and training strategies for ChatIR. Our comparison includes strong baselines derived from related applications trained with Reinforcement Learning. Our system is capable of retrieving the target image from a pool of 50K images with over 78% success rate after 5 dialogue rounds, compared to 75% when questions are asked by humans, and 64% for a single shot text-to-image retrieval. Extensive evaluations reveal the strong capabilities and examine the limitations of CharIR under different settings. Project repository is available at https://github.com/levymsn/ChatIR.

The user's answers provide additional information for finding the desired image in a large collection.

The system uses a large language model to generate those questions. summary.tldr: ChatIR improves image retrieval by using language-model-generated follow-up questions to clarify the user's search.

title: Chatting Makes Perfect: Chat-based Image Retrieval

abstract: The recently developed sparse network training methods, such as Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) and its variants, have shown impressive learning capacity by finding sparse sub-networks from a dense one. While these methods could largely sparsify deep networks, they generally focus more on realizing comparable accuracy to dense counterparts yet neglect network calibration. However, how to achieve calibrated network predictions lies at the core of improving model reliability, especially when it comes to addressing the overconfident issue and out-of-distribution cases. In this study, we propose a novel Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) framework to achieve an ensemble of lottery tickets towards calibrated network sparsification. Specifically, the proposed DRO ensemble aims to learn multiple diverse and complementary sparse sub-networks (tickets) with the guidance of uncertainty sets, which encourage tickets to gradually capture different data distributions from easy to hard and naturally complement each other. We theoretically justify the strong calibration performance by showing how the proposed robust training process guarantees to lower the confidence of incorrect predictions. Extensive experimental results on several benchmarks show that our proposed lottery ticket ensemble leads to a clear calibration improvement without sacrificing accuracy and burdening inference costs. Furthermore, experiments on OOD datasets demonstrate the robustness of our approach in the open-set environment.

paragraphs: Sparse network training seeks small subnetworks that retain the predictive ability of a larger network. This paper focuses on calibration: whether a model's confidence appropriately reflects its predictions' reliability. Preserving accuracy alone does not address overconfident mistakes, especially when inputs come from outside the training distribution.

The proposed method trains an ensemble of sparse subnetworks, or lottery tickets, through distributionally robust optimization. Uncertainty sets guide the tickets toward different data distributions, progressing from easier to harder ones. This encourages diverse subnetworks whose predictions complement one another. The theoretical analysis explains how the robust training procedure guarantees reduced confidence on incorrect predictions.

Across several benchmarks, the ensemble improves calibration without sacrificing accuracy or adding an inference-cost burden in the reported experiments. Tests on out-of-distribution datasets also demonstrate robustness in an open-set setting. The findings support training sparse models with confidence quality as an explicit concern, and show how diversity among tickets can contribute to that goal.
summary.tldr: A distributionally robust ensemble of sparse subnetworks improves reported calibration while preserving accuracy and avoiding additional inference-cost burdens.

title: Distributionally Robust Ensemble of Lottery Tickets Towards Calibrated Sparse Network Training

abstract: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has shown promising results across several domains. Despite this promise, MARL policies often lack robustness and are therefore sensitive to small changes in their environment. This presents a serious concern for the real world deployment of MARL algorithms, where the testing environment may slightly differ from the training environment. In this work we show that we can gain robustness by controlling a policy’s Lipschitz constant, and under mild conditions, establish the existence of a Lipschitz and close-to-optimal policy. Motivated by these insights, we propose a new robust MARL framework, ERNIE, that promotes the Lipschitz continuity of the policies with respect to the state observations and actions by adversarial regularization. The ERNIE framework provides robustness against noisy observations, changing transition dynamics, and malicious actions of agents. However, ERNIE’s adversarial regularization may introduce some training instability. To reduce this instability, we reformulate adversarial regularization as a Stackelberg game. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework with extensive experiments in traffic light control and particle environments. In addition, we extend ERNIE to mean-field MARL with a formulation based on distributionally robust optimization that outperforms its non-robust counterpart and is of independent interest. Our code is available at https://github.com/abukharin3/ERNIE.

Together, the theory and algorithms connect smoother policy responses with practical robustness, while explicitly addressing the training difficulties introduced by the robustness mechanism.
summary.tldr: ERNIE improves multi-agent policy robustness through adversarial regularization and uses a game formulation to reduce training instability.

title: Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Adversarial Regularization: Theoretical Foundation and Stable Algorithms

abstract: Recent research has observed that in machine learning optimization, gradient descent (GD) often operates at the edge of stability (EoS) [Cohen et al., 2021], where the stepsizes are set to be large, resulting in non-monotonic losses induced by the GD iterates. This paper studies the convergence and implicit bias of constant-stepsize GD for logistic regression on linearly separable data in the EoS regime. Despite the presence of local oscillations, we prove that the logistic loss can be minimized by GD with any constant stepsize over a long time scale. Furthermore, we prove that with any constant stepsize, the GD iterates tend to infinity when projected to a max-margin direction (the hard-margin SVM direction) and converge to a fixed vector that minimizes a strongly convex potential when projected to the orthogonal complement of the max-margin direction. In contrast, we also show that in the EoS regime, GD iterates may diverge catastrophically under the exponential loss, highlighting the superiority of the logistic loss. These theoretical findings are in line with numerical simulations and complement existing theories on the convergence and implicit bias of GD for logistic regression, which are only applicable when the stepsizes are sufficiently small.

paragraphs: Large gradient-descent steps can make training loss oscillate instead of decreasing at every iteration. This paper studies that edge-of-stability behavior for logistic regression on linearly separable data. It asks both whether learning still converges over longer timescales and which solution direction the optimization process implicitly favors.

The authors prove that logistic loss can be minimized over a long timescale with any constant stepsize, despite local oscillations. They also decompose the parameter trajectory into two parts. Its component along the hard-margin support-vector-machine direction grows without bound, while its component perpendicular to that direction converges to a fixed vector minimizing a strongly convex potential.

These findings explain how increasing parameter magnitude and a stable directional preference can coexist with irregular short-term loss behavior. The paper also shows that exponential loss may instead lead to catastrophic divergence in this regime. Numerical simulations agree with the theoretical results. The conclusions extend small-stepsize analyses for logistic regression, with linear separability and the choice of loss remaining essential parts of the stated setting.
summary.tldr: For linearly separable logistic regression, any constant gradient-descent stepsize retains long-term loss minimization and a max-margin directional bias.

title: Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent for Logistic Regression at the Edge of Stability

abstract: In _cross-domain few-shot classification_ (CFC), recent works mainly focus on adapting a simple transformation head on top of a frozen pre-trained backbone with few labeled data to project embeddings into a task-specific metric space where classification can be performed by measuring similarities between image instance and prototype representations. Technically, an _assumption_ implicitly adopted in such a framework is that the prototype and image instance embeddings share the same representation transformation. However, in this paper, we find that there naturally exists a gap, which resembles the modality gap, between the prototype and image instance embeddings extracted from the frozen pre-trained backbone, and simply applying the same transformation during the adaptation phase constrains exploring the optimal representation distributions and shrinks the gap between prototype and image representations. To solve this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method, _contrastive prototype-image adaptation_ (CoPA), to adapt different transformations for prototypes and images similarly to CLIP by treating prototypes as text prompts. Extensive experiments on Meta-Dataset demonstrate that CoPA achieves the _state-of-the-art_ performance more efficiently. Meanwhile, further analyses also indicate that CoPA can learn better representation clusters, enlarge the gap, and achieve the minimum validation loss at the enlarged gap.

paragraphs: Cross-domain few-shot classification adapts a model to a new classification task using few labeled examples. A common approach freezes the pretrained backbone and learns a transformation that makes image embeddings comparable to class prototypes. This paper questions the implicit assumption that prototypes and individual images should undergo the same transformation.

The authors identify a representation gap between prototypes and image instances produced by the frozen backbone. Applying one shared transformation restricts the distributions that adaptation can explore and shrinks that gap. Their proposed contrastive prototype-image adaptation method, CoPA, learns different transformations for the two representation types, treating prototypes analogously to text prompts in CLIP.

Experiments on Meta-Dataset report state-of-the-art performance with greater efficiency. Additional analyses find better representation clusters and an enlarged prototype-image gap, with the lowest validation loss occurring at that enlarged gap. These findings suggest that forcing the two representation types closer together can be counterproductive in this setting; separate transformations allow their distinct roles to be preserved during adaptation.
summary.tldr: CoPA improves cross-domain few-shot classification by adapting class prototypes and image embeddings with separate transformations.

title: Mind the Gap Between Prototypes and Images in Cross-domain Finetuning

abstract: The efficacy of video generation models heavily depends on the quality of their training datasets. Most previous video generation models are trained on short video clips, while recently there has been increasing interest in training long video generation models directly on longer videos. However, the lack of such high-quality long videos impedes the advancement long video generation. To promote research in long video generation, we desire a new dataset with four key features essential for training long video generation models: (1) long videos covering at least 10 seconds, (2) long-take videos without cuts, (3) large motion and diverse contents, and (4) temporally dense captions. To achieve this, we introduce a new pipeline for filtering high-quality long-take videos and generating temporally dense captions. Specifically, we define a set of metrics to quantitatively assess video quality including scene cuts, dynamic degrees, and semantic-level scores, enabling us to filter high-quality long-take videos from a large amount of source videos. Subsequently, we develop a hierarchical video captioning pipeline to annotate long videos with temporally-dense captions. With this pipeline, we curate the first long-take video dataset, LVD-2M, comprising 2 million long-take videos, each covering more than 10 seconds and annotated with temporally dense captions. We further validate the effectiveness of LVD-2M by fine-tuning video generation models to generate long videos with dynamic motions. We believe it will significantly contribute to future research in long video generation.

paragraphs: Training models to generate long videos requires examples that capture events over time. Short clips provide a different kind of training material, and high-quality long videos are scarce. This paper targets videos that last at least ten seconds, contain no cuts, show substantial motion and varied content, and include detailed captions across time.

The authors build a pipeline that filters source videos using quantitative assessments of scene cuts, motion, and semantic content. A hierarchical captioning procedure then supplies temporally dense descriptions for the selected videos. The two stages address complementary needs: choosing suitable continuous footage and describing what happens throughout it.

The resulting LVD-2M dataset contains two million long-take videos, each longer than ten seconds and paired with temporally dense captions. The authors assess its usefulness by fine-tuning video-generation models to produce longer videos with dynamic motion. summary.tldr: LVD-2M provides two million continuous videos longer than ten seconds, with dense temporal captions for long-video generation research.

title: LVD-2M: A Long-take Video Dataset with Temporally Dense Captions

abstract: Robots are often built from standardized assemblies, (e.g. arms, legs, or fingers), but each robot must be trained from scratch to control all the actuators of all the parts together. In this paper we demonstrate a new approach that takes a single robot and its controller as input and produces a set of modular controllers for each of these assemblies such that when a new robot is built from the same parts, its control can be quickly learned by reusing the modular controllers. We achieve this with a framework called MeMo which learns (Me)aningful, (Mo)dular controllers. Specifically, we propose a novel modularity objective to learn an appropriate division of labor among the modules. We demonstrate that this objective can be optimized simultaneously with standard behavior cloning loss via noise injection. We benchmark our framework in locomotion and grasping environments on simple to complex robot morphology transfer. We also show that the modules help in task transfer. On both structure and task transfer, MeMo achieves improved training efficiency to graph neural network and Transformer baselines.

paragraphs: Robots can reuse standard physical assemblies such as arms, legs, and fingers, yet their controllers are often trained from scratch for each overall body. MeMo seeks a similar kind of reuse in control. Given one robot and its controller, it learns separate controller modules associated with assemblies that can later be reused in a new robot built from the same parts.

The key ingredient is a modularity objective that encourages an appropriate division of labor among those controllers. The authors show that noise injection allows this objective to be optimized together with a standard behavior-cloning loss. The training process therefore aims both to reproduce the original controller's behavior and to organize that behavior into useful modules.

Evaluations cover locomotion and grasping, including transfers between robot structures of varying complexity. The modules also help when transferring between tasks. Across structure and task transfer, MeMo improves training efficiency relative to graph neural network and Transformer baselines, supporting controller reuse as a way to learn new combinations more efficiently.
summary.tldr: MeMo uses noise injection to learn reusable controller modules that improve training efficiency when transferring to new robot structures or tasks.

title: MeMo: Meaningful, Modular Controllers via Noise Injection

abstract: The security threat of backdoor attacks is a central concern for deep neural networks (DNNs). Recently, without poisoned data, unlearning models with clean data and then learning a pruning mask have contributed to backdoor defense. Additionally, vanilla fine-tuning with those clean data can help recover the lost clean accuracy. However, the behavior of clean unlearning is still under-explored, and vanilla fine-tuning unintentionally induces back the backdoor effect. In this work, we first investigate model unlearning from the perspective of weight changes and gradient norms, and find two interesting observations in the backdoored model: 1) the weight changes between poison and clean unlearning are positively correlated, making it possible for us to identify the backdoored-related neurons without using poisoned data; 2) the neurons of the backdoored model are more active (*i.e.*, larger gradient norm) than those in the clean model, suggesting the need to suppress the gradient norm during fine-tuning. Then, we propose an effective two-stage defense method. In the first stage, an efficient *Neuron Weight Change (NWC)-based Backdoor Reinitialization* is proposed based on observation 1). In the second stage, based on observation 2), we design an *Activeness-Aware Fine-Tuning* to replace the vanilla fine-tuning. Extensive experiments, involving eight backdoor attacks on three benchmark datasets, demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method compared to recent state-of-the-art backdoor defense approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/linweiii/TSBD.git.

paragraphs: Backdoor defenses can use clean data to unlearn model behavior and identify components to remove, without access to poisoned examples. However, later fine-tuning intended to restore clean accuracy can bring back the backdoor effect. This paper investigates weight changes and gradient norms to guide both identification and recovery.

The authors observe that weight changes during clean-data unlearning correlate positively with changes during poisoned-data unlearning. This makes clean unlearning useful for identifying neurons associated with a backdoor. They also find larger gradient norms in backdoored models than in clean models, suggesting that activity measured this way should be suppressed during fine-tuning.

Second, activeness-aware fine-tuning replaces ordinary fine-tuning to account for the gradient-norm observation. Experiments covering eight attacks on three benchmark datasets report better performance than recent state-of-the-art defenses. The method links two measured behaviors of compromised networks to complementary interventions, addressing both backdoor-related components and their potential reactivation during recovery.
summary.tldr: A two-stage backdoor defense uses clean-unlearning weight changes for reinitialization and activity-aware fine-tuning to reduce backdoor revival.

title: Unveiling and Mitigating Backdoor Vulnerabilities based on Unlearning Weight Changes and Backdoor Activeness

abstract: Learning-based simulators show great potential for simulating particle dynamics when 3D groundtruth is available, but per-particle correspondences are not always accessible. The development of neural rendering presents a new solution to this field to learn 3D dynamics from 2D images by inverse rendering. However, existing approaches still suffer from ill-posed natures resulting from the 2D to 3D uncertainty, for example, specific 2D images can correspond with various 3D particle distributions. To mitigate such uncertainty, we consider a conventional, mechanically interpretable framework as the physical priors and extend it to a learning-based version. In brief, we incorporate the learnable graph kernels into the classic Discrete Element Analysis (DEA) framework to implement a novel mechanics-informed network architecture. In this case, the graph networks are only used for approximating some specific mechanical operators in the DEA framework rather than the whole dynamics mapping. By integrating the strong physics priors, our methods can effectively learn the dynamics of various materials from the partial 2D observations in a unified manner. Experiments show that our approach outperforms other learned simulators by a large margin in this context and is robust to different renderers, fewer training samples, and fewer camera views.

paragraphs: DEL learns three-dimensional particle dynamics from partial two-dimensional observations. Neural rendering makes this possible by connecting simulated 3D configurations to images, but the inverse problem is ambiguous: different particle arrangements can explain the same image. The paper addresses this uncertainty by building a learned simulator around an established mechanical framework.

The architecture extends Discrete Element Analysis with learnable graph kernels. These graph networks approximate particular mechanical operators within the framework, leaving the broader organization of the dynamics grounded in physical structure. This focuses learning on selected components of the simulation and supplies a mechanically interpretable prior for reconstructing dynamics from incomplete visual evidence.

The authors report that this combination learns the dynamics of different materials within a unified approach. In the setting of partial 2D supervision, experiments show a large advantage over other learned simulators. They also demonstrate robustness across renderers and when training samples or camera views are reduced. The results support incorporating strong mechanical structure when visual observations leave the underlying 3D dynamics uncertain.
summary.tldr: DEL combines mechanical simulation structure with learned graph operators to recover 3D particle dynamics from partial 2D observations.

title: DEL: Discrete Element Learner for Learning 3D Particle Dynamics with Neural Rendering

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is critical for deploying machine learning models in the open world. To design scoring functions that discern OOD data from the in-distribution (ID) cases from a pre-trained discriminative model, existing methods tend to make rigorous distributional assumptions either explicitly or implicitly due to the lack of knowledge about the learned feature space in advance. The mismatch between the learned and assumed distributions motivates us to raise a fundamental yet under-explored question: \textit{Is it possible to deterministically model the feature distribution while pre-training a discriminative model?}This paper gives an affirmative answer to this question by presenting a Distributional Representation Learning (\texttt{DRL}) framework for OOD detection. In particular, \texttt{DRL} explicitly enforces the underlying feature space to conform to a pre-defined mixture distribution, together with an online approximation of normalization constants to enable end-to-end training. Furthermore, we formulate \texttt{DRL} into a provably convergent Expectation-Maximization algorithm to avoid trivial solutions and rearrange the sequential sampling to guide the training consistency. Extensive evaluations across mainstream OOD detection benchmarks empirically manifest the superiority of the proposed \texttt{DRL} over its advanced counterparts.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the kinds of data a model was trained to handle. Many detectors assume a particular distribution for a pretrained model’s internal features. This paper targets the mismatch that can arise when those assumptions do not fit the feature space the model actually learned.

Distributional Representation Learning, or DRL, shapes that feature space during pretraining. It explicitly encourages features to follow a predefined mixture distribution, making the distributional model part of representation learning itself. An online approximation of normalization constants enables end-to-end training, connecting the prescribed distribution to the optimization of the discriminative model.

The authors formulate DRL as an Expectation-Maximization algorithm with a convergence proof, addressing trivial solutions, and rearrange sequential sampling to support training consistency. Evaluations on mainstream out-of-distribution detection benchmarks report improvements over advanced comparison methods. The approach’s significance is that it brings feature learning and detection assumptions into the same training framework, with empirical evidence that this coordination improves detection in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: DRL trains model features to follow a predefined mixture distribution, aligning representation learning with out-of-distribution detection.

title: Learning to Shape In-distribution Feature Space for Out-of-distribution Detection

abstract: The state space models, employing recursively propagated features, demonstrate strong representation capabilities comparable to Transformer models and superior efficiency.However, constrained by the inherent geometric constraints of sequences, it still falls short in modeling long-range dependencies.To address this issue, we propose the MambaTree network, which first dynamically generates a tree topology based on spatial relationships and input features.Then, feature propagation is performed based on this graph, thereby breaking the original sequence constraints to achieve stronger representation capabilities.Additionally, we introduce a linear complexity dynamic programming algorithm to enhance long-range interactions without increasing computational cost.MambaTree is a versatile multimodal framework that can be applied to both visual and textual tasks.Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing structured state space models on image classification, object detection and segmentation.Besides, by fine-tuning large language models, our approach achieves consistent improvements in multiple textual tasks at minor training cost.

paragraphs: State space models propagate information recursively and can provide strong representations efficiently. The paper argues that organizing this propagation along a sequence restricts how well distant inputs interact. MambaTree changes the structure over which features move, aiming to improve long-range dependencies while retaining the computational appeal of state space modeling.

For each input, the network dynamically constructs a tree using spatial relationships and input features. It then propagates features along that tree, moving beyond the original sequence geometry. A dynamic programming algorithm performs the computation with linear complexity, supporting stronger long-range interactions without increasing the computational cost as described by the authors.

The framework applies to both images and text. Experiments report significant improvements over existing structured state space models in image classification, object detection, and segmentation. Fine-tuning large language models with the approach also produces consistent gains across multiple text tasks at a small training cost. The results support changing information-flow structure as a useful design choice across the evaluated modalities.
summary.tldr: MambaTree propagates features through an input-dependent tree to improve long-range interactions while retaining linear computational complexity.

title: MambaTree: Tree Topology is All You Need in State Space Model

abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are amortized samplers of unnormalized distributions over compositional objects with applications to causal discovery, NLP, and drug design. Recently, it was shown that GFlowNets can be framed as a hierarchical variational inference (HVI) method for discrete distributions. Despite this equivalence, attempts to train GFlowNets using traditional divergence measures as learning objectives were unsuccessful. Instead, current approaches for training these models rely on minimizing the log-squared difference between a proposal (forward policy) and a target (backward policy) distributions. In this work, we first formally extend the relationship between GFlowNets and HVI to distributions on arbitrary measurable topological spaces. Then, we empirically show that the ineffectiveness of divergence-based learning of GFlowNets is due to large gradient variance of the corresponding stochastic objectives. To address this issue, we devise a collection of provably variance-reducing control variates for gradient estimation based on the REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator. Our experimental results suggest that the resulting algorithms often accelerate training convergence when compared against previous approaches. All in all, our work contributes by narrowing the gap between GFlowNet training and HVI, paving the way for algorithmic advancements inspired by the divergence minimization viewpoint.

Recently, it was shown that GFlowNets can be framed as a hierarchical variational inference (HVI) method for discrete distributions. Despite this equivalence, attempts to train GFlowNets using traditional divergence measures as learning objectives were unsuccessful. Instead, current approaches for training these models rely on minimizing the log-squared difference between a proposal (forward policy) and a target (backward policy) distributions. In this work, we first formally extend the relationship between GFlowNets and HVI to distributions on arbitrary measurable topological spaces. Then, we empirically show that the ineffectiveness of divergence-based learning of GFlowNets is due to large gradient variance of the corresponding stochastic objectives. To address this issue, we devise a collection of provably variance-reducing control variates for gradient estimation based on the REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator. Our experimental results suggest that the resulting algorithms often accelerate training convergence when compared against previous approaches. All in all, our work contributes by narrowing the gap between GFlowNet training and HVI, paving the way for algorithmic advancements inspired by the divergence minimization viewpoint.

paragraphs: GFlowNets learn reusable samplers for distributions over objects assembled through a sequence of decisions. Although they are connected to hierarchical variational inference, traditional divergence-based training objectives have proved ineffective in earlier attempts. Common training methods instead minimize squared differences between log quantities associated with forward and backward policies. This paper investigates the gap between the theoretical connection and practical training.

The authors first extend the connection beyond discrete distributions to arbitrary measurable topological spaces. They then provide empirical evidence that high variance in stochastic gradient estimates explains the difficulty of divergence-based learning. To reduce that noise, they develop control variates based on the REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator and prove that these adjustments reduce variance.

Experiments suggest that the resulting algorithms often converge faster than previous approaches. That is a qualified empirical finding, rather than a guarantee of faster training in every setting. The broader contribution is to make divergence minimization a more practical route for GFlowNet training, bringing its algorithms closer to the variational inference framework already linked to them theoretically.
summary.tldr: Variance-reducing gradient estimators make divergence-based GFlowNet training more effective and often accelerate convergence in the reported experiments.

title: On Divergence Measures for Training GFlowNets

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a prevalent machine learning paradigm designed to address challenges posed by heterogeneous client data while preserving data privacy. Unlike distributed training, it typically orchestrates resource-constrained edge devices to communicate via a low-bandwidth communication network with a central server. This urges the development of more computation and communication efficient training algorithms. In this paper, we propose an efficient FL paradigm, where the local models in the clients are trained with low-precision operations and communicated with the server in low precision format, while only the model aggregation in the server is performed with high-precision computation. We surprisingly find that high precision models can be recovered from the low precision local models with proper aggregation in the server. In this way, both the workload in the client-side and the communication cost can be significantly reduced. We theoretically show that our proposed paradigm can converge to the optimal solution as the training goes on, which demonstrates that low precision local training is enough for FL. Our paradigm can be integrated with existing FL algorithms flexibly. Experiments across extensive benchmarks are conducted to showcase the effectiveness of our proposed method. Notably, the models trained by our method with the precision as low as 8 bits are comparable to those from the full precision training. As a by-product, we show that low precision local training can relieve the over-fitting issue in local training, which under heterogeneous client data can cause the client models drift further away from each other and lead to the failure in model aggregation. Code is released at https://github.com/digbangbang/LPT-FL.

This paper proposes reducing numerical precision in both local training and model communication. They provide a theoretical convergence result showing that their proposed paradigm can approach the optimal solution as training continues. The approach can also be incorporated into existing federated learning algorithms, offering a way to reduce client workload and communication costs.

The authors also find that low-precision local training can reduce local overfitting. With heterogeneous client data, such overfitting can push clients’ models farther apart and undermine aggregation, so this effect addresses an additional difficulty beyond resource consumption.
summary.tldr: Low-precision client training and communication, paired with high-precision server aggregation, produce competitive federated models while reducing resource demands.

title: Low Precision Local Training is Enough for Federated Learning

abstract: Given the vast number of classifiers that have been (and continue to be) proposed, reliable methods for comparing them are becoming increasingly important. The desire for reliability is broken down into three main aspects: (1) Comparisons should allow for different quality metrics simultaneously. (2) Comparisons should take into account the statistical uncertainty induced by the choice of benchmark suite. (3) The robustness of the comparisons under small deviations in the underlying assumptions should be verifiable. To address (1), we propose to compare classifiers using a generalized stochastic dominance ordering (GSD) and present the GSD-front as an information-efficient alternative to the classical Pareto-front. For (2), we propose a consistent statistical estimator for the GSD-front and construct a statistical test for whether a (potentially new) classifier lies in the GSD-front of a set of state-of-the-art classifiers. For (3), we relax our proposed test using techniques from robust statistics and imprecise probabilities. We illustrate our concepts on the benchmark suite PMLB and on the platform OpenML.

paragraphs: Comparing classifiers reliably involves more than choosing a single score. This paper addresses three requirements: considering multiple quality metrics, accounting for uncertainty from the benchmark suite, and checking robustness to small changes in assumptions. It develops a statistical framework that brings these requirements into the comparison process.

The framework uses generalized stochastic dominance to order classifiers and introduces the GSD-front as an information-efficient alternative to the classical Pareto-front. The authors provide a consistent estimator for this front and a statistical test for whether a classifier belongs to it. This includes assessing a potentially new classifier against a collection of state-of-the-art alternatives.

To examine robustness, the authors relax the test using tools from robust statistics and imprecise probabilities. They illustrate the framework using PMLB and OpenML. The contribution makes uncertainty and assumptions part of multicriteria benchmarking, allowing claims about competitive classifiers to be assessed statistically while retaining the fact that quality is being judged along several dimensions.
summary.tldr: The GSD-front provides a statistical framework for comparing classifiers across multiple metrics while accounting for benchmark uncertainty and assumption sensitivity.

title: Statistical Multicriteria Benchmarking via the GSD-Front

abstract: The expressive power of graph learning architectures based on the $k$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman ($k$-WL) hierarchy is well understood. However, such architectures often fail to deliver solid predictive performance on real-world tasks, limiting their practical impact. In contrast, global attention-based models such as graph transformers demonstrate strong performance in practice, but comparing their expressive power with the $k$-WL hierarchy remains challenging, particularly since these architectures rely on positional or structural encodings for their expressivity and predictive performance. To address this, we show that the recently proposed Edge Transformer, a global attention model operating on node pairs instead of nodes, has 3-WL expressive power when provided with the right tokenization. Empirically, we demonstrate that the Edge Transformer surpasses other theoretically aligned architectures regarding predictive performance while not relying on positional or structural encodings.

This paper analyzes the Edge Transformer, a global-attention architecture that operates on pairs of nodes rather than individual nodes. The authors show that it has 3-WL expressive power when supplied with the appropriate tokenization. That condition is central: the theoretical characterization depends on how graph information is represented for the model to process.

Empirical results show the Edge Transformer outperforming other theoretically aligned architectures without relying on positional or structural encodings. The contribution brings a practical attention model into a familiar theoretical framework while also testing its predictive behavior. Together, the proof and experiments connect a specific representation choice, a clear expressivity characterization, and strong performance in the evaluated graph-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: With appropriate tokenization, the Edge Transformer has 3-WL expressive power and performs strongly without positional or structural encodings.

title: Towards Principled Graph Transformers

abstract: The influence maximization (IM) problem aims to identify a budgeted set of nodes with the highest potential to influence the largest number of users in a cascade model, a key challenge in viral marketing. Traditional \emph{IM} approaches consider each user/node independently as a potential target customer. However, in many scenarios, the target customers comprise motifs, where activating only one or a few users within a motif is insufficient for effective viral marketing, which, nevertheless, receives little attention. For instance, if a motif of three friends planning to dine together, targeting all three simultaneously is crucial for a restaurant advertisement to succeed.In this paper, we address the motif-oriented influence maximization problem under the linear threshold model. We prove that the motif-oriented IM problem is NP-hard and that the influence function is neither supermodular nor submodular, in contrast to the classical \emph{IM} setting.To simplify the problem, we establish the submodular upper and lower bounds for the influence function. By leveraging the submodular property, we propose a natural greedy strategy that simultaneously maximizes both bounds. Our algorithm has an approximation ratio of $\tau\cdot (1-1/e-\varepsilon)$ and a near-linear time complexity of $O((k+l)(m+\eta)\log \eta/\varepsilon^2)$.Experimental results on diverse datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach in motif maximization.

paragraphs: Influence maximization selects a limited set of people to start a cascade that reaches many others. This paper studies situations where success depends on activating an entire connected group, or motif. For example, an advertisement aimed at friends planning a meal may need to influence all of them to achieve its purpose.

Under the linear threshold model, the authors prove that this motif-oriented problem is NP-hard. They also show that its influence function is neither submodular nor supermodular, so it lacks structural properties that could simplify optimization. To make progress, they construct submodular upper and lower bounds on the function and propose a greedy strategy that maximizes both bounds simultaneously.

The algorithm has a stated approximation ratio of tau times one minus one over e minus epsilon, together with near-linear time complexity. Experiments on diverse datasets support its effectiveness at maximizing activated motifs. The paper's contribution is to align the optimization target with group-level marketing success and provide an algorithm with theoretical guarantees for this harder objective.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a greedy algorithm with approximation guarantees for spreading influence to whole social-network motifs rather than counting users individually.

title: Motif-oriented influence maximization for viral marketing in large-scale social networks

abstract: Training generalist agents capable of solving diverse tasks is challenging, often requiring large datasets of expert demonstrations. This is particularly problematic in robotics, where each data point requires physical execution of actions in the real world. Thus, there is a pressing need for architectures that can effectively leverage the available training data. In this work, we present BAKU, a simple transformer architecture that enables efficient learning of multi-task robot policies. BAKU builds upon recent advancements in offline imitation learning and meticulously combines observation trunks, action chunking, multi-sensory observations, and action heads to substantially improve upon prior work. Our experiments on 129 simulated tasks across LIBERO, Meta-World suite, and the Deepmind Control suite exhibit an overall 18% absolute improvement over RT-1 and MT-ACT, with a 36% improvement on the harder LIBERO benchmark. On 30 real-world manipulation tasks, given an average of just 17 demonstrations per task, BAKU achieves a 91% success rate. Videos of the robot are best viewed at baku-robot.github.io.

paragraphs: Teaching a robot many tasks often requires substantial collections of expert demonstrations. Collecting those demonstrations is costly because actions must be physically performed. BAKU addresses this challenge through the design of the policy architecture, aiming to extract more useful learning from available demonstrations while supporting multiple tasks within one transformer-based system.

The architecture combines components from offline imitation learning: observation-processing trunks, multiple sensory inputs, action heads, and action chunking. Action chunking organizes outputs into groups of actions. The contribution is the careful combination of these components into a simple architecture for learning robot policies, with attention to how observations become actions across different tasks.

Across 129 simulated tasks from LIBERO, Meta-World, and the DeepMind Control suite, the authors report an overall absolute improvement of 18% over RT-1 and MT-ACT, and a 36% improvement on the harder LIBERO benchmark. On 30 real-world manipulation tasks, BAKU reaches 91% success with an average of 17 demonstrations per task. These results support its effectiveness in the evaluated settings where demonstrations are relatively scarce.
summary.tldr: BAKU combines transformer policy components to improve multitask robot learning, achieving 91% success on 30 real-world tasks.

title: BAKU: An Efficient Transformer for Multi-Task Policy Learning

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated decent generation quality, yet their deployment in federated learning scenarios remains challenging. Due to data heterogeneity and a large number of parameters, conventional parameter averaging schemes often fail to achieve stable collaborative training of diffusion models. We reframe collaborative synthetic data generation as a cooperative sampling procedure from a mixture of decentralized distributions, each encoded by a pre-trained local diffusion model. This leverages the connection between diffusion and energy-based models, which readily supports compositional generation thereof. Consequently, we can directly obtain refined synthetic dataset, optionally with differential privacy guarantee, even without exchanging diffusion model parameters. Our framework reduces communication overhead while maintaining the generation quality, realized through an unadjusted Langevin algorithm with a convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: Collaboratively training diffusion models across decentralized data sources is difficult when those sources contain different kinds of data. The models also have many parameters, making conventional parameter averaging an unstable way to combine their learning. This paper changes the collaborative task from merging model parameters to jointly generating a synthetic dataset.

Each source contributes through a pretrained local diffusion model representing its own data distribution. The framework treats generation as sampling from a mixture of these decentralized distributions. It uses the relationship between diffusion models and energy-based models to support this composition, allowing the participants to produce a refined synthetic dataset without exchanging diffusion model parameters.

The sampling procedure uses an unadjusted Langevin algorithm, for which the authors provide a convergence guarantee. The framework reduces communication overhead while maintaining generation quality, and it can optionally provide differential privacy. Privacy is therefore an available configuration rather than an automatic property of every use. The contribution offers a way to collaborate through generated data while keeping the locally trained diffusion models separate.
summary.tldr: The framework combines local diffusion distributions through cooperative sampling to generate synthetic data without exchanging model parameters.

title: Diffusion Federated Dataset

abstract: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) ensure interpretability by decomposing predictions into human interpretable concepts. Yet the annotations used for training CBMs that enable this transparency are often noisy, and the impact of such corruption is not well understood. In this study, we present the first systematic study of noise in CBMs and show that even moderate corruption simultaneously impairs prediction performance, interpretability, and the intervention effectiveness. Our analysis identifies a susceptible subset of concepts whose accuracy declines far more than the average gap between noisy and clean supervision and whose corruption accounts for most performance loss. To mitigate this vulnerability we propose a two-stage framework. During training, sharpness-aware minimization stabilizes the learning of noise-sensitive concepts. During inference, where clean labels are unavailable, we rank concepts by predictive entropy and correct only the most uncertain ones, using uncertainty as a proxy for susceptibility. Theoretical analysis and extensive ablations elucidate why sharpness-aware training confers robustness and why uncertainty reliably identifies susceptible concepts, providing a principled basis that preserves both interpretability and resilience in the presence of noise.

Their usefulness therefore depends on learning those concepts reliably, even when the annotations used for supervision contain mistakes. This study finds that moderate annotation corruption can damage prediction accuracy, interpretability, and the effectiveness of interventions on the concepts.

The damage is concentrated in a particularly susceptible subset of concepts. Their accuracy deteriorates much more than the average difference between clean and noisy supervision, and their corruption accounts for most of the performance loss. At inference, when clean labels are unavailable, predictive entropy ranks concepts by uncertainty so that correction focuses on the most uncertain ones. Theoretical analysis and ablations support both the robustness mechanism and uncertainty as a proxy for susceptibility. The stated result links preserving the model's interpretable intermediate representation with maintaining its predictive resilience.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies noise-sensitive concepts and combines robust training with uncertainty-guided correction to protect concept bottleneck models.

title: An Analysis of Concept Bottleneck Models: Measuring, Understanding, and Mitigating the Impact of Noisy Annotations

abstract: Recent advances in 3D point cloud transformers have led to state-of-the-art results in tasks such as semantic segmentation and reconstruction. However, these models typically rely on dense token representations, incurring high computational and memory costs during training and inference. In this work, we present the finding that tokens are remarkably redundant, leading to substantial inefficiency. We introduce an efficient token merging method and illustrate that it can reduce the token count by up to 90–95% while maintaining competitive performance. This finding challenges the prevailing assumption that more tokens inherently yield better performance and highlights that many current models are over-tokenized and under-optimized for scalability. We validate our method across multiple 3D vision tasks and show consistent improvements in computational efficiency. This work is the first to assess redundancy in large-scale 3D transformer models, providing insights into the development of more efficient 3D foundation architectures. Our code and checkpoints are publicly available at https://gitmerge3d.github.io.

paragraphs: Transformers for 3D point clouds often represent scenes with dense collections of tokens. These representations have supported strong results in tasks such as segmentation and reconstruction, but they also impose substantial computation and memory costs. This paper asks whether the large token counts actually provide enough useful information to justify that expense.

The authors find considerable redundancy and introduce a token-merging method to reduce it. Their approach can remove up to 90–95% of tokens while retaining competitive performance. The key implication is that the number of tokens alone is a poor guide to the usefulness of a representation: much of the processing in the studied models can be spent on redundant information.

Evaluations across multiple 3D vision tasks show consistent improvements in computational efficiency. The reported reductions are achievable results rather than a guarantee for every model or task. Together, the findings challenge the assumption that denser tokenization inherently improves performance and motivate more efficient token representations for large-scale 3D foundation architectures.
summary.tldr: A token-merging method cuts token counts by up to 90–95% in tested 3D point-cloud Transformers while preserving competitive performance.

title: How Many Tokens Do 3D Point Cloud Transformer Architectures Really Need?

abstract: We propose Flow-GRPO, the first method to integrate online policy gradient reinforcement learning (RL) into flow matching models. Our approach uses two key strategies: (1) an ODE-to-SDE conversion that transforms a deterministic Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) into an equivalent Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) that matches the original model's marginal distribution at all timesteps, enabling statistical sampling for RL exploration; and (2) a Denoising Reduction strategy that reduces training denoising steps while retaining the original number of inference steps, significantly improving sampling efficiency without sacrificing performance. Empirically, Flow-GRPO is effective across multiple text-to-image tasks. For compositional generation, RL-tuned SD3.5-M generates nearly perfect object counts, spatial relations, and fine-grained attributes, increasing GenEval accuracy from $63\%$ to $95\%$. In visual text rendering, accuracy improves from $59\%$ to $92\%$, greatly enhancing text generation. Flow-GRPO also achieves substantial gains in human preference alignment. Notably, very little reward hacking occurred, meaning rewards did not increase at the cost of appreciable image quality or diversity degradation.

The challenge addressed by its first mechanism is that a deterministic generation process does not directly provide the stochastic exploration used by reinforcement learning. The method converts the model's ordinary differential equation into a stochastic differential equation while preserving its marginal distribution at every timestep.

A second mechanism reduces the number of denoising steps used during training while keeping the original inference-step count. The authors report that this makes sampling more efficient without sacrificing performance. summary.tldr: Flow-GRPO enables online reinforcement learning for flow matching and substantially improves the reported text-to-image generation results.

title: Flow-GRPO: Training Flow Matching Models via Online RL

abstract: Semantic segmentation neural networks (SSNs) are increasingly essential in high-stakes fields such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and environmental monitoring, where robustness to input uncertainties and adversarial examples is crucial for ensuring safety and reliability. However, traditional probabilistic verification methods struggle to scale effectively with the size and depth of modern SSNs, especially when dealing with their high-dimensional, structured inputs/outputs. As the output dimension increases, these methods tend to become overly conservative, resulting in unnecessarily restrictive safety guarantees. In this work, we propose a probabilistic, data-driven verification algorithm that is architecture-agnostic and scalable, capable of handling the high-dimensional outputs of SSNs without introducing conservative and loose guarantees. We leverage efficient sampling-based reachability analysis to explore the space of possible outputs while maintaining computational feasibility. Our methodology is based on Conformal Inference (CI), which is known for its high data efficiency. However, CI tends to be overly conservative in high-dimensional spaces. To address this, in this paper, we introduce techniques to mitigate these sources of conservatism, enabling us to provide less conservative yet provable guarantees for SSNs. We validate our approach on large segmentation models applied to CamVid, OCTA-500 and Lung\_Segmentation, and Cityscapes datasets, showing that it can offer reliable safety guarantees while lowering the conservatism inherent in traditional methods. We also provide a public GitHub repository for this approach, to support reproducibility.

This paper develops a data-driven verification algorithm intended to handle large segmentation models without that degree of looseness.

The method is architecture-agnostic, allowing its verification strategy to apply across network designs.

Evaluations use large segmentation models on CamVid, OCTA-500, Lung_Segmentation, and Cityscapes. The authors report reliable safety guarantees with less conservatism than traditional methods. The contribution is a way to make probabilistic robustness analysis more computationally practical and informative for structured prediction, where overly broad output uncertainty can otherwise limit the usefulness of verification.
summary.tldr: A sampling-based conformal verification method provides less conservative probabilistic robustness guarantees for large semantic segmentation networks.

title: Scaling Data-Driven Probabilistic Robustness Analysis for Semantic Segmentation Neural Networks

abstract: Harmful fine-tuning poses critical safety risks to fine-tuning-as-a-service for large language models. Existing defense strategies preemptively build robustness via attack simulation but suffer from fundamental limitations: (i) the infeasibility of extending attack simulations beyond bounded threat models due to the inherent difficulty of anticipating unknown attacks, and (ii) limited adaptability to varying attack settings, as simulation fails to capture their variability and complexity. To address these challenges, we propose Bayesian Data Scheduler (BDS), an adaptive tuning-stage defense strategy with no need for attack simulation. BDS formulates harmful fine-tuning defense as a Bayesian inference problem, learning the posterior distribution of each data point's safety attribute, conditioned on the fine-tuning and alignment datasets. The fine-tuning process is then constrained by weighting data with their safety attributes sampled from the posterior, thus mitigating the influence of harmful data. By leveraging the post hoc nature of Bayesian inference, the posterior is conditioned on the fine-tuning dataset, enabling BDS to tailor its defense to the specific dataset, thereby achieving adaptive defense. Furthermore, we introduce a neural scheduler based on amortized Bayesian learning, enabling efficient transfer to new data without retraining. Comprehensive results across diverse attack and defense settings demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our approach. Code is available at https://github.com/Egg-Hu/Bayesian-Data-Scheduler.

paragraphs: Harmful fine-tuning can undermine a language model’s safety behavior after its initial alignment. Existing defenses often prepare by simulating attacks, but those simulations cover bounded threats and may not capture unfamiliar attack settings. This paper introduces Bayesian Data Scheduler, a defense that adapts during fine-tuning without requiring attack simulation.

The method treats each training example’s safety as something uncertain that must be inferred. It learns a posterior distribution over that safety attribute using both the fine-tuning dataset and alignment data. Training examples receive weights based on safety attributes sampled from these distributions, reducing the influence of harmful data during the tuning process.

Because the inference incorporates the actual fine-tuning dataset, the defense can respond to that dataset’s characteristics. A neural scheduler trained through amortized Bayesian learning supports efficient transfer to new data without retraining. Across diverse evaluated attack and defense settings, the authors report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is an adaptive way to constrain training using inferred data safety, with effectiveness demonstrated across the studied settings.
summary.tldr: Bayesian Data Scheduler adapts fine-tuning defenses by inferring each example’s safety and weighting its training influence without simulated attacks.

title: Adaptive Defense against Harmful Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models via Bayesian Data Scheduler

abstract: The advent of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has expanded AI capabilities to visual modalities, yet existing evaluation benchmarks remain limited to single-video understanding, overlooking the critical need for multi-video understanding in real-world scenarios (e.g., sports analytics and autonomous driving). To address this significant gap, we introduce **MVU-Eval**, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating **M**ulti-**V**ideo **U**nderstanding for MLLMs. Specifically, our MVU-Eval mainly assesses eight core competencies through 1,824 meticulously curated question-answer pairs spanning 4,959 videos from diverse domains, addressing both fundamental perception tasks and high-order reasoning tasks. These capabilities are rigorously aligned with real-world applications such as multi-sensor synthesis in autonomous systems and cross-angle sports analytics. Through extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art open-source and closed-source models, we reveal significant performance discrepancies and limitations in current MLLMs' ability to perform understanding across multiple videos.The benchmark will be made publicly available to foster future research.
