paragraphs: MVU-Eval tests how well multimodal language models understand information spread across multiple videos. Existing evaluations centered on single videos leave this capability insufficiently examined. Applications such as sports analysis across camera angles and synthesis of multiple sensors require models to combine evidence across video inputs.

The benchmark contains 1,824 curated question-answer pairs spanning 4,959 videos from varied domains. It assesses eight competencies, covering both basic perception and more demanding reasoning. The authors align these abilities with practical uses, including cross-angle sports analysis and multi-sensor interpretation in autonomous systems. This gives the evaluation a broader target than recognizing content within an isolated clip.

Tests of leading open-source and closed-source models reveal substantial differences in performance and limitations in multi-video understanding. The findings show that this setting exposes capabilities that need direct evaluation rather than being inferred from single-video results. The paper’s main contribution is a structured benchmark for measuring those abilities and comparing systems; it does not introduce a model that resolves the observed weaknesses.
summary.tldr: MVU-Eval tests eight multi-video understanding competencies and reveals substantial performance gaps among current multimodal language models.

title: MVU-Eval: Towards Multi-Video Understanding Evaluation for Multimodal LLMs

abstract: Generative models for structure-based drug design are often limited to a specific modality, restricting their broader applicability. To address this challenge, we introduce FuncBind, a framework based on computer vision to generate target-conditioned, all-atom molecules across atomic systems. FuncBind uses neural fields to represent molecules as continuous atomic densities and employs score-based generative models with modern architectures adapted from the computer vision literature. This modality-agnostic representation allows a single unified model to be trained on diverse atomic systems, from small to large molecules, and handle variable atom/residue counts, including non-canonical amino acids. FuncBind achieves competitive in silico performance in generating small molecules, macrocyclic peptides, and antibody complementarity-determining region loops, conditioned on target structures. FuncBind also generated in vitro novel antibody binders via de novo redesign of the complementarity-determining region H3 loop of two chosen co-crystal structures. As a final contribution, we introduce a new dataset and benchmark for structure-conditioned macrocyclic peptide generation.

paragraphs: Generative models for structure-based drug design often specialize in one molecular category, limiting their broader use. FuncBind introduces a shared representation for generating target-conditioned molecules across different atomic systems. It represents molecules as continuous atomic densities through neural fields and uses score-based generative models with architectures adapted from computer vision.

This representation allows a single model to train on both small and large molecular systems. It accommodates varying numbers of atoms or residues, including non-canonical amino acids. The authors report competitive computational performance for target-conditioned generation of small molecules, macrocyclic peptides, and antibody complementarity-determining region loops, demonstrating the framework across substantially different molecular forms.

This supplies experimental evidence for those antibody-design cases alongside the broader computational evaluations. Finally, the authors introduce a dataset and benchmark for structure-conditioned macrocyclic peptide generation, extending the contribution from a unified generation framework to an additional resource for evaluating molecular design.
summary.tldr: FuncBind uses continuous atomic-density representations to generate diverse target-conditioned molecules, with competitive computational results and experimentally tested antibody binders.

title: Unified all-atom molecule generation with neural fields

abstract: Measuring the alignment between representations lets us understand similarities between the feature spaces of different models, such as Vision Transformers trained under diverse paradigms. However, traditional measures for representational alignment yield only scalar values that obscure how these spaces agree in terms of learned features. To address this, we combine alignment analysis with concept discovery, allowing a fine-grained breakdown of alignment into individual concepts. This approach reveals both universal concepts across models and each representation’s internal concept structure. We introduce a new definition of concepts as non-linear manifolds, hypothesizing they better capture the geometry of the feature space. A sanity check demonstrates the advantage of this manifold-based definition over linear baselines for concept-based alignment. Finally, our alignment analysis of four different ViTs shows that increased supervision tends to reduce semantic organization in learned representations.

paragraphs: Comparing two models often involves reducing the similarity of their internal representations to one number. That number summarizes agreement, but it does not explain which learned features the models share. This paper combines representation comparison with concept discovery to make those similarities more interpretable.

The method breaks alignment down into individual concepts, exposing both concepts shared across models and the organization of concepts within each model. The authors define concepts as nonlinear manifolds: structures that can follow curved shapes within a representation space. They hypothesize that this definition fits the geometry of learned features better than linear alternatives. A sanity check supports its advantage for the concept-based comparison they study.

The authors apply the analysis to four vision transformers. In this comparison, greater supervision tends to accompany less semantic organization in the learned representations. The finding is a tendency in the studied models, while the broader contribution is a way to explain what representational agreement consists of instead of reporting only its overall magnitude.
summary.tldr: Concept-based alignment reveals which features vision transformers share and how those features are organized.

title: Beyond Scalars: Concept-Based Alignment Analysis in Vision Transformers

abstract: The Conditional Sequence Modeling (CSM) paradigm, benefiting from the transformer's powerful distribution modeling capabilities, has demonstrated considerable promise in Reinforcement Learning (RL) tasks. However, much of the work has focused on applying CSM to single online or offline settings, with the general architecture rarely explored. Additionally, existing methods primarily focus on deterministic trajectory modeling, overlooking the randomness of state transitions and the diversity of future trajectory distributions. Fortunately, value-based methods offer a viable solution for CSM, further bridging the potential gap between offline and online RL. In this paper, we propose Value-Guided Decision Transformer (VDT), which leverages value functions to perform advantage-weighting and behavior regularization on the Decision Transformer (DT), guiding the policy toward upper-bound optimal decisions during the offline training phase. In the online tuning phase, VDT further integrates value-based policy improvement with behavior cloning under the CSM architecture through limited interaction and data collection, achieving performance improvement within minimal timesteps. The predictive capability of value functions for future returns is also incorporated into the sampling process. Our method achieves competitive performance on various standard RL benchmarks, providing a feasible solution for developing CSM architectures in general scenarios. Code is available at here.

paragraphs: Decision Transformers approach reinforcement learning through conditional sequence modeling, using trajectories to learn behavior. Much prior work treats offline learning from existing data and online learning through interaction separately. The paper also highlights a weakness of deterministic trajectory modeling: it can overlook randomness in transitions and the variety of possible futures.

Value-Guided Decision Transformer introduces value functions into this sequence-modeling framework. During offline training, advantage weighting and behavior regularization guide the policy toward the paper's upper-bound optimal decisions. During online tuning, value-based policy improvement is combined with behavior cloning using limited interaction and data collection. Predictions of future returns also inform sampling.

The method achieves competitive results across standard reinforcement-learning benchmarks and improves performance within a small number of online timesteps. Its contribution is a common architecture for learning from stored trajectories and subsequently improving through experience. Value estimates provide guidance across training and sampling, connecting the transformer's ability to model behavior distributions with reinforcement learning's estimates of future reward.
summary.tldr: VDT integrates value-based guidance into Decision Transformers to support offline training, efficient online improvement, and return-informed sampling.

title: Value-Guided Decision Transformer: A Unified Reinforcement Learning Framework for Online and Offline Settings

abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities by integrating visual perception with language understanding, enabling applications such as image-grounded dialogue, visual question answering, and scientific analysis. However, most MLLMs adopt a static inference paradigm, encoding the entire image into fixed visual tokens upfront, which limits their ability to iteratively refine understanding or adapt to context during inference. This contrasts sharply with human perception, which is dynamic, selective, and feedback-driven. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for inference-time visual token scaling that enables MLLMs to perform iterative, verifier-guided reasoning over visual content. We formulate the problem as a Markov Decision Process, involving a reasoner that proposes visual actions and a verifier—trained via multi-step Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)—that evaluates these actions and determines when reasoning should terminate. To support this, we present a new dataset, VTS, comprising supervised reasoning trajectories (VTS-SFT) and preference-labeled reasoning comparisons (VTS-DPO). Our method significantly outperforms existing approaches across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks, offering not only improved accuracy but also more interpretable and grounded reasoning processes. These results demonstrate the promise of dynamic inference mechanisms for enabling fine-grained, context-aware visual reasoning in next-generation MLLMs. Code and datasets are publicly released at https://vts-v.github.io/.

paragraphs: Many multimodal language models encode an image into a fixed collection of visual tokens before reasoning begins. This static representation limits their ability to refine visual understanding as the task develops. The paper introduces an inference-time framework in which visual processing proceeds iteratively and a verifier guides the reasoning process.

The framework casts this process as a Markov Decision Process. A reasoner proposes visual actions, while a verifier evaluates them and decides when reasoning should stop. The verifier is trained with multi-step Direct Preference Optimization. To support training, the authors introduce VTS, containing both supervised reasoning trajectories and preference-labeled comparisons between reasoning sequences.

The authors report significant improvements over existing approaches across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks, alongside more interpretable and visually grounded reasoning. The contribution connects decisions about what visual processing to perform with decisions about whether enough reasoning has occurred. These findings support dynamic visual inference as a promising way to make image understanding more responsive to the context of a particular task.
summary.tldr: Verifier-guided visual actions let multimodal models refine their understanding during inference, improving accuracy and grounding on visual reasoning benchmarks.

title: Multi-step Visual Reasoning with Visual Tokens Scaling and Verification

abstract: Privileged learning efficiently tackles high-dimensional, partially observable decision-making problems by first training a privileged policy (PP) on low-dimensional privileged observations, and then deriving a deployment policy (DP) either by imitating the PP or coupling it with an observation encoder. However, since the DP relies on local and partial observations, a behavioral divergence (BD) often emerges between the DP and the PP, ultimately degrading deployment performance. A promising strategy is to train a PP to learn the optimal behaviors attainable under the DP’s observation space by applying reward penalties in regions with large BD. However, producing these behaviors is challenging for the PP because they rely on the DP’s information-gathering progress, which is invisible to the PP. In this paper, we quantify the DP’s information-gathering progress by estimating the prediction uncertainty of privileged observations reconstructed from partial observations, and accordingly propose the framework of Uncertainty-Sensitive Privileged Learning (USPL). USPL feeds this uncertainty estimation to the PP and combines reward transformation with privileged-observation blurring, driving the PP to choose actions that actively reduce uncertainty and thus gather the necessary information. Experiments across nine tasks demonstrate that USPL significantly reduces the behavioral discrepancies, achieving superior deployment performance compared to baselines. Additional visualization results show that the DP accurately quantifies its uncertainty, and the PP effectively adapts to uncertainty variations. Code is available at https://github.com/FanmingL/USPL.

paragraphs: Privileged learning trains a policy with access to informative observations, then derives a deployment policy that must act using partial observations. The two can behave differently because the deployed policy lacks information available during privileged training. Simply penalizing that behavioral gap is difficult when the privileged policy cannot see how much information its counterpart has gathered.

Uncertainty-Sensitive Privileged Learning estimates this information-gathering progress through uncertainty in reconstructing privileged observations from partial ones. It supplies the uncertainty estimate to the privileged policy. Reward transformation and blurring of privileged observations then encourage actions that reduce uncertainty, guiding the policy toward gathering information needed for successful behavior under the deployment observation constraints.

Across nine tasks, the authors report significantly smaller behavioral discrepancies and better deployment performance than the evaluated baselines. Visualizations show the deployment policy quantifying its uncertainty and the privileged policy responding to changes in it. The results support making the learner’s information state visible during privileged training so that training behavior better reflects what deployment can achieve.
summary.tldr: USPL exposes deployment uncertainty to a privileged training policy, encouraging information gathering and reducing the reported training-to-deployment behavior gap.

title: Uncertainty-Sensitive Privileged Learning

abstract: In reinforcement learning with sparse rewards, demonstrations can accelerate learning, but determining when to imitate them remains challenging. We propose Smooth Policy Regularisation from Demonstrations (SPReD), a framework that addresses the fundamental question: when should an agent imitate a demonstration versus follow its own policy? SPReD uses ensemble methods to explicitly model Q-value distributions for both demonstration and policy actions, quantifying uncertainty for comparisons. We develop two complementary uncertainty-aware methods: a probabilistic approach estimating the likelihood of demonstration superiority, and an advantage-based approach scaling imitation by statistical significance. Unlike prevailing methods (e.g. Q-filter) that make binary imitation decisions, SPReD applies continuous, uncertainty-proportional regularisation weights, reducing gradient variance during training. Despite its computational simplicity, SPReD achieves remarkable gains in experiments across eight robotics tasks, outperforming existing approaches by up to a factor of 14 in complex tasks while maintaining robustness to demonstration quality and quantity. Our code is available at https://github.com/YujieZhu7/SPReD.

paragraphs: Demonstrations can help a reinforcement-learning agent when rewards are rare, but imitating every demonstrated action may be inappropriate. SPReD addresses the decision of how strongly to imitate versus follow the agent’s current policy. It compares both actions using distributions of estimated Q-values, which represent expected return, rather than relying on single estimates.

Ensembles provide the uncertainty information for these comparisons. One version estimates the probability that the demonstrated action is better; another scales imitation according to the statistical significance of its advantage. Both produce continuous regularization weights. This replaces a hard yes-or-no imitation decision with a graded influence that reflects uncertainty and reduces training gradient variance.

Experiments across eight robotics tasks report gains over existing approaches, reaching up to a factor of 14 on complex tasks. The method also remains robust to changes in demonstration quality and quantity in the evaluated settings. The result suggests that a small demonstration collection can be more useful when its influence is adjusted according to the strength of the available evidence.
summary.tldr: SPReD uses uncertainty in action-value estimates to adjust imitation smoothly, improving learning from limited demonstrations in robotics experiments.

title: Uncertainty-Based Smooth Policy Regularisation for Reinforcement Learning with Few Demonstrations

abstract: There is growing interest in using machine learning (ML) to support clinical diagnosis, but most approaches rely on static, fully observed datasets and fail to reflect the sequential, resource-aware reasoning clinicians use in practice. Diagnosis remains complex and error prone, especially in high-pressure or resource-limited settings, underscoring the need for frameworks that help clinicians make timely and cost-effective decisions. We propose ACTMED (Adaptive Clinical Test selection via Model-based Experimental Design), a diagnostic framework that integrates Bayesian Experimental Design (BED) with large language models (LLMs) to better emulate real-world diagnostic reasoning. At each step, ACTMED selects the test expected to yield the greatest reduction in diagnostic uncertainty for a given patient. LLMs act as flexible simulators, generating plausible patient state distributions and supporting belief updates without requiring structured, task-specific training data. Clinicians can remain in the loop; reviewing test suggestions, interpreting intermediate outputs, and applying clinical judgment throughout. We evaluate ACTMED on real-world datasets and show it can optimize test selection to improve diagnostic accuracy, interpretability, and resource use. This represents a step toward transparent, adaptive, and clinician-aligned diagnostic systems that generalize across settings with reduced reliance on domain-specific data.

Models trained on fully observed, static datasets do not directly capture that process or its resource constraints. ACTMED frames diagnosis as adaptive test selection, using the information already available for an individual patient to guide the next step.

The framework combines Bayesian Experimental Design with language models. At each step, it selects the test expected to reduce diagnostic uncertainty most. Language models serve as simulators that generate plausible distributions over patient states and support updates to diagnostic beliefs, without requiring structured training data tailored to each task. summary.tldr: ACTMED combines Bayesian experimental design and language-model simulation to select informative clinical tests sequentially while supporting clinician involvement.

title: Timely Clinical Diagnosis through Active Test Selection

abstract: Deploying reinforcement learning (RL) safely in the real world is challenging, as policies trained in simulators must face the inevitable *sim-to-real gap*. Robust safe RL techniques are provably safe, however difficult to scale, while domain randomization is more practical yet prone to unsafe behaviors. We address this gap by proposing SPiDR, short for Sim-to-real via Pessimistic Domain Randomization—a scalable algorithm with provable guarantees for safe sim-to-real transfer. SPiDR uses domain randomization to incorporate the uncertainty about the sim-to-real gap into the safety constraints, making it versatile and highly compatible with existing training pipelines. Through extensive experiments on sim-to-sim benchmarks and two distinct real-world robotic platforms, we demonstrate that SPiDR effectively ensures safety despite the sim-to-real gap while maintaining strong performance.

paragraphs: SPiDR addresses the safety problem that arises when a reinforcement-learning policy moves from simulation into the real world. A simulator inevitably differs from the system being controlled. The paper describes a tension between robust safe-learning methods, which offer proofs but are difficult to scale, and practical domain randomization, which can still produce unsafe behavior.

The proposed method uses pessimistic domain randomization to bring uncertainty about this simulation gap into the safety constraints themselves. Its design combines a scalable training algorithm with provable guarantees for safe transfer. Because it builds on domain randomization, the authors describe it as versatile and compatible with existing training pipelines.

Evaluation includes transfers between simulated settings and experiments on two distinct physical robotic platforms. The authors report that SPiDR maintains safety despite the simulation gap while preserving strong performance. These results support incorporating uncertainty directly into safety-constrained training. The contribution joins formal guarantees with practical transfer evidence, addressing the gap between scalable training methods and methods designed around explicit safety requirements.
summary.tldr: SPiDR incorporates simulation-to-reality uncertainty into safety constraints, combining scalable domain randomization with provable transfer guarantees.

title: SPiDR: A Simple Approach for Zero-Shot Safety in Sim-to-Real Transfer

abstract: Understanding the evolution of cellular microenvironments in spatiotemporal data is essential for deciphering tissue development and disease progression. While experimental techniques like spatial transcriptomics now enable high-resolution mapping of tissue organization across space and time, current methods that model cellular evolution operate at the single-cell level, overlooking the coordinated development of cellular states in a tissue. We introduce NicheFlow, a flow-based generative model that infers the temporal trajectory of cellular microenvironments across sequential spatial slides. By representing local cell neighborhoods as point clouds, NicheFlow jointly models the evolution of cell states and spatial coordinates using optimal transport and Variational Flow Matching. Our approach successfully recovers both global spatial architecture and local microenvironment composition across diverse spatiotemporal datasets, from embryonic to brain development.

By representing local cell neighborhoods as point clouds, NicheFlow jointly models the evolution of cell states and spatial coordinates using optimal transport and Variational Flow Matching. Spatial transcriptomics captures tissue organization across space and time, but methods focused on individual cells can overlook this neighborhood-level evolution. NicheFlow models cellular microenvironments to capture the joint development of nearby cells.

It uses optimal transport and Variational Flow Matching to jointly model changes in cell states and spatial coordinates. title: Modeling Microenvironment Trajectories on Spatial Transcriptomics with NicheFlow

abstract: Uncertainty estimation is crucial for ensuring the reliability of machine learning models in safety-critical applications. Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) offers a principled framework by modeling predictive uncertainty through Dirichlet distributions over class probabilities. However, existing EDL methods predominantly rely on level-0 hard labels, which supervised a uncertainty-aware model with full certainty. We argue that hard labels not only fail to capture epistemic uncertainty but also obscure the aleatoric uncertainty arising from inherent data noise and label ambiguity. As a result, EDL models often produce degenerate Dirichlet distributions that collapse to near-deterministic outputs. To overcome these limitations, we propose a vicinal risk minimization paradigm for EDL by incorporating level-1 supervision in the form of vicinally smoothed conditional label distributions. This richer supervision exposes the model to local label uncertainty, enhancing aleatoric uncertainty quantification, while also mitigating the degeneration of the Dirichlet distribution into a Dirac delta function, thereby improving epistemic uncertainty modeling. Extensive experiments show that our approach consistently outperforms standard EDL baselines across synthetic datasets, covariate-shifted out-of-distribution generalization tasks, and out-of-distribution detection benchmarks, providing more reliable uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Evidential deep learning represents uncertainty using Dirichlet distributions over class probabilities. This paper argues that training such models with completely certain hard labels creates a mismatch: the target provides no direct expression of ambiguity. The resulting distributions can become nearly deterministic, obscuring uncertainty from noisy data as well as uncertainty associated with the model.

The proposed approach replaces hard-label-only supervision with locally smoothed conditional label distributions through vicinal risk minimization. These richer targets expose the model to label uncertainty in a sample’s neighborhood. The aim is to better represent aleatoric uncertainty, which comes from data noise and ambiguity, while preventing distributional collapse that undermines epistemic uncertainty modeling.

Experiments compare the approach with standard evidential learning baselines on synthetic data, generalization under covariate shift, and out-of-distribution detection. The authors report consistently better performance and more reliable uncertainty estimates. The contribution places emphasis on the information supplied by training targets: uncertainty-aware outputs benefit from supervision that itself expresses local uncertainty, rather than asking the model to recover that uncertainty from fully certain labels.
summary.tldr: Locally smoothed label distributions improve evidential models’ estimates of both data uncertainty and model uncertainty.

title: Vicinal Label Supervision for Reliable Aleatoric and Epistemic Uncertainty Estimation

abstract: Plant traits such as leaf carbon content and leaf mass are essential variables in the study of biodiversity and climate change. However, conventional field sampling cannot feasibly cover trait variation at ecologically meaningful spatial scales. Machine learning represents a valuable solution for plant trait prediction across ecosystems, leveraging hyperspectral data from remote sensing.Nevertheless, trait prediction from hyperspectral data is challenged by label scarcity and substantial domain shifts (\eg across sensors, ecological distributions), requiring robust cross-domain methods.Here, we present GreenHyperSpectra, a pretraining dataset encompassing real-world cross-sensor and cross-ecosystem samples designed to benchmark trait prediction with semi- and self-supervised methods. We adopt an evaluation framework encompassing in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. We successfully leverage GreenHyperSpectra to pretrain label-efficient multi-output regression models that outperform the state-of-the-art supervised baseline. Our empirical analyses demonstrate substantial improvements in learning spectral representations for trait prediction, establishing a comprehensive methodological framework to catalyze research at the intersection of representation learning and plant functional traits assessment. We also share the dataset\footnotemark[1], code and pretrained model objects for this study \href{https://github.com/echerif18/HyspectraSSL}{here}.\footnotetext[1]{GreenHyperSpectra dataset: \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/Avatarr05/GreenHyperSpectra}{https://huggingface.co/datasets/Avatarr05/GreenHyperSpectra}}

paragraphs: Plant traits such as leaf carbon content and leaf mass help researchers study biodiversity and climate change. Field measurements alone cannot feasibly capture their variation across ecologically meaningful areas. Hyperspectral remote sensing offers data for predicting these traits, but labeled examples are scarce and measurements differ across sensors and ecosystems.

GreenHyperSpectra is a pretraining dataset designed around those cross-sensor and cross-ecosystem differences. It supports benchmarking methods that learn from partly labeled or unlabeled data. The accompanying evaluation framework includes both familiar distributions and shifted ones, making transfer across data conditions an explicit part of assessing trait prediction.

The authors use the dataset to pretrain regression models that predict multiple traits while making efficient use of labels. These models outperform the compared state-of-the-art supervised baseline. Their empirical analyses also show improved spectral representations for trait prediction. The contribution combines data and evaluation methodology, providing a setting in which researchers can study how representation learning addresses scarce labels and the domain shifts encountered in vegetation monitoring.
summary.tldr: GreenHyperSpectra supports label-efficient vegetation trait prediction by providing hyperspectral pretraining data and evaluation across sensors and ecosystems.

title: GreenHyperSpectra: A multi-source hyperspectral dataset for global vegetation trait prediction

abstract: Extracting neural signals at the single motor neuron level provides an optimal control signal for neuroprosthetic applications. However, current algorithms to decompose motor units from high-density electromyography (HD-EMG) are time-consuming and inconsistent, limiting their application to controlled scenarios in a research setting. We introduce MUelim, an algorithm for efficient motor unit decomposition that uses approximate joint diagonalization with a subtractive approach to rapidly identify and refine candidate sources. The algorithm incorporates an extend-lag procedure to augment data for enhanced source separability prior to diagonalization. By systematically iterating and eliminating redundant or noisy sources, MUelim achieves high decomposition accuracy while significantly reducing computational complexity, making it well-suited for real-time applications. We validate MUelim by demonstrating its ability to extract motor units in both simulated and physiological HD-EMG grid data. Across six healthy participants performing ramp and maximum voluntary contraction paradigms, MUelim achieves up to a 36$\times$ speed increase compared to existing state-of-the-art methods while decomposing a similar number of high signal-to-noise sources. Furthermore, we showcase a real-world application of MUelim in a clinical setting in which an individual with spinal cord injury controlled an EMG-driven neuroprosthetic to perform functional tasks. We demonstrate the ability to decode motor intent in real-time using a spiking neural network trained on the decomposed motor unit spike trains to trigger functional electrical stimulation patterns that evoke hand movements during task practice therapy. We show that motor unit-based decoding enables nuanced motor control, highlighting the potential of MUelim to advance assistive neurotechnology and rehabilitation through precise, intention-driven neuroprosthetic systems.

title: Decomposing motor units through elimination for real-time intention driven assistive neurotechnology

abstract: To address these challenges, we propose the Reconfigurable Continuum Gaussian Stream, dubbed ReCon-GS, a novel storage-aware framework that enables high-fidelity online dynamic scene reconstruction and real-time rendering. Specifically, we dynamically allocate multi-level Anchor Gaussians in a density-adaptive fashion to capture inter-frame geometric deformations, thereby decomposing scene motion into compact coarse-to-fine representations. Then, we design a dynamic hierarchy reconfiguration strategy that preserves localized motion expressiveness through on-demand anchor re-hierarchization, while ensuring temporal consistency through intra-hierarchical deformation inheritance that confines transformation priors to their respective hierarchy levels. Furthermore, we introduce a storage-aware optimization mechanism that flexibly adjusts the density of Anchor Gaussians at different hierarchy levels, enabling a controllable trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and memory usage. Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets demonstrate that, compared to state‐of‐the‐art methods, ReCon-GS improves training efficiency by approximately 15% and achieves superior FVV synthesis quality with enhanced robustness and stability. Moreover, at equivalent rendering quality, ReCon-GS slashes memory requirements by over 50% compared to leading state‑of‑the‑art methods. Code is avaliable at: https://github.com/jyfu-vcl/ReCon-GS/.

paragraphs: ReCon-GS reconstructs changing scenes online while accounting for the memory needed to store them. It represents motion through multiple levels of Anchor Gaussians, allocated adaptively according to density. This breaks geometric changes between frames into a compact hierarchy ranging from coarse motion to finer local deformation.

The hierarchy can be reorganized on demand to retain expressive local motion. Deformation information is inherited within the appropriate hierarchy levels to preserve temporal consistency. A storage-aware optimization mechanism also adjusts anchor density at different levels, giving control over the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and memory use while supporting real-time rendering.

Across three datasets, the authors report approximately 15% better training efficiency than leading methods, alongside improved free-viewpoint video synthesis quality, robustness, and stability. At equivalent rendering quality, memory requirements fall by more than 50%. These results support the combination of adaptive motion hierarchy and storage-aware optimization as a way to make dynamic reconstruction more compact without sacrificing the reported rendering quality.
summary.tldr: ReCon-GS uses adaptive Gaussian motion hierarchies to improve dynamic reconstruction efficiency and reduce memory by over 50% at equivalent rendering quality.

title: ReCon-GS: Continuum-Preserved Gaussian Streaming for Fast and Compact Reconstruction of Dynamic Scenes

abstract: We introduce Parametric Density Path Optimization (PDPO), a novel method for computing action-minimizing paths between probability densities. The core idea is to represent the target probability path as the pushforward of a reference density through a parametric map, transforming the original infinite-dimensional optimization over densities to a finite-dimensional one over the parameters of the map. We derive a static formulation of the dynamic problem of action minimization and propose cubic spline interpolation of the path in parameter space to solve the static problem. Theoretically, we establish an error bound of the action under proper assumptions on the regularity of the parameter path. Empirically, we find that using 3–5 control points of the spline interpolation suffices to accurately resolve both multimodal and high-dimensional problems. We demonstrate that PDPO can flexibly accommodate a wide range of potential terms, including those modeling obstacles, mean-field interactions, stochastic control, and higher-order dynamics. Our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in benchmark tasks, demonstrating superior computational efficiency and solution quality.

paragraphs: PDPO computes paths that transform one probability density into another while minimizing an action, the objective assigned to the whole transformation. Directly optimizing such a path involves an infinite-dimensional space of densities. The paper makes the problem finite-dimensional by representing each density as the result of applying a parameterized map to a reference density.

The optimization then concerns how the map's parameters change along the path. The authors derive a static formulation of the original dynamic problem and solve it using cubic spline interpolation in parameter space. Under appropriate regularity assumptions on the parameter path, they establish an error bound for the action. This provides theoretical support for approximating a continuous path with a compact parameterization.

In experiments, three to five spline control points suffice to accurately resolve the tested multimodal and high-dimensional problems. PDPO also accommodates potential terms for obstacles, mean-field interactions, stochastic control, and higher-order dynamics. Benchmark results show better computational efficiency and solution quality than existing state-of-the-art approaches, suggesting that a small spline representation can be effective across varied action-minimization settings.
summary.tldr: PDPO turns optimization over probability-density paths into a compact spline optimization over map parameters, improving efficiency and solution quality.

title: PDPO: Parametric Density Path Optimization

abstract: While deep learning has achieved remarkable success across many domains, it has historically underperformed on tabular learning tasks, which remain dominated by gradient boosting decision trees. However, recent advancements are paving the way for Tabular Foundation Models, which can leverage real-world knowledge and generalize across diverse datasets, particularly when the data contains free-text. Although incorporating language model capabilities into tabular tasks has been explored, most existing methods utilize static, target-agnostic textual representations, limiting their effectiveness. We introduce TabSTAR: a Tabular Foundation Model with Semantically Target-Aware Representations. TabSTAR is designed to enable transfer learning on tabular data with textual features, with an architecture free of dataset-specific parameters. It unfreezes a pretrained text encoder and takes as input target tokens, which provide the model with the context needed to learn task-specific embeddings. TabSTAR achieves state-of-the-art performance for both medium- and large-sized datasets across known benchmarks of classification tasks with text features, and its pretraining phase exhibits scaling laws in the number of datasets, offering a pathway for further performance improvements.

paragraphs: TabSTAR focuses on tables that contain free-text fields alongside other data. Language models offer a way to bring semantic knowledge into these prediction tasks, but many existing approaches use fixed text representations that do not account for the prediction target. The same textual information may therefore be represented without regard to what the model needs to infer.

TabSTAR makes its representations target-aware. It allows a pretrained text encoder to update during learning and supplies target tokens that describe the task context. This enables embeddings to adapt to the prediction objective. Its architecture also avoids dataset-specific parameters, supporting transfer learning across different tables while retaining a shared model structure.

On established classification benchmarks with text features, the authors report state-of-the-art performance for both medium-sized and large datasets. They also observe scaling laws as the number of pretraining datasets grows. These findings support combining task-sensitive language representations with cross-dataset pretraining, and suggest that expanding dataset coverage offers a path toward further improvements.
summary.tldr: TabSTAR learns target-aware text representations for tabular classification, reporting strong transfer performance and scaling with more pretraining datasets.

title: TabSTAR: A Tabular Foundation Model for Tabular Data with Text Fields

abstract: We provide efficient algorithms for learning disjunctions in the semi-supervised setting under a natural regularity assumption introduced by (Balcan & Blum, 2005). We prove bounds on the sample complexity of our algorithms under a mild restriction on the data distribution. We also give an active learning algorithm with improved sample complexity and extend all our algorithms to the random classification noise setting.
originalAbstract: We provide efficient algorithms for learning disjunctions in the semi-supervised setting under a natural regularity assumption introduced by (Balcan & Blum, 2005). We prove bounds on the sample complexity of our algorithms under a mild restriction on the data distribution. We also give an active learning algorithm with improved sample complexity and extend all our algorithms to the random classification noise setting.

paragraphs: A disjunction is a rule that accepts an example when at least one of its constituent conditions holds. This paper studies how to learn such rules efficiently in a semi-supervised setting, where the learning problem includes unlabeled information. The algorithms operate under a stated regularity assumption, so the results concern a structured learning setting.

The authors prove sample-complexity bounds under an additional mild restriction on the data distribution. These bounds describe how much data the algorithms require to learn. They also develop an active learning algorithm with improved sample complexity, connecting the learning task to a setting in which the learner can select examples for labeling.

All of the algorithms are extended to random classification noise, addressing labels that may be randomly corrupted. The contribution therefore covers efficient learning, data requirements, and a noisy-label extension within one family of prediction rules. Its guarantees depend on the stated regularity and distributional conditions; the abstract does not claim unrestricted learnability for arbitrary data.
summary.tldr: The paper gives efficient semi-supervised and active algorithms for learning disjunctions under stated assumptions, including extensions to random label noise.

title: Efficient Semi-supervised and Active Learning of Disjunctions

abstract: Both max-margin and Bayesian methods have been extensively studied in multi-task learning, but have rarely been considered together. We present Bayesian max-margin multi-task learning, which conjoins the two schools of methods, thus allowing the discriminative max-margin methods to enjoy the great flexibility of Bayesian methods on incorporating rich prior information as well as performing nonparametric Bayesian feature learning with the latent dimensionality resolved from data. We develop Gibbs sampling algorithms by exploring data augmentation to deal with the non-smooth hinge loss. For nonparametric models, our algorithms do not need to make mean-field assumptions or truncated approximation. Empirical results demonstrate superior performance than competitors in both multi-task classification and regression.

paragraphs: The paper combines Bayesian modeling and max-margin learning for problems involving multiple tasks. Max-margin methods supply a discriminative learning objective, while Bayesian methods offer ways to incorporate prior information. Bringing them together allows the learning framework to use both kinds of structure when fitting related prediction tasks.

The framework also supports nonparametric Bayesian feature learning, in which the dimensionality of the latent representation is resolved from data. A computational obstacle is the hinge loss, whose non-smooth form complicates inference. The authors use data augmentation to develop Gibbs sampling algorithms that can handle this loss within the Bayesian formulation.

For the nonparametric models, the proposed algorithms avoid mean-field assumptions and truncated approximations. This is a specific feature of their inference approach, alongside the ability to infer latent dimensionality. Experiments cover both multi-task classification and regression, with reported performance above the evaluated competitors. The findings support the practical value of combining margin-based prediction with flexible Bayesian representations in those tested settings.
summary.tldr: The paper combines Bayesian flexibility with max-margin multi-task learning using data augmentation and Gibbs sampling.

title: Bayesian Max-margin Multi-Task Learning with Data Augmentation

abstract: We study online boosting, the task of converting any weak online learner into a strong online learner. Based on a novel and natural definition of weak online learnability, we develop two online boosting algorithms. The first algorithm is an online version of boost-by-majority. By proving a matching lower bound, we show that this algorithm is essentially optimal in terms of the number of weak learners and the sample complexity needed to achieve a specified accuracy. The second algorithm is adaptive and parameter-free, albeit not optimal.
originalAbstract: We study online boosting, the task of converting any weak online learner into a strong online learner. Based on a novel and natural definition of weak online learnability, we develop two online boosting algorithms. The first algorithm is an online version of boost-by-majority. By proving a matching lower bound, we show that this algorithm is essentially optimal in terms of the number of weak learners and the sample complexity needed to achieve a specified accuracy. The second algorithm is adaptive and parameter-free, albeit not optimal.

paragraphs: Online boosting aims to convert a weak online learner into a strong one as learning proceeds over time. The paper begins by introducing a definition of weak online learnability that supports this goal. That definition supplies the foundation for two algorithms with different strengths: one emphasizes provable resource efficiency, while the other emphasizes adaptation.

The first algorithm adapts boost-by-majority to the online setting. The authors prove a matching lower bound, showing that its requirements are essentially optimal in both the number of weak learners and the sample complexity needed for a specified accuracy. The lower bound matters because it compares the algorithm's resource use with what the problem fundamentally requires under the framework.

The second algorithm is adaptive and parameter-free, but does not achieve the same optimality claim. The paper thus presents two distinct outcomes within a common theory of online boosting. One establishes how efficiently strong learning can be achieved; the other offers an adaptive procedure without parameter specification, while explicitly retaining the distinction between adaptability and optimality.
summary.tldr: Two online boosting algorithms offer either essentially optimal resource requirements or parameter-free adaptation.

title: Optimal and Adaptive Algorithms for Online Boosting

abstract: Black box variational inference allows researchers to easily prototype and evaluate an array of models. Recent advances allow such algorithms to scale to high dimensions. However, a central question remains: How to specify an expressive variational distribution that maintains efficient computation? To address this, we develop hierarchical variational models (HVMs). HVMs augment a variational approximation with a prior on its parameters, which allows it to capture complex structure for both discrete and continuous latent variables. The algorithm we develop is black box, can be used for any HVM, and has the same computational efficiency as the original approximation. We study HVMs on a variety of deep discrete latent variable models. HVMs generalize other expressive variational distributions and maintains higher fidelity to the posterior.

However, a central question remains: How to specify an expressive variational distribution that maintains efficient computation? To address this, we develop hierarchical variational models (HVMs). HVMs augment a variational approximation with a prior on its parameters, which allows it to capture complex structure for both discrete and continuous latent variables. The algorithm we develop is black box, can be used for any HVM, and has the same computational efficiency as the original approximation. We study HVMs on a variety of deep discrete latent variable models. HVMs generalize other expressive variational distributions and maintains higher fidelity to the posterior.

paragraphs: The paper tackles a central design problem in variational inference: how to make an approximate posterior expressive without sacrificing computational efficiency. Black-box methods make it easier to evaluate different probabilistic models, but their usefulness still depends on the distribution chosen to approximate the posterior. A restrictive approximation can miss complex latent structure.

Hierarchical variational models add a prior over the parameters of an existing variational approximation. This additional layer allows the approximation to represent more complex structure for both discrete and continuous latent variables. The authors also develop a black-box inference algorithm that applies to any hierarchical variational model and retains the computational efficiency of the original approximation.

The study examines these models on several deep models with discrete latent variables. The authors report greater fidelity to the posterior and show that the framework generalizes other expressive variational distributions. The contribution is a reusable way to enrich an approximation, together with an inference procedure intended to preserve the computational advantages that made the starting approximation useful.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical variational models enrich posterior approximations by placing priors on their parameters while retaining computational efficiency.

title: Hierarchical Variational Models

abstract: Learning a classifier from private data distributed across multiple parties is an important problem that has many potential applications. How can we build an accurate and differentially private global classifier by combining locally-trained classifiers from different parties, without access to any party’s private data? We propose to transfer the “knowledge” of the local classifier ensemble by first creating labeled data from auxiliary unlabeled data, and then train a global differentially private classifier. We show that majority voting is too sensitive and therefore propose a new risk weighted by class probabilities estimated from the ensemble. Relative to a non-private solution, our private solution has a generalization error bounded by O(ε^-2 M^-2). This allows strong privacy without performance loss when the number of participating parties M is large, such as in crowdsensing applications. We demonstrate the performance of our framework with realistic tasks of activity recognition, network intrusion detection, and malicious URL detection.

Relative to a non-private solution, our private solution has a generalization error bounded by O(ε^-2 M^-2). This allows strong privacy without performance loss when the number of participating parties M is large, such as in crowdsensing applications. We demonstrate the performance of our framework with realistic tasks of activity recognition, network intrusion detection, and malicious URL detection.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to build a global classifier when private training data remain with multiple parties. Each party contributes a locally trained classifier, while the global learning procedure has no access to the underlying private data. The challenge is to combine their knowledge accurately while providing differential privacy.

The proposed framework uses the local ensemble to create labeled training information from auxiliary unlabeled data. A global private classifier then learns from that information. The authors find majority voting too sensitive for this purpose, so they introduce a risk function weighted by class probabilities estimated from the ensemble. This changes how local predictions guide global training.

Relative to a non-private solution, the stated generalization-error bound scales as O(epsilon^-2 M^-2), where M is the number of participating parties. The result supports strong privacy without performance loss when participation is sufficiently large. Evaluations on activity recognition, network intrusion detection, and malicious URL detection demonstrate the framework across realistic tasks, linking the privacy analysis with practical classification settings.
summary.tldr: A private global classifier learns from local-model predictions on auxiliary data, with an error bound that improves as participation grows.

title: Learning privately from multiparty data

abstract: We examined the sequence of decision problems that are encountered in the game of Tetris and found that most of the problems are easy in the following sense: One can choose well among the available actions without knowing an evaluation function that scores well in the game. This is a consequence of three conditions that are prevalent in the game: simple dominance, cumulative dominance, and noncompensation. These conditions can be exploited to develop faster and more effective learning algorithms. In addition, they allow certain types of domain knowledge to be incorporated with ease into a learning algorithm. Among the sequential decision problems we encounter, it is unlikely that Tetris is unique or rare in having these properties.

paragraphs: The paper examines the individual decision problems that arise during Tetris and finds that most are easy in a particular sense. A player or learning algorithm can often choose well among the available moves without already knowing an evaluation function that performs well over the whole game. Local choices can therefore be simpler than learning an effective overall scoring rule.

The authors attribute this to three conditions that occur frequently in the game: simple dominance, cumulative dominance, and noncompensation. These conditions provide structure for comparing actions, reducing dependence on a fully learned evaluation function. Their importance is that the available moves themselves can contain enough structure to support a good choice before the complete scoring problem has been solved.

The paper argues that exploiting these properties can produce faster and more effective learning algorithms and make certain forms of domain knowledge easy to incorporate. The authors also suggest that Tetris is unlikely to be unusual among sequential decision problems in possessing these properties. That broader relevance is proposed as a possibility rather than demonstrated for all such problems.
summary.tldr: Many Tetris choices can be made well without a strong overall evaluation function because recurring structural conditions simplify action comparisons.

title: Why Most Decisions Are Easy in Tetris—And Perhaps in Other Sequential Decision Problems, As Well

abstract: Although RNNs have been shown to be power- ful tools for processing sequential data, finding architectures or optimization strategies that al- low them to model very long term dependencies is still an active area of research. In this work, we carefully analyze two synthetic datasets orig- inally outlined in (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) which are used to evaluate the ability of RNNs to store information over many time steps. We explicitly construct RNN solutions to these problems, and using these constructions, illumi- nate both the problems themselves and the way in which RNNs store different types of information in their hidden states. These constructions fur- thermore explain the success of recent methods that specify unitary initializations or constraints on the transition matrices.

These constructions fur- thermore explain the success of recent methods that specify unitary initializations or constraints on the transition matrices.

paragraphs: The paper examines how recurrent neural networks retain information over long sequences. It focuses on two synthetic datasets used to evaluate long-term memory. Rather than relying only on observed training outcomes, the authors explicitly construct recurrent networks that solve these problems, making it possible to inspect how a successful solution stores the information it needs.

These constructions clarify both the demands of the tasks and the roles of information held in the hidden state. A hidden state carries information from one time step to the next, so understanding its contents is central to understanding long-memory behavior. The constructed solutions reveal how different kinds of information can be represented within that state.

The analysis also explains the success of recent methods using unitary initializations or constraints on transition matrices. Its contribution is therefore explanatory: concrete solutions help connect task structure, memory representation, and recurrent-network design. The findings concern the two analyzed synthetic problems and use their solutions to illuminate why those approaches can work well.
summary.tldr: Explicit RNN solutions to two long-memory tasks explain hidden-state storage and the success of unitary transition initializations or constraints.

title: Recurrent Orthogonal Networks and Long-Memory Tasks

abstract: Our goal is to improve the \it training and \it prediction time of Nyström method, which is a widely-used technique for generating low-rank kernel matrix approximations. When applying the Nyström approximation for large-scale applications, both training and prediction time is dominated by computing kernel values between a data point and all landmark points. With m landmark points, this computation requires Θ(md) time (flops), where d is the input dimension. In this paper, we propose the use of a family of fast transforms to generate structured landmark points for Nyström approximation. By exploiting fast transforms, e.g., Haar transform and Hadamard transform, our modified Nyström method requires only Θ(m) or Θ(m\log d) time to compute the kernel values between a given data point and m landmark points. This improvement in time complexity can significantly speed up kernel approximation and benefit prediction speed in kernel machines. For instance, on the webspam data (more than 300,000 data points), our proposed algorithm enables kernel SVM prediction to deliver 98% accuracy and the resulting prediction time is 1000 times faster than LIBSVM and only 10 times slower than linear SVM prediction (which yields only 91% accuracy).

paragraphs: Nyström approximation makes kernel methods more manageable by constructing a low-rank approximation to a kernel matrix. This paper targets a remaining bottleneck: computing kernel values between each input and every landmark point. With m landmarks and input dimension d, that calculation ordinarily takes time proportional to m times d.

The authors generate structured landmarks using fast transforms, including Haar and Hadamard transforms. Exploiting that structure reduces the stated kernel-evaluation cost to time proportional to m or m log d. The change directly targets a computation that dominates both training and prediction, so it can benefit more than the initial construction of the approximation.

On the webspam dataset, containing over 300,000 points, the proposed method enables kernel SVM prediction with 98% accuracy. Its reported prediction time is 1,000 times faster than LIBSVM and ten times slower than a linear SVM, which achieves 91% accuracy. This example illustrates a favorable accuracy–speed balance in the evaluated setting, alongside the broader computational improvement from structured landmarks.
summary.tldr: Fast-transform landmarks reduce Nyström kernel-evaluation costs and substantially accelerate prediction in the reported experiment.

title: Computationally Efficient Nyström Approximation using Fast Transforms

abstract: State-space models (SSMs) are a highly expressive model class for learning patterns in time series data and for system identification. Deterministic versions of SSMs (e.g., LSTMs) proved extremely successful in modeling complex time series data. Fully probabilistic SSMs, however, are often found hard to train, even for smaller problems. We propose a novel model formulation and a scalable training algorithm based on doubly stochastic variational inference and Gaussian processes. This combination allows efficient incorporation of latent state temporal correlations, which we found to be key to robust training. The effectiveness of the proposed PR-SSM is evaluated on a set of real-world benchmark datasets in comparison to state-of-the-art probabilistic model learning methods. Scalability and robustness are demonstrated on a high dimensional problem.

We propose a novel model formulation and a scalable training algorithm based on doubly stochastic variational inference and Gaussian processes. This combination allows efficient incorporation of latent state temporal correlations, which we found to be key to robust training. The effectiveness of the proposed PR-SSM is evaluated on a set of real-world benchmark datasets in comparison to state-of-the-art probabilistic model learning methods. Scalability and robustness are demonstrated on a high dimensional problem.

paragraphs: State-space models describe patterns in time series through an evolving internal state and are useful for system identification. Deterministic versions have been successful on complex sequences, but fully probabilistic models can be difficult to train even on smaller problems. This paper targets that training difficulty with a new formulation and scalable algorithm.

The proposed probabilistic recurrent state-space model combines Gaussian processes with doubly stochastic variational inference. A key feature is efficient treatment of temporal correlations among latent states. The authors find that retaining these relationships across time is important for robust training, making them central to the design rather than incidental structure.

The method is evaluated on real-world benchmark datasets against state-of-the-art probabilistic model-learning approaches. A high-dimensional problem also demonstrates scalability and robustness. These findings support the combination of a probabilistic state representation and an inference procedure that accounts for temporal dependence. The abstract's central explanation for the training improvement is the effective incorporation of correlations between hidden states over time.
summary.tldr: PR-SSM combines Gaussian processes and variational inference to train probabilistic state-space models while retaining temporal correlations.

title: Probabilistic Recurrent State-Space Models

abstract: We introduce multi-frequency vector diffusion maps (MFVDM), a new framework for organizing and analyzing high dimensional data sets. The new method is a mathematical and algorithmic generalization of vector diffusion maps (VDM) and other non-linear dimensionality reduction methods. The idea of MFVDM is to incorporates multiple unitary irreducible representations of the alignment group which introduces robustness to noise. We illustrate the efficacy of MFVDM on synthetic and cryo-EM image datasets, achieving better nearest neighbors search and alignment estimation than other baselines as VDM and diffusion maps (DM), especially on extremely noisy data.

The idea of MFVDM is to incorporates multiple unitary irreducible representations of the alignment group which introduces robustness to noise. We illustrate the efficacy of MFVDM on synthetic and cryo-EM image datasets, achieving better nearest neighbors search and alignment estimation than other baselines as VDM and diffusion maps (DM), especially on extremely noisy data.

paragraphs: Organizing high-dimensional data involves finding which observations are related and, when relevant, how they align. Noise can make both judgments difficult. This paper introduces multi-frequency vector diffusion maps as a framework for analyzing such data, extending vector diffusion maps and other methods for nonlinear dimensionality reduction.

The central construction incorporates multiple unitary irreducible representations of the alignment group. These are mathematical ways to represent the transformations involved in alignment. Using several representations gives the framework multiple descriptions of that transformation structure. The authors identify this combination as the mechanism that introduces robustness to noise, connecting data organization with information about alignment.

The method is evaluated on synthetic data and cryo-electron microscopy image datasets. In those evaluations it improves nearest-neighbor search and alignment estimation compared with vector diffusion maps and diffusion maps, with especially strong benefits on extremely noisy data. The findings support using multiple representations of alignment structure to improve these two related tasks, rather than evaluating the framework only as a dimensionality-reduction construction.
summary.tldr: Multi-frequency vector diffusion maps combine representations of alignment transformations to improve neighbor search and alignment estimation in noisy data.

title: Multi-Frequency Vector Diffusion Maps

abstract: Trained generative models have shown remarkable performance as priors for inverse problems in imaging – for example, Generative Adversarial Network priors permit recovery of test images from 5-10x fewer measurements than sparsity priors. Unfortunately, these models may be unable to represent any particular image because of architectural choices, mode collapse, and bias in the training dataset. In this paper, we demonstrate that invertible neural networks, which have zero representation error by design, can be effective natural signal priors at inverse problems such as denoising, compressive sensing, and inpainting. Given a trained generative model, we study the empirical risk formulation of the desired inverse problem under a regularization that promotes high likelihood images, either directly by penalization or algorithmically by initialization. For compressive sensing, invertible priors can yield higher accuracy than sparsity priors across almost all undersampling ratios, and due to their lack of representation error, invertible priors can yield better reconstructions than GAN priors for images that have rare features of variation within the biased training set, including out-of-distribution natural images. We additionally compare performance for compressive sensing to unlearned methods, such as the deep decoder, and we establish theoretical bounds on expected recovery error in the case of a linear invertible model.

paragraphs: Generative models can guide image reconstruction from incomplete or corrupted measurements by favoring images that resemble their training data. However, architectural restrictions, mode collapse, or training-set bias can leave some images outside a model's representational reach. The paper investigates invertible neural networks, which have zero representation error by design, as priors for these inverse problems.

The authors study denoising, compressive sensing, and inpainting using a trained invertible model. Their formulations encourage high-likelihood images either through an explicit penalty or through the reconstruction algorithm's initialization. This allows the learned model to guide the reconstruction while retaining the representational capacity supplied by invertibility.

For compressive sensing, the results show that invertible priors can outperform sparsity priors across almost all undersampling ratios. They can also improve on GAN priors for images with rare variations in biased training data, including out-of-distribution natural images. The paper additionally compares against unlearned methods and gives expected-recovery-error bounds for a linear invertible model.
summary.tldr: Invertible generative priors avoid representation error and can improve image reconstruction, including for rare features poorly represented in training data.

title: Invertible generative models for inverse problems: mitigating representation error and dataset bias

abstract: Normalizing flows transform a latent distribution through an invertible neural network for a flexible and pleasingly simple approach to generative modelling, while preserving an exact likelihood. We propose FlowGMM, an end-to-end approach to generative semi supervised learning with normalizing flows, using a latent Gaussian mixture model. FlowGMM is distinct in its simplicity, unified treatment of labelled and unlabelled data with an exact likelihood, interpretability, and broad applicability beyond image data. We show promising results on a wide range of applications, including AG-News and Yahoo Answers text data, tabular data, and semi-supervised image classification. We also show that FlowGMM can discover interpretable structure, provide real-time optimization-free feature visualizations, and specify well calibrated predictive distributions.

We propose FlowGMM, an end-to-end approach to generative semi supervised learning with normalizing flows, using a latent Gaussian mixture model. FlowGMM is distinct in its simplicity, unified treatment of labelled and unlabelled data with an exact likelihood, interpretability, and broad applicability beyond image data. We show promising results on a wide range of applications, including AG-News and Yahoo Answers text data, tabular data, and semi-supervised image classification. paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines examples with labels and examples without them. FlowGMM approaches this through a generative model built from a normalizing flow: an invertible neural transformation that connects data to a latent distribution while keeping likelihood exactly computable. The latent distribution is a Gaussian mixture, giving the model a structured space in which to represent data.

The approach trains end to end and treats labeled and unlabeled observations within one likelihood-based framework. Its appeal is the combination of a relatively simple construction, interpretable latent structure, and applicability beyond images. Exact likelihood supplies a common modeling basis for the two kinds of training data.

The authors report promising results on AG-News and Yahoo Answers text, tabular datasets, and semi-supervised image classification. They also show that the model can uncover interpretable structure, produce real-time feature visualizations without additional optimization, and yield well-calibrated predictive distributions. These findings present FlowGMM as a broadly applicable semi-supervised approach, with demonstrated interpretability and uncertainty-related capabilities alongside classification results.
summary.tldr: FlowGMM combines normalizing flows with a latent Gaussian mixture to learn jointly from labeled and unlabeled data across several data types.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning with Normalizing Flows

abstract: Likelihood-free (a.k.a. simulation-based) inference problems are inverse problems with expensive, or intractable, forward models. ODE inverse problems are commonly treated as likelihood-free, as their forward map has to be numerically approximated by an ODE solver. This, however, is not a fundamental constraint but just a lack of functionality in classic ODE solvers, which do not return a likelihood but a point estimate. To address this shortcoming, we employ Gaussian ODE filtering (a probabilistic numerical method for ODEs) to construct a local Gaussian approximation to the likelihood. This approximation yields tractable estimators for the gradient and Hessian of the (log-)likelihood. Insertion of these estimators into existing gradient-based optimization and sampling methods engenders new solvers for ODE inverse problems. We demonstrate that these methods outperform standard likelihood-free approaches on three benchmark-systems.

paragraphs: Inverse problems for ordinary differential equations work backward from observations to the quantities that could have produced them. They are often approached as likelihood-free problems because computing the forward behavior requires numerical solution. This paper argues that the obstacle partly reflects what conventional solvers return: a point estimate rather than a likelihood.

The authors use Gaussian ODE filtering, a probabilistic numerical method, to construct a local Gaussian approximation to the likelihood. This approximation makes it possible to estimate both its gradient and its Hessian. These describe how the likelihood changes as the unknown quantities change, supplying information useful for directing inference.

Inserting those estimators into existing gradient-based optimization and sampling methods produces new solvers for ODE inverse problems. On three benchmark systems, the resulting methods outperform standard likelihood-free approaches. The contribution is to make derivative information available through probabilistic numerical approximation, allowing inference methods to exploit structure that a conventional point-valued solver does not provide. The likelihood remains a local approximation.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic ODE filtering supplies approximate likelihood derivatives that improve optimization and sampling on three inverse-problem benchmarks.

title: Differentiable Likelihoods for Fast Inversion of ’Likelihood-Free’ Dynamical Systems

abstract: Data tracing determines whether particular data samples have been used to train a model. We propose a new technique, radioactive data, that makes imperceptible changes to these samples such that any model trained on them will bear an identifiable mark. Given a trained model, our technique detects the use of radioactive data and provides a level of confidence (p-value). Experiments on large-scale benchmarks (Imagenet), with standard architectures (Resnet-18, VGG-16, Densenet-121) and training procedures, show that we detect radioactive data with high confidence (p<0.0001) when only 1% of the data used to train a model is radioactive. Our radioactive mark is resilient to strong data augmentations and variations of the model architecture. As a result, it offers a much higher signal-to-noise ratio than data poisoning and backdoor methods.

As a result, it offers a much higher signal-to-noise ratio than data poisoning and backdoor methods.

paragraphs: Data tracing asks whether particular samples were used to train a model. This paper proposes modifying samples imperceptibly so that training on them leaves an identifiable mark in the resulting model. The authors call these marked samples radioactive data, emphasizing that evidence of their use persists through training.

Given a trained model, the technique tests for that mark and reports a p-value expressing statistical evidence for detection. On ImageNet experiments using standard training procedures and ResNet-18, VGG-16, and DenseNet-121 architectures, the authors detect marked data with p-values below 0.0001 even when only one percent of the training data is radioactive.

The reported mark withstands strong data augmentation and changes in model architecture. The authors also report a substantially higher signal-to-noise ratio than data poisoning and backdoor methods. These findings show that small changes to a limited portion of a training set can produce a detectable training trace in the evaluated settings. The measured confidence comes from the detection test; the reported percentages and p-values describe the experiments rather than a universal detection rate.
summary.tldr: Imperceptibly marked training samples leave detectable model traces, with high-confidence detection reported when only one percent of training data is marked.

title: Radioactive data: tracing through training

abstract: Policy learning using historical observational data is an important problem that has found widespread applications. However, existing literature rests on the crucial assumption that the future environment where the learned policy will be deployed is the same as the past environment that has generated the data{–}an assumption that is often false or too coarse an approximation. In this paper, we lift this assumption and aim to learn a distributionally robust policy with bandit observational data. We propose a novel learning algorithm that is able to learn a robust policy to adversarial perturbations and unknown covariate shifts. We first present a policy evaluation procedure in the ambiguous environment and also give a heuristic algorithm to solve the distributionally robust policy learning problems efficiently. Additionally, we provide extensive simulations to demonstrate the robustness of our policy.
