However, existing literature rests on the crucial assumption that the future environment where the learned policy will be deployed is the same as the past environment that has generated the data{–}an assumption that is often false or too coarse an approximation. In this paper, we lift this assumption and aim to learn a distributionally robust policy with bandit observational data. We propose a novel learning algorithm that is able to learn a robust policy to adversarial perturbations and unknown covariate shifts. We first present a policy evaluation procedure in the ambiguous environment and also give a heuristic algorithm to solve the distributionally robust policy learning problems efficiently. Additionally, we provide extensive simulations to demonstrate the robustness of our policy.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from historical observational data is useful when decisions must be improved using existing records. A major difficulty is that the environment producing those records may differ from the environment where the policy will operate. This paper addresses that mismatch in offline contextual bandits, rather than relying on the deployment environment being identical to the historical one.

The authors develop a distributionally robust learning approach aimed at handling adversarial perturbations and unknown shifts in the covariates. They first provide a procedure for evaluating a policy when the environment is ambiguous. That evaluation step makes uncertainty about the future environment part of how a candidate policy is assessed.

They then give a heuristic algorithm for efficiently solving the robust policy learning problem. Extensive simulations demonstrate robustness of the resulting policy. The two components address complementary needs: assessing decisions under environmental uncertainty and searching for a policy that performs robustly under that uncertainty. The findings support the approach in the simulated settings, with the efficient learning procedure explicitly presented as a heuristic.
summary.tldr: A distributionally robust approach evaluates and learns offline contextual-bandit policies for environments that may differ from the historical data.

title: Distributionally Robust Policy Evaluation and Learning in Offline Contextual Bandits

abstract: Deep neural networks for natural language processing tasks are vulnerable to adversarial input perturbations. In this paper, we present a versatile language for programmatically specifying string transformations—e.g., insertions, deletions, substitutions, swaps, etc.—that are relevant to the task at hand. We then present an approach to adversarially training models that are robust to such user-defined string transformations. Our approach combines the advantages of search-based techniques for adversarial training with abstraction-based techniques. Specifically, we show how to decompose a set of user-defined string transformations into two component specifications, one that benefits from search and another from abstraction. We use our technique to train models on the AG and SST2 datasets and show that the resulting models are robust to combinations of user-defined transformations mimicking spelling mistakes and other meaning-preserving transformations.
originalAbstract: Deep neural networks for natural language processing tasks are vulnerable to adversarial input perturbations. In this paper, we present a versatile language for programmatically specifying string transformations—e.g., insertions, deletions, substitutions, swaps, etc.—that are relevant to the task at hand. We then present an approach to adversarially training models that are robust to such user-defined string transformations. Our approach combines the advantages of search-based techniques for adversarial training with abstraction-based techniques. Specifically, we show how to decompose a set of user-defined string transformations into two component specifications, one that benefits from search and another from abstraction. We use our technique to train models on the AG and SST2 datasets and show that the resulting models are robust to combinations of user-defined transformations mimicking spelling mistakes and other meaning-preserving transformations.

paragraphs: Text models can be sensitive to input changes that should leave the intended meaning intact. This paper addresses robustness to task-relevant edits through a language for specifying string transformations programmatically. Users can describe changes such as insertions, deletions, substitutions, and swaps, making the desired robustness target explicit.

The training approach combines search-based adversarial techniques with abstraction-based techniques. It decomposes a user-defined transformation specification into two components, choosing one suited to search and another suited to abstraction. This allows the method to use the advantages of both approaches within a single adversarial-training procedure rather than treating all specified transformations identically.

The authors train models on AG and SST2 and show robustness to combinations of transformations that imitate spelling mistakes and other meaning-preserving changes. The contribution is both a flexible way to express relevant perturbations and a method for training against them. The reported robustness concerns the user-defined combinations studied, with the specification determining which kinds of input changes the training addresses.
summary.tldr: A programmable transformation language and combined search-and-abstraction training improve text-model robustness to specified combinations of string edits.

title: Robustness to Programmable String Transformations via Augmented Abstract Training

abstract: Machine learning applications often require calibrated predictions, e.g. a 90% credible interval should contain the true outcome 90% of the times. However, typical definitions of calibration only require this to hold on average, and offer no guarantees on predictions made on individual samples. Thus, predictions can be systematically over or under confident on certain subgroups, leading to issues of fairness and potential vulnerabilities. We show that calibration for individual samples is possible in the regression setup if and only if the predictions are randomized, i.e. outputting randomized credible intervals. Randomization removes systematic bias by trading off bias with variance. We design a training objective to enforce individual calibration and use it to train randomized regression functions. The resulting models are more calibrated for arbitrarily chosen subgroups of the data, and can achieve higher utility in decision making against adversaries that exploit miscalibrated predictions.
originalAbstract: Machine learning applications often require calibrated predictions, e.g. a 90% credible interval should contain the true outcome 90% of the times. However, typical definitions of calibration only require this to hold on average, and offer no guarantees on predictions made on individual samples. Thus, predictions can be systematically over or under confident on certain subgroups, leading to issues of fairness and potential vulnerabilities. We show that calibration for individual samples is possible in the regression setup if and only if the predictions are randomized, i.e. outputting randomized credible intervals. Randomization removes systematic bias by trading off bias with variance. We design a training objective to enforce individual calibration and use it to train randomized regression functions. The resulting models are more calibrated for arbitrarily chosen subgroups of the data, and can achieve higher utility in decision making against adversaries that exploit miscalibrated predictions.

paragraphs: A prediction interval can have the correct coverage averaged over a dataset while remaining systematically overconfident or underconfident for particular groups. This paper studies a stronger requirement: calibration for individual samples in regression. The goal is to address errors that aggregate calibration can conceal and that can affect fairness or decisions made from predictions.

The authors show that individual calibration is possible in their regression setup if and only if predictions are randomized. In particular, the model outputs randomized credible intervals. Randomization removes systematic bias by exchanging it for variance, so the method changes the nature of prediction uncertainty rather than simply adjusting a fixed interval.

The paper designs a training objective that enforces this individual calibration requirement and uses it to learn randomized regression functions. The resulting models are better calibrated for arbitrarily selected subgroups. They can also provide higher decision-making utility against adversaries that exploit miscalibration, connecting the stronger calibration objective to consequences beyond average prediction coverage.
summary.tldr: Randomized regression forecasts enable individual calibration and can improve subgroup calibration and decisions against adversaries exploiting miscalibration.

title: Individual Calibration with Randomized Forecasting

abstract: Retrieving relevant targets from an extremely large target set under computational limits is a common challenge for information retrieval and recommendation systems. Tree models, which formulate targets as leaves of a tree with trainable node-wise scorers, have attracted a lot of interests in tackling this challenge due to their logarithmic computational complexity in both training and testing. Tree-based deep models (TDMs) and probabilistic label trees (PLTs) are two representative kinds of them. Though achieving many practical successes, existing tree models suffer from the training-testing discrepancy, where the retrieval performance deterioration caused by beam search in testing is not considered in training. This leads to an intrinsic gap between the most relevant targets and those retrieved by beam search with even the optimally trained node-wise scorers. We take a first step towards understanding and analyzing this problem theoretically, and develop the concept of Bayes optimality under beam search and calibration under beam search as general analyzing tools for this purpose. Moreover, to eliminate the discrepancy, we propose a novel algorithm for learning optimal tree models under beam search. Experiments on both synthetic and real data verify the rationality of our theoretical analysis and demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm compared to state-of-the-art methods.

The authors develop concepts of Bayes optimality and calibration specifically under beam search, providing tools for analyzing retrieval quality in terms of the procedure actually used at test time.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the theoretical analysis and show improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The central implication is that tree-model training should account for how candidates are searched, because optimal node scoring alone can leave an intrinsic retrieval gap.

title: Learning Optimal Tree Models under Beam Search

abstract: The automation of probabilistic reasoning is one of the primary aims of machine learning. Recently, the confluence of variational inference and deep learning has led to powerful and flexible automatic inference methods that can be trained by stochastic gradient descent. In particular, normalizing flows are highly parameterized deep models that can fit arbitrarily complex posterior densities. However, normalizing flows struggle in highly structured probabilistic programs as they need to relearn the forward-pass of the program. Automatic structured variational inference (ASVI) remedies this problem by constructing variational programs that embed the forward-pass. Here, we combine the flexibility of normalizing flows and the prior-embedding property of ASVI in a new family of variational programs, which we named cascading flows. A cascading flows program interposes a newly designed highway flow architecture in between the conditional distributions of the prior program such as to steer it toward the observed data. These programs can be constructed automatically from an input probabilistic program and can also be amortized automatically. We evaluate the performance of the new variational programs in a series of structured inference problems. We find that cascading flows have much higher performance than both normalizing flows and ASVI in a large set of structured inference problems.

paragraphs: Automatic probabilistic inference must adapt a model's prior beliefs to observed data. Normalizing flows offer flexible distributions for this task, but can struggle with highly structured probabilistic programs because they must relearn the program's forward computation. Automatic structured variational inference addresses that problem by retaining the forward computation inside the approximation.

Cascading flows combine these two ideas. They preserve the prior program's structure while inserting a new highway flow architecture between its conditional distributions. These inserted transformations steer the program toward the observations, supplying flexibility without discarding the relationships already encoded in the original probabilistic program.

The resulting variational programs can be constructed automatically from an input program and can also be amortized automatically, allowing inference to be shared across cases. In evaluations on a large set of structured inference problems, the authors report substantially better performance than both normalizing flows and automatic structured variational inference. The finding supports combining structural information with flexible transformations for the kinds of inference problems studied.
summary.tldr: Cascading flows combine a probabilistic program's prior structure with flexible flow transformations, improving performance across the structured inference problems evaluated.

title: Automatic variational inference with cascading flows

abstract: As humans interact with autonomous agents to perform increasingly complicated, potentially risky tasks, it is important to be able to efficiently evaluate an agent’s performance and correctness. In this paper we formalize and theoretically analyze the problem of efficient value alignment verification: how to efficiently test whether the behavior of another agent is aligned with a human’s values? The goal is to construct a kind of "driver’s test" that a human can give to any agent which will verify value alignment via a minimal number of queries. We study alignment verification problems with both idealized humans that have an explicit reward function as well as problems where they have implicit values. We analyze verification of exact value alignment for rational agents, propose and test heuristics for value alignment verification in gridworlds and a continuous autonomous driving domain, and prove that there exist sufficient conditions such that we can verify epsilon-alignment in any environment via a constant-query-complexity alignment test.

paragraphs: As autonomous agents take on complicated and potentially risky tasks, checking whether their behavior matches human values becomes important. This paper formalizes value alignment verification as a testing problem. The aim is a compact assessment, analogous to a driver’s test, that verifies alignment using as few queries as possible.

The authors consider both idealized humans with an explicit reward function and humans whose values remain implicit. They analyze exact alignment verification for rational agents and develop heuristics tested in gridworlds and a continuous autonomous driving domain. These settings separate a mathematically explicit version of the problem from more practical testing procedures.

A theoretical result establishes sufficient conditions under which approximate, or epsilon, alignment can be verified in any environment with constant query complexity. The conditions are essential: this is not an unconditional guarantee that a short test certifies every agent. The contribution identifies circumstances permitting efficient verification while also exploring heuristic approaches for settings where practical evaluation is needed.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes efficient alignment testing and proves that sufficient conditions permit constant-query verification of approximate value alignment.

title: Value Alignment Verification

abstract: Through sequential construction of posteriors on observing data online, Bayes’ theorem provides a natural framework for continual learning. We develop Variational Auto-Regressive Gaussian Processes (VAR-GPs), a principled posterior updating mechanism to solve sequential tasks in continual learning. By relying on sparse inducing point approximations for scalable posteriors, we propose a novel auto-regressive variational distribution which reveals two fruitful connections to existing results in Bayesian inference, expectation propagation and orthogonal inducing points. Mean predictive entropy estimates show VAR-GPs prevent catastrophic forgetting, which is empirically supported by strong performance on modern continual learning benchmarks against competitive baselines. A thorough ablation study demonstrates the efficacy of our modeling choices.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires updating a model as tasks arrive sequentially while retaining useful knowledge from earlier tasks. Bayesian inference offers a natural formulation: each new batch of evidence updates the current posterior. This paper develops Variational Auto-Regressive Gaussian Processes, or VAR-GPs, as a principled mechanism for carrying out those sequential updates.

The method uses sparse inducing-point approximations to make posterior representations scalable. Its distinctive component is an autoregressive variational distribution, which structures the approximation used during updating. The authors show connections between this construction and two existing Bayesian ideas, expectation propagation and orthogonal inducing points, helping situate the proposed mechanism within established inference methods.

Mean predictive entropy estimates indicate that VAR-GPs prevent catastrophic forgetting, and strong performance against competitive baselines on continual-learning benchmarks provides empirical support. An ablation study further supports the modeling choices. These findings connect the posterior-updating design to observed retention across tasks: the evidence comes from uncertainty estimates, benchmark performance, and experiments that examine the contribution of the method's components.
summary.tldr: VAR-GPs use structured Bayesian posterior updates for continual learning, with empirical evidence supporting resistance to catastrophic forgetting.

title: Variational Auto-Regressive Gaussian Processes for Continual Learning

abstract: Multi-layered network exploration (MuLaNE) problem is an important problem abstracted from many applications. In MuLaNE, there are multiple network layers where each node has an importance weight and each layer is explored by a random walk. The MuLaNE task is to allocate total random walk budget $B$ into each network layer so that the total weights of the unique nodes visited by random walks are maximized. We systematically study this problem from offline optimization to online learning. For the offline optimization setting where the network structure and node weights are known, we provide greedy based constant-ratio approximation algorithms for overlapping networks, and greedy or dynamic-programming based optimal solutions for non-overlapping networks. For the online learning setting, neither the network structure nor the node weights are known initially. We adapt the combinatorial multi-armed bandit framework and design algorithms to learn random walk related parameters and node weights while optimizing the budget allocation in multiple rounds, and prove that they achieve logarithmic regret bounds. Finally, we conduct experiments on a real-world social network dataset to validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to divide a limited exploration budget across several network layers. A random walk explores each layer, and every node has an importance weight. The objective is to maximize the combined weight of distinct nodes visited, so repeated visits do not contribute additional value to the objective.

When network structures and node weights are known, the authors develop algorithms according to whether the layers overlap. For overlapping networks, greedy-based methods provide constant-ratio approximation guarantees. For non-overlapping networks, greedy or dynamic-programming approaches provide optimal solutions. These results distinguish settings where the proposed methods approximate the best allocation from those where they attain it.

The paper also considers repeated exploration when neither network structure nor node weights are initially known. Using a combinatorial multi-armed bandit framework, the algorithms learn random-walk parameters and node weights while allocating the budget. The authors prove logarithmic regret bounds and evaluate their methods on a real-world social network dataset. The overall contribution joins budget allocation with learning, covering both full-information planning and decisions made while the relevant network information is still being discovered.
summary.tldr: The paper develops guaranteed methods for allocating random-walk budgets across network layers with known or initially unknown information.

title: Multi-layered Network Exploration via Random Walks: From Offline Optimization to Online Learning

abstract: Imitation learning trains control policies by mimicking pre-recorded expert demonstrations. In partially observable settings, imitation policies must rely on observation histories, but many seemingly paradoxical results show better performance for policies that only access the most recent observation. Recent solutions ranging from causal graph learning to deep information bottlenecks have shown promising results, but failed to scale to realistic settings such as visual imitation. We propose a solution that outperforms these prior approaches by upweighting demonstration keyframes corresponding to expert action changepoints. This simple approach easily scales to complex visual imitation settings. Our experimental results demonstrate consistent performance improvements over all baselines on image-based Gym MuJoCo continuous control tasks. Finally, on the CARLA photorealistic vision-based urban driving simulator, we resolve a long-standing issue in behavioral cloning for driving by demonstrating effective imitation from observation histories. Supplementary materials and code at: \url{https://tinyurl.com/imitation-keyframes}.

paragraphs: Imitation learning trains a policy from recorded expert behavior. When a single observation does not reveal the full situation, a policy needs observation history. Yet prior results have sometimes found that policies using only the latest observation perform better. This paper tackles that tension in visual imitation, where earlier proposed remedies had struggled to scale.

The approach gives additional training weight to demonstration keyframes at which the expert's action changes. This places greater emphasis on moments marking a change in behavior. The method is simple enough to apply to complex visual inputs, making action changepoints a practical source of structure in demonstration data.

Experiments report consistent improvements over all tested baselines on image-based Gym MuJoCo continuous-control tasks. In the CARLA urban-driving simulator, the method also demonstrates effective imitation using observation histories, addressing a longstanding behavioral-cloning issue described by the authors. These results support selective weighting of demonstration moments as a scalable way to improve learning from visual histories.
summary.tldr: Giving extra weight to expert action-change keyframes improves visual imitation and enables effective use of observation histories in simulated driving.

title: Keyframe-Focused Visual Imitation Learning

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks have demonstrated dermatologist-level performance in the classification of melanoma from skin lesion images, but prediction irregularities due to biases seen within the training data are an issue that should be addressed before widespread deployment is possible. In this work, we robustly remove bias and spurious variation from an automated melanoma classification pipeline using two leading bias unlearning techniques. We show that the biases introduced by surgical markings and rulers presented in previous studies can be reasonably mitigated using these bias removal methods. We also demonstrate the generalisation benefits of unlearning spurious variation relating to the imaging instrument used to capture lesion images. Our experimental results provide evidence that the effects of each of the aforementioned biases are notably reduced, with different debiasing techniques excelling at different tasks.

paragraphs: A melanoma classifier can perform well while still relying on misleading patterns in its training images. This paper examines biases associated with visible surgical markings, rulers, and the instrument used to capture lesion images. Such influences can create irregular predictions even when convolutional networks achieve dermatologist-level classification performance.

The authors apply two leading bias-unlearning techniques within an automated melanoma classification pipeline. Their goal is to reduce the influence of these unwanted image variations on the classifier. They show that the effects of surgical markings and rulers identified in previous studies can be reasonably mitigated using the methods.

They also demonstrate generalization benefits from unlearning variation associated with the imaging instrument. Across the experiments, the effects of all three kinds of bias are notably reduced, while different techniques perform best on different tasks. These results support debiasing as a useful part of the pipeline, with evidence of mitigation rather than a claim that the studied biases have been completely eliminated.
summary.tldr: Two bias-unlearning methods reduce melanoma classifiers’ sensitivity to image artifacts and imaging instruments, with different strengths across tasks.

title: Skin Deep Unlearning: Artefact and Instrument Debiasing in the Context of Melanoma Classification

abstract: In this paper, we extend the remarkable M-estimator of Catoni \citep{Cat12} to situations where the variance is infinite. In particular, given a sequence of i.i.d random variables $\{X_i\}_{i=1}^n$ from distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathbb{R}$ with mean $\mu$, we only assume the existence of a known upper bound $\upsilon_{\varepsilon} > 0$ on the $(1+\varepsilon)^{th}$ central moment of the random variables, namely, for $\varepsilon \in (0,1]$ \[ \mathbb{E}_{X_1 \sim \mathcal{D}} \Big| X_1 - \mu \Big|^{1+\varepsilon} \leq \upsilon_{\varepsilon}. \]{The} extension is non-trivial owing to the difficulty in characterizing the roots of certain polynomials of degree smaller than $2$. The proposed estimator has the same order of magnitude and the same asymptotic constant as in \citet{Cat12}, but for the case of bounded moments. We further propose a version of the estimator that does not require even the knowledge of $\upsilon_{\varepsilon}$, but adapts the moment bound in a data-driven manner. Finally, to illustrate the usefulness of the derived non-asymptotic confidence bounds, we consider an application in multi-armed bandits and propose best arm identification algorithms, in the fixed confidence setting, that outperform the state of the art.

paragraphs: This paper extends Catoni’s mean estimator to distributions that may have infinite variance. It considers independent, identically distributed real-valued observations and initially assumes a known bound on their central moment of order one plus epsilon. For epsilon below one, this assumption permits settings where a finite-variance requirement would be too restrictive.

The extension requires resolving difficulties involving roots of polynomials with degree below two. The resulting estimator preserves the order of magnitude and asymptotic constant of Catoni’s earlier result in the bounded-moment setting considered here. The authors also propose an adaptive version that learns the moment bound from data, removing the need to supply that bound in advance.

The work provides confidence bounds that apply at finite sample sizes. To demonstrate their usefulness, the authors develop best-arm identification algorithms for multi-armed bandits under a fixed-confidence requirement. They report improvements over the state of the art. The contribution links robust mean estimation under weak moment conditions to decisions that require controlled uncertainty.
summary.tldr: An extension of Catoni’s estimator handles potentially infinite variance, supports an adaptive moment bound, and improves fixed-confidence best-arm identification.

title: Nearly Optimal Catoni’s M-estimator for Infinite Variance

abstract: In contrast to SGD, adaptive gradient methods like Adam allow robust training of modern deep networks, especially large language models. However, the use of adaptivity not only comes at the cost of extra memory but also raises the fundamental question: can non-adaptive methods like SGD enjoy similar benefits? In this paper, we provide an affirmative answer to this question by proposing to achieve both robust and memory-efficient training via the following general recipe: (1) modify the architecture and make it scale invariant, (2) train with SGD and weight decay, and optionally (3) clip the global gradient norm proportional to weight norm multiplied by $\sqrt{\frac{2\lambda}{\eta}}$, where $\eta$ is learning rate and $\lambda$ is weight decay. We show that this general approach is robust to rescaling of parameter and loss by proving that its convergence only depends logarithmically on the scale of initialization and loss, whereas the standard SGD might not even converge for many initializations. Following our recipe, we design a scale invariant version of BERT, called SIBERT, which when trained simply by vanilla SGD achieves performance comparable to BERT trained by adaptive methods like Adam on downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adam can make deep-network training robust, but require extra memory. This paper asks whether ordinary stochastic gradient descent can obtain similar benefits through architectural changes. Its proposed recipe makes the architecture scale invariant and trains it with SGD and weight decay.

The recipe optionally clips the global gradient norm using a threshold proportional to the weight norm times the square root of twice the weight decay divided by the learning rate. The authors prove robustness to parameter and loss rescaling: convergence depends only logarithmically on initialization and loss scales. By comparison, standard SGD may fail to converge for many initializations.

To demonstrate the approach, the authors construct SIBERT, a scale-invariant version of BERT. Trained with vanilla SGD, it achieves downstream-task performance comparable to BERT trained with adaptive methods such as Adam. The contribution links an architectural property to optimization robustness, showing how changing the network can help a memory-efficient optimizer work effectively in the reported setting.
summary.tldr: Scale-invariant architectures let SGD with weight decay train robustly, with SIBERT matching adaptive-optimizer BERT performance on reported downstream tasks.

title: Robust Training of Neural Networks Using Scale Invariant Architectures

abstract: Minwise hashing (MinHash) is an important and practical algorithm for generating random hashes to approximate the Jaccard (resemblance) similarity in massive binary (0/1) data. The basic theory of MinHash requires applying hundreds or even thousands of independent random permutations to each data vector in the dataset, in order to obtain reliable results for (e.g.,) building large-scale learning models or approximate near neighbor search. In this paper, we propose Circulant MinHash (C-MinHash) and provide the surprising theoretical results that using only two independent random permutations in a circulant manner leads to uniformly smaller Jaccard estimation variance than that of the classical MinHash with K independent permutations. Experiments are conducted to show the effectiveness of the proposed method. We also propose a more convenient C-MinHash variant which reduces two permutations to just one, with extensive numerical results to validate that it achieves essentially the same estimation accuracy as using two permutations.

paragraphs: MinHash produces compact random summaries for estimating Jaccard similarity in large binary datasets. This similarity measures resemblance between sets of present features. Classical MinHash theory relies on many independent random permutations, potentially hundreds or thousands per data vector, to obtain reliable estimates for tasks such as approximate neighbor search.

Circulant MinHash changes how those permutations are constructed and reused. It starts from only two independent random permutations and applies them in a circulant arrangement. The paper proves that this construction yields uniformly smaller variance in Jaccard estimates than classical MinHash using K independent permutations. Thus, reducing the number of independent permutations does not require accepting noisier estimates in the stated theoretical comparison.

Experiments support the proposed construction. The authors also introduce a simpler variant that uses just one permutation. Extensive numerical results show essentially the same estimation accuracy as the two-permutation version. The distinction matters: the two-permutation method has the stated variance theorem, while the one-permutation variant’s comparable accuracy is supported empirically.
summary.tldr: C-MinHash uses two independent permutations in a circulant construction to provably reduce Jaccard estimation variance relative to classical MinHash.

title: C-MinHash: Improving Minwise Hashing with Circulant Permutation

abstract: Neural networks (NNs) are known to be vulnerable against adversarial perturbations, and thus there is a line of work aiming to provide robustness certification for NNs, such as randomized smoothing, which samples smoothing noises from a certain distribution to certify the robustness for a smoothed classifier. However, as previous work shows, the certified robust radius in randomized smoothing suffers from scaling to large datasets ("curse of dimensionality"). To overcome this hurdle, we propose a Double Sampling Randomized Smoothing (DSRS) framework, which exploits the sampled probability from an additional smoothing distribution to tighten the robustness certification of the previous smoothed classifier. Theoretically, under mild assumptions, we prove that DSRS can certify $\Theta(\sqrt d)$ robust radius under $\ell_2$ norm where $d$ is the input dimension, which implies that DSRS may be able to break the curse of dimensionality of randomized smoothing. We instantiate DSRS for a generalized family of Gaussian smoothing and propose an efficient and sound computing method based on customized dual optimization considering sampling error. Extensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet verify our theory and show that DSRS certifies larger robust radii than existing baselines consistently under different settings. Code is available at https://github.com/llylly/DSRS.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing certifies a classifier’s robustness by evaluating its behavior under randomly sampled input noise. Its certified radius can suffer from dimensionality-related limits. Double Sampling Randomized Smoothing adds information from a second noise distribution to tighten the robustness certificate for the existing smoothed classifier.

The added distribution supplies another sampled probability that constrains the certification problem. Under stated mild assumptions, the authors prove that DSRS can certify an ℓ2 radius scaling as Θ(√d), where d is input dimension. This result suggests that the framework may overcome the dimensionality barrier; the conclusion remains tied to the assumptions of the analysis.

The paper instantiates the framework for a generalized Gaussian smoothing family and develops a customized dual-optimization procedure that accounts for sampling error. This provides an efficient, sound way to compute the certificate from estimated probabilities. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet support the theory and consistently produce larger certified radii than the compared baselines across the studied settings.
summary.tldr: DSRS tightens randomized-smoothing robustness certificates using an additional noise distribution, with conditional theory and experiments supporting larger certified radii.

title: Double Sampling Randomized Smoothing

abstract: We introduce ProxSkip—a surprisingly simple and provably efficient method for minimizing the sum of a smooth ($f$) and an expensive nonsmooth proximable ($\psi$) function. The canonical approach to solving such problems is via the proximal gradient descent (ProxGD) algorithm, which is based on the evaluation of the gradient of $f$ and the prox operator of $\psi$ in each iteration. In this work we are specifically interested in the regime in which the evaluation of prox is costly relative to the evaluation of the gradient, which is the case in many applications. ProxSkip allows for the expensive prox operator to be skipped in most iterations: while its iteration complexity is $\mathcal{O}(\kappa \log \nicefrac{1}{\varepsilon})$, where $\kappa$ is the condition number of $f$, the number of prox evaluations is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\kappa} \log \nicefrac{1}{\varepsilon})$ only. Our main motivation comes from federated learning, where evaluation of the gradient operator corresponds to taking a local GD step independently on all devices, and evaluation of prox corresponds to (expensive) communication in the form of gradient averaging. In this context, ProxSkip offers an effective acceleration of communication complexity. Unlike other local gradient-type methods, such as FedAvg, SCAFFOLD, S-Local-GD and FedLin, whose theoretical communication complexity is worse than, or at best matching, that of vanilla GD in the heterogeneous data regime, we obtain a provable and large improvement without any heterogeneity-bounding assumptions.

summary.tldr: ProxSkip provably reduces expensive proximal evaluations, yielding federated communication acceleration without heterogeneity-bounding assumptions.

title: ProxSkip: Yes! Local Gradient Steps Provably Lead to Communication Acceleration! Finally!

abstract: Recent years have witnessed a surge of interest in developing trustworthy methods to evaluate the value of data in many real-world applications (e.g., collaborative machine learning, data marketplaces). Existing data valuation methods typically valuate data using the generalization performance of converged machine learning models after their long-term model training, hence making data valuation on large complex deep neural networks (DNNs) unaffordable. To this end, we theoretically derive a domain-aware generalization bound to estimate the generalization performance of DNNs without model training. We then exploit this theoretically derived generalization bound to develop a novel training-free data valuation method named data valuation at initialization (DAVINZ) on DNNs, which consistently achieves remarkable effectiveness and efficiency in practice. Moreover, our training-free DAVINZ, surprisingly, can even theoretically and empirically enjoy the desirable properties that training-based data valuation methods usually attain, thus making it more trustworthy in practice.

paragraphs: Data valuation asks how useful data is for learning, a question relevant to collaborative machine learning and data marketplaces. Existing approaches commonly assess that usefulness through the generalization performance of fully trained models. For large neural networks, the resulting training expense can make valuation unaffordable before the value of the data has even been established.

DAVINZ moves the assessment to model initialization. The authors derive a domain-aware generalization bound that estimates neural-network generalization performance without training the model, then use that bound as the basis of a valuation method. The method’s central computational advantage comes from avoiding the long optimization process used by training-based valuation approaches.

The authors report strong practical effectiveness and efficiency. They also provide theoretical and empirical support that DAVINZ can possess desirable properties normally attained by training-based valuation methods. The stated findings therefore concern both computation and valuation quality: avoiding training can still support useful, theoretically motivated assessments of data rather than merely cheaper calculations.
summary.tldr: DAVINZ uses a domain-aware generalization bound to value data with neural networks at initialization, avoiding model training.

title: DAVINZ: Data Valuation using Deep Neural Networks at Initialization

abstract: Collaborative learning algorithms, such as distributed SGD (or D-SGD), are prone to faulty machines that may deviate from their prescribed algorithm because of software or hardware bugs, poisoned data or malicious behaviors. While many solutions have been proposed to enhance the robustness of D-SGD to such machines, previous works either resort to strong assumptions (trusted server, homogeneous data, specific noise model) or impose a gradient computational cost that is several orders of magnitude higher than that of D-SGD. We present MoNNA, a new algorithm that (a) is provably robust under standard assumptions and (b) has a gradient computation overhead that is linear in the fraction of faulty machines, which is conjectured to be tight. Essentially, MoNNA uses Polyak’s momentum of local gradients for local updates and nearest-neighbor averaging (NNA) for global mixing, respectively. While MoNNA is rather simple to implement, its analysis has been more challenging and relies on two key elements that may be of independent interest. Specifically, we introduce the mixing criterion of $(\alpha, \lambda)$-reduction to analyze the non-linear mixing of non-faulty machines, and present a way to control the tension between the momentum and the model drifts. We validate our theory by experiments on image classification and make our code available at https://github.com/LPD-EPFL/robust-collaborative-learning.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning can be disrupted by machines that send faulty updates because of bugs, poisoned data, or malicious behavior. Existing defenses may rely on strong assumptions or substantially increase gradient computation. This paper introduces MoNNA, aiming to provide robustness with an overhead that grows linearly with the fraction of faulty machines.

MoNNA combines momentum applied to local gradients with nearest-neighbor averaging for mixing information across machines. Its analysis introduces a mixing criterion called alpha-lambda reduction to study the nonlinear interaction among non-faulty machines. It also develops a way to control the tension between momentum and divergence among local models, which is important to establishing the robustness result.

The authors prove robustness under their standard assumptions and validate the theory with image-classification experiments. They conjecture that the linear gradient overhead is tight; the abstract does not present that optimality as proved. The contribution is a relatively simple algorithm paired with an analysis that links fault tolerance to a controlled additional gradient-computation cost.
summary.tldr: MoNNA combines momentum and nearest-neighbor averaging to provide provable collaborative-learning robustness with gradient overhead linear in the faulty-machine fraction.

title: Robust Collaborative Learning with Linear Gradient Overhead

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have greatly advanced the semi-supervised node classification task on graphs. The majority of existing GNNs are trained in an end-to-end manner that can be viewed as tackling a bi-level optimization problem. This process is often inefficient in computation and memory usage. In this work, we propose a new optimization framework for semi-supervised learning on graphs from a multi-view learning perspective. The proposed framework can be conveniently solved by the alternating optimization algorithms, resulting in significantly improved efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve comparable or better performance with state-of-the-art baselines while it has significantly better computation and memory efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational cost of training graph neural networks for semi-supervised node classification. In this task, a model learns to classify graph nodes using a limited supply of labels. The authors argue that the usual end-to-end training process can be understood as a two-level optimization problem, and that solving it this way often consumes substantial computation and memory.

They introduce a different optimization framework based on a multi-view learning perspective. Its structure allows the learning problem to be handled through alternating optimization: different parts of the problem are updated in turn. The contribution therefore concerns how graph learning is organized and optimized, with efficiency as a central objective.

Extensive experiments show comparable or better predictive performance than the state-of-the-art baselines considered, together with substantially improved computation and memory efficiency. These findings suggest that changing the optimization framework can preserve strong node classification performance while reducing training demands. The reported advantage combines predictive quality and resource use, rather than relying on efficiency alone.
summary.tldr: An alternating optimization framework makes semi-supervised graph learning more efficient while matching or improving the tested baselines’ predictive performance.

title: Alternately Optimized Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is the problem of learning a symbolic expression from numerical data. Recently, deep neural models trained on procedurally-generated synthetic datasets showed competitive performance compared to more classical Genetic Programming (GP) ones. Unlike their GP counterparts, these neural approaches are trained to generate expressions from datasets given as context. This allows them to produce accurate expressions in a single forward pass at test time. However, they usually do not benefit from search abilities, which result in low performance compared to GP on out-of-distribution datasets. In this paper, we propose a novel method which provides the best of both worlds, based on a Monte-Carlo Tree Search procedure using a context-aware neural mutation model, which is initially pre-trained to learn promising mutations, and further refined from successful experiences in an online fashion. The approach demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the well-known SRBench benchmark.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression seeks a mathematical expression that explains numerical data. Neural approaches can generate accurate expressions in a single forward pass after training on synthetic examples. However, the authors identify a weakness: these approaches usually lack search capabilities and perform worse than genetic programming on datasets outside their training distribution.

The proposed method combines a learned expression-mutation model with Monte Carlo Tree Search. The neural model uses the dataset as context when proposing promising changes to an expression. It is first pretrained to make useful mutations, then refined online using successful experiences. Search and learning therefore contribute jointly to the process of finding expressions.

This design brings data-conditioned neural proposals into an explicit search procedure, addressing the stated gap between fast neural generation and the search abilities of genetic programming. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on SRBench. That benchmark result supports the combined approach as an effective symbolic regression method, while the mechanism explains how it can continue exploring beyond an initial generated expression.
summary.tldr: A neural mutation model guides Monte Carlo Tree Search to find symbolic expressions, achieving state-of-the-art SRBench performance.

title: Deep Generative Symbolic Regression with Monte-Carlo-Tree-Search

abstract: We consider test-time adaptation (TTA), the task of adapting a trained model to an arbitrary test domain using unlabeled input data on-the-fly during testing. A common practice of TTA is to disregard data used in training due to large memory demand and privacy leakage. However, the training data are the only source of supervision. This motivates us to investigate a proper way of using them while minimizing the side effects. To this end, we propose two lightweight yet informative proxies of the training data and a TTA method fully exploiting them. One of the proxies is composed of a small number of images synthesized (hence, less privacy-sensitive) by data condensation which minimizes their domain-specificity to capture a general underlying structure over a wide spectrum of domains. Then, in TTA, they are translated into labeled test data by stylizing them to match styles of unlabeled test samples. This enables virtually supervised test-time training. The other proxy is inter-class relations of training data, which are transferred to target model during TTA. On four public benchmarks, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art ones at remarkably less computation and memory.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a trained model using unlabeled inputs from a new domain. Training data are often excluded because retaining them consumes memory and raises privacy concerns, yet they contain the original supervision. This paper proposes preserving useful information from those data in two lightweight proxies.

The first proxy is a small collection of synthetic images produced through data condensation. Their construction reduces domain-specific characteristics to capture structure shared across domains. During adaptation, the images are stylized to match incoming test samples, turning them into labeled examples suited to the test domain and enabling a form of supervised test-time training.

The second proxy preserves relationships between classes and transfers those relationships to the adapting model. Together, the proxies supply both labeled synthetic examples and information about class structure. On four public benchmarks, the method outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches while using substantially less computation and memory. The synthetic images are described as less privacy-sensitive, so the contribution is reduced reliance on stored original data rather than a formal privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: Synthetic training images and stored class relationships provide compact supervision for efficient test-time adaptation.

title: Leveraging Proxy of Training Data for Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: Bayesian approaches for learning deep neural networks (BNN) have been received much attention and successfully applied to various applications. Particularly, BNNs have the merit of having better generalization ability as well as better uncertainty quantification. For the success of BNN, search an appropriate architecture of the neural networks is an important task, and various algorithms to find good sparse neural networks have been proposed. In this paper, we propose a new node-sparse BNN model which has good theoretical properties and is computationally feasible. We prove that the posterior concentration rate to the true model is near minimax optimal and adaptive to the smoothness of the true model. In particular the adaptiveness is the first of its kind for node-sparse BNNs. In addition, we develop a novel MCMC algorithm which makes the Bayesian inference of the node-sparse BNN model feasible in practice.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty over a model rather than relying on a single fitted network. Choosing a suitable architecture remains important, and sparse networks offer one way to control that structure. This paper proposes a node-sparse Bayesian model, making the selection of active nodes part of the modeling approach.

The theoretical contribution concerns posterior concentration: how quickly the model’s posterior distribution gathers around the true model as data accumulate. The authors prove a rate that is near minimax optimal and adapts to the true model’s smoothness. In practical terms, the guarantee adjusts to this property of the underlying target rather than being tied to only one smoothness level. The authors identify this adaptivity result as the first for node-sparse Bayesian neural networks.

The paper also introduces a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for posterior inference in the proposed model. This addresses the computational side of using the sparse Bayesian formulation. Together, the contributions combine an adaptive statistical guarantee with an inference procedure intended to make that formulation feasible in practice.
summary.tldr: A node-sparse Bayesian neural network combines near-optimal, smoothness-adaptive posterior concentration with a practical MCMC inference algorithm.

title: Masked Bayesian Neural Networks : Theoretical Guarantee and its Posterior Inference

abstract: This paper addresses unsupervised representation learning on tabular data containing multiple views generated by distinct sources of measurement. Traditional methods, which tackle this problem using the multi-view framework, are constrained by predefined assumptions that assume feature sets share the same information and representations should learn globally shared factors. However, this assumption is not always valid for real-world tabular datasets with complex dependencies between feature sets, resulting in localized information that is harder to learn. To overcome this limitation, we propose a data-driven approach that learns feature set dependencies by representing feature sets as graph nodes and their relationships as learnable edges. Furthermore, we introduce $\texttt{LEGATO}$, a novel hierarchical graph autoencoder that learns a smaller, latent graph to aggregate information from multiple views dynamically. This approach results in latent graph components that specialize in capturing localized information from different regions of the input, leading to superior downstream performance.

paragraphs: Tabular datasets can contain several views produced by different measurement sources. Traditional multi-view representation learning often assumes these feature groups share information and should be explained by globally shared factors. The paper addresses cases where dependencies are more complex and useful information is localized to particular groups.

The proposed approach represents feature sets as graph nodes and learns the edges that describe their relationships. LEGATO, its hierarchical graph autoencoder, then learns a smaller latent graph that dynamically combines information from the input views. This makes the relationships among feature groups something learned from data instead of relying on a predefined pattern of globally shared information.

Components of the latent graph specialize in information from different regions of the input. The authors report that this leads to superior downstream performance. The result supports allowing a representation to retain several localized sources of information, particularly when the assumptions used by traditional multi-view methods do not match the dependencies present in the dataset.
summary.tldr: LEGATO learns relationships among tabular feature groups and uses a latent graph to capture localized information.

title: Learning Representations without Compositional Assumptions

abstract: Masked Image Modeling (MIM) is a promising self-supervised learning approach that enables learning from unlabeled images. Despite its recent success, learning good representations through MIM remains challenging because it requires predicting the right semantic content in accurate locations. For example, given an incomplete picture of a dog, we can guess that there is a tail, but we cannot determine its exact location. In this work, we propose to incorporate location uncertainty to MIM by using stochastic positional embeddings (StoP). Specifically, we condition the model on stochastic masked token positions drawn from a gaussian distribution. We show that using StoP reduces overfitting to location features and guides the model toward learning features that are more robust to location uncertainties. Quantitatively, using StoP improves downstream MIM performance on a variety of downstream tasks. For example, linear probing on ImageNet using ViT-B is improved by $+1.7%$, and by $2.5%$ for ViT-H using 1% of the data.

paragraphs: Masked image modeling learns from unlabeled images by predicting missing content. That task mixes two demands: recognizing what belongs in the image and locating it precisely. The visible content may support a plausible semantic prediction without determining its exact position, creating uncertainty that a model’s training should account for.

The paper introduces stochastic positional embeddings, called StoP, to represent that uncertainty. Instead of conditioning only on fixed masked-token positions, the model receives positions sampled from a Gaussian distribution. The authors show that this reduces overfitting to location features and encourages representations that remain useful when location is uncertain. The change directly targets the positional information supplied during masked-image learning.

StoP improves downstream performance on a variety of tasks in the reported experiments. Examples include a reported 1.7% improvement in ImageNet linear probing with ViT-B and 2.5% with ViT-H using 1% of the data. These results support treating location uncertainty as part of representation learning, with benefits measured through the usefulness of the resulting features on downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: Sampling masked-token positions from a Gaussian distribution reduces location overfitting and improves masked-image representations.

title: Stochastic positional embeddings improve masked image modeling

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) aligns language models to human preferences by employing a singular reward model derived from preference data. However, the single reward model overlooks the rich diversity of human preferences inherent in data collected from multiple users. In this work, we first derive an impossibility result of alignment with single reward RLHF, thereby highlighting its insufficiency in representing diverse human preferences. Next, we propose to learn a mixture of reward models via an expectation-maximization algorithm and solve a MaxMin alignment objective inspired by the Egalitarian principle in social choice theory to better honor diverse human preferences. We present comprehensive experimental results on small-scale (GPT-2) and large-scale language (with Tulu2-7B)) and show the efficacy of the proposed approach in the presence of diversity among human preferences. We remark that our findings in this work are not only limited to language models but also extend to reinforcement learning in general.

paragraphs: Human feedback can contain different and conflicting preferences, yet conventional RLHF combines that feedback into a single reward model. This paper examines the consequences of that compression. The authors derive an impossibility result for alignment using a single reward, highlighting its insufficiency for representing diverse human preferences in the setting they study.

Their alternative learns a mixture of reward models using expectation-maximization. This allows the preference data to be represented through multiple reward models instead of one shared evaluation. The alignment step then uses a MaxMin objective inspired by the egalitarian principle in social choice: it gives attention to the least well-served preferences represented by the objective.

The authors evaluate the method with GPT-2 and Tulu2-7B and report that it is effective when human preferences are diverse. These experiments connect the representational argument to language-model alignment at different scales. The paper also states that its findings extend to reinforcement learning more generally, where representing several human preferences can likewise matter for defining what an agent should optimize.
summary.tldr: MaxMin-RLHF combines multiple reward models with an egalitarian objective to better account for diverse human preferences.

title: MaxMin-RLHF: Alignment with Diverse Human Preferences

abstract: Performative prediction, as introduced by Perdomo et al., is a framework for studying social prediction in which the data distribution itself changes in response to the deployment of a model. Existing work in this field usually hinges on three assumptions that are easily violated in practice: that the performative risk is convex over the deployed model, that the mapping from the model to the data distribution is known to the model designer in advance, and the first-order information of the performative risk is available. In this paper, we initiate the study of performative prediction problems that do not require these assumptions. Specifically, we develop a parameterization framework that parametrizes the performative prediction objective as a function of the induced data distribution. We also develop a two-level zeroth-order optimization procedure, where the first level performs iterative optimization on the distribution parameter space, and the second level learns the model that induced a particular target distribution parameter at each iteration. Under mild conditions, this reparameterization allows us to transform the non-convex objective into a convex one and achieve provable regret guarantees. In particular, we provide a regret bound that is sublinear in the total number of performative samples taken and is only polynomial in the dimension of the model parameter.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, deploying a model changes the data distribution it will encounter. Optimizing such a model therefore requires accounting for its influence on the environment. This paper addresses settings where the objective need not be convex in model parameters, the model’s effect on the distribution is unknown, and gradient information is unavailable.

The proposed framework rewrites the objective in terms of parameters describing the induced data distribution. A two-level procedure then operates without gradients. One level optimizes over distribution parameters; the other learns a model that induces the target distribution selected at that iteration. This separates choosing a desirable distribution from finding a model that produces it.

Under the paper’s stated mild conditions, this reparameterization turns the nonconvex objective into a convex one and enables provable regret guarantees. The regret bound is sublinear in the number of performative samples and polynomial in the dimension of the model parameters. The result establishes a conditional route to learning with limited feedback while avoiding several assumptions commonly used in earlier analyses.
summary.tldr: Optimizing over induced data distributions enables conditional regret guarantees for performative prediction without known distribution responses or gradients.

title: Performative Prediction with Bandit Feedback: Learning through Reparameterization

abstract: In contrast to close-set scenarios that restore images from a predefined set of degradations, open-set image restoration aims to handle the unknown degradations that were unforeseen during the pretraining phase, which is less-touched as far as we know. This work study this challenging problem and reveal its essence as unidentified distribution shifts between the test and training data. Recently, test-time adaptation has emerged as a fundamental method to address this inherent disparities. Inspired by it, we propose a test-time degradation adaptation framework for open-set image restoration, which consists of three components, i.e., i) a pre-trained and degradation-agnostic diffusion model for generating clean images, ii) a test-time degradation adapter adapts the unknown degradations based on the input image during the testing phase, and iii) the adapter-guided image restoration guides the model through the adapter to produce the corresponding clean image. Through experiments on multiple degradations, we show that our method achieves comparable even better performance than those task-specific methods. The code is available at https://github.com/XLearning-SCU/2024-ICML-TAO.

paragraphs: Image restoration often assumes that the kinds of degradation encountered during use were represented during training. Open-set restoration instead deals with previously unforeseen degradations. This paper interprets that challenge as an unidentified distribution shift between training images and the damaged image presented at test time.

The proposed framework has three components. A pretrained diffusion model supplies a degradation-agnostic model of clean images. A test-time adapter uses the input image to adapt to its unknown degradation. Finally, the adapter guides the diffusion model's restoration process toward a corresponding clean image. This connects a reusable clean-image model with adaptation to the particular input.

The results support adapting the degradation handling during inference when pretraining cannot anticipate the corruption encountered. The contribution is the integration of that adaptation with guided restoration, allowing the clean-image generator to be used in the studied open-set conditions.
summary.tldr: A test-time degradation adapter guides a pretrained diffusion model to restore images affected by previously unseen degradations.

title: Test-Time Degradation Adaptation for Open-Set Image Restoration

abstract: Predictive models are often introduced to decision-making tasks under the rationale that they improve performance over an existing decision-making policy. However, it is challenging to compare predictive performance against an existing decision-making policy that is generally under-specified and dependent on unobservable factors. These sources of uncertainty are often addressed in practice by making strong assumptions about the data-generating mechanism. In this work, we propose a method to compare the predictive performance of decision policies under a variety of modern identification approaches from the causal inference and off-policy evaluation literatures (e.g., instrumental variable, marginal sensitivity model, proximal variable). Key to our method is the insight that there are regions of uncertainty that we can safely ignore in the policy comparison. We develop a practical approach for finite-sample estimation of regret intervals under no assumptions on the parametric form of the status quo policy. We verify our framework theoretically and via synthetic data experiments. We conclude with a real-world application using our framework to support a pre-deployment evaluation of a proposed modification to a healthcare enrollment policy.

paragraphs: A proposed predictive policy is often justified by claiming it will outperform the current decision process. That comparison is difficult when the existing policy is incompletely specified or depends on unobserved factors. This paper develops a way to compare policies while retaining uncertainty about those factors.

The key insight is that some uncertain regions can be safely ignored for the comparison, even if they matter for characterizing policies individually. The framework accommodates several causal identification approaches, including instrumental variables, marginal sensitivity models, and proximal variables. It estimates finite-sample regret intervals without assuming a particular parametric form for the status quo policy.

Those intervals express uncertainty in comparative predictive performance instead of forcing a single fully determined answer. The authors verify the framework theoretically and through synthetic-data experiments, then apply it to evaluating a proposed healthcare enrollment-policy change before deployment. The contribution makes comparison possible under multiple identification approaches while avoiding a specific structural assumption about the existing policy; it does not remove the assumptions attached to those approaches.
summary.tldr: The framework estimates policy-performance differences under confounding by ignoring uncertainty irrelevant to the comparison and reporting regret intervals.

title: Predictive Performance Comparison of Decision Policies Under Confounding

abstract: Optimization problems with access to only zeroth-order information of the objective function on Riemannian manifolds arise in various applications, spanning from statistical learning to robot learning. While various zeroth-order algorithms have been proposed in Euclidean space, they are not inherently designed to handle the challenging constraints imposed by Riemannian manifolds. The proper adaptation of zeroth-order techniques to Riemannian manifolds remained unknown until the pioneering work of (Li et al., 2023a). However, zeroth-order algorithms are widely observed to converge slowly and be unstable in practice. To alleviate these issues, we propose a Riemannian accelerated zeroth-order algorithm with improved robustness. Regarding efficiency, our accelerated algorithm has the function query complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-7/4}d)$ for finding an $\epsilon$-approximate first-order stationary point. By introducing a small perturbation, it exhibits a function query complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-7/4}d)$ for seeking a second-order stationary point with a high probability, matching state-of-the-art result in Euclidean space. Moreover, we further establish the almost sure convergence in the asymptotic sense through the Stable Manifold Theorem. Regarding robustness, our algorithm requires larger smoothing parameters in the order of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{7/8}d^{-1/2})$, improving the existing result by a factor of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{3/4})$.

The paper develops an accelerated zeroth-order method to address slow convergence and instability in this setting.

For an epsilon-approximate first-order stationary point, the method requires O(epsilon^(-7/4) d) function queries. The authors also establish almost-sure asymptotic convergence through the Stable Manifold Theorem.

The robustness analysis permits larger smoothing parameters, with a stated scale of approximately epsilon^(7/8) d^(-1/2), up to logarithmic factors. This improves the existing result by the factor reported in the abstract. Together, the results extend strong query-efficiency guarantees to manifold-constrained optimization while strengthening the smoothing behavior associated with robustness. The conclusions concern stationary points and distinguish finite-query probabilistic guarantees from asymptotic convergence.
summary.tldr: An accelerated derivative-free manifold optimizer improves query complexity and smoothing robustness, with first- and second-order stationarity guarantees.

title: Riemannian Accelerated Zeroth-order Algorithm: Improved Robustness and Lower Query Complexity

abstract: People grasp flexible visual concepts from a few examples. We explore a neurosymbolic system that learns how to infer programs that capture visual concepts in a domain-general fashion. We introduce Template Programs: programmatic expressions from a domain-specific language that specify structural and parametric patterns common to an input concept. Our framework supports multiple concept-related tasks, including few-shot generation and co-segmentation through parsing. We develop a learning paradigm that allows us to train networks that infer Template Programs directly from visual datasets that contain concept groupings. We run experiments across multiple visual domains: 2D layouts, Omniglot characters, and 3D shapes. We find that our method outperforms task-specific alternatives, and performs competitively against domain-specific approaches for the limited domains where they exist.

paragraphs: A visual concept can include examples that share an underlying organization while differing in their details. This paper studies how to capture that shared organization in a program inferred from a small set of examples. Its neurosymbolic approach combines learned inference with explicit programmatic representations of visual structure.

The proposed Template Programs use expressions from a domain-specific language to describe structural and parameter patterns common to a concept. The authors develop a learning procedure that trains networks to infer these programs directly from visual datasets organized into concept groups. The resulting representation supports multiple tasks, including generating examples from limited input and parsing related examples to identify corresponding segments.

Experiments span two-dimensional layouts, Omniglot characters, and three-dimensional shapes. The method outperforms task-specific alternatives and is competitive with domain-specific approaches in the limited domains where those approaches exist. These findings support template programs as a reusable representation across visual tasks and domains, with shared structure serving both the interpretation of existing examples and the generation of new ones.
summary.tldr: Learned template programs capture shared visual structure to support generation and segmentation across several visual domains.

title: Learning to Infer Generative Template Programs for Visual Concepts

abstract: In this work, we propose a novel method for modeling numerous speakers, which enables expressing the overall characteristics of speakers in detail like a trained multi-speaker model without additional training on the target speaker’s dataset. Although various works with similar purposes have been actively studied, their performance has not yet reached that of trained multi-speaker models due to their fundamental limitations. To overcome previous limitations, we propose effective methods for feature learning and representing target speakers’ speech characteristics by discretizing the features and conditioning them to a speech synthesis model. Our method obtained a significantly higher similarity mean opinion score (SMOS) in subjective similarity evaluation than seen speakers of a high-performance multi-speaker model, even with unseen speakers. The proposed method also outperforms a zero-shot method by significant margins. Furthermore, our method shows remarkable performance in generating new artificial speakers. In addition, we demonstrate that the encoded latent features are sufficiently informative to reconstruct an original speaker’s speech completely. It implies that our method can be used as a general methodology to encode and reconstruct speakers’ characteristics in various tasks.

paragraphs: ELF aims to represent a speaker’s overall vocal characteristics in detail without additional training on that target speaker’s dataset. The motivation is a gap between methods designed to handle new speakers and models trained specifically to synthesize speech from multiple known speakers. The paper seeks a representation that can support detailed voice characteristics even for unseen speakers.

The method learns speech features, discretizes them, and uses the resulting representation to condition a speech-synthesis model. This places the speaker’s characteristics in an encoded form that the synthesizer can use. The authors also investigate whether those features contain enough information to reconstruct the original speaker’s speech and whether they can support newly created artificial speakers.

Subjective evaluations report higher speaker-similarity scores for unseen speakers than for seen speakers of a high-performance multispeaker model, as well as substantial gains over a zero-shot method. The paper also reports strong artificial-speaker generation and complete reconstruction of original speech from the encoded features. These findings motivate a possible broader role for the representation in encoding and reconstructing speaker characteristics.
summary.tldr: ELF encodes speaker characteristics into discrete speech features, reporting strong unseen-speaker similarity without additional target-speaker training.

title: ELF: Encoding Speaker-Specific Latent Speech Feature for Speech Synthesis

abstract: With increasingly serious data privacy concerns and strict regulations, privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) has emerged to securely execute machine learning tasks without violating privacy. Unfortunately, the computational cost to securely execute nonlinear computations in PPML remains significant, calling for new model architecture designs with fewer nonlinear operations. We propose Seesaw, a novel neural architecture search method tailored for PPML. Seesaw exploits a previously unexplored opportunity to leverage more linear computations and nonlinear result reuse, in order to compensate for the accuracy loss due to nonlinear reduction. It incorporates specifically designed pruning and search strategies, not only to efficiently handle the much larger design space of both linear and nonlinear operators, but also to achieve a better balance between the model accuracy and the online/offline execution latencies. Compared to the state-of-the-art design for image classification on ImageNet, Seesaw achieves 1.68$\times$ lower online latency and 1.55$\times$ lower total online + offline latency at 71% iso-accuracy, or 3.65% higher accuracy at iso-latency of 190 seconds, while using much simpler and faster search and training methods.
