paragraphs: Language models store information from earlier tokens in a key-value cache so they can use it during generation. As context grows, this storage becomes costly. Removing selected tokens helps control the cost, but can also remove useful information. ARM introduces a fixed-size memory whose contents and access patterns are learned.

The memory is organized through a hierarchical router. A differentiable selection mechanism lets training adjust which memory slots receive information. Gated updates blend incoming information with what is already stored, reducing the information loss associated with hard eviction. This makes memory management part of the learned computation rather than only a rule for deleting old entries.

ARM also trains a policy that chooses how much memory to access during inference. This allows different inputs to receive different amounts of retrieval effort, including inputs requiring deeper reasoning. Experiments on commonsense and long-context reasoning benchmarks report better performance and efficiency than fixed caching approaches. The findings support learning both memory updates and access decisions while controlling storage and generation latency.
summary.tldr: ARM learns how to update and access a fixed-size memory, improving reasoning performance and efficiency in the reported evaluations.

title: Attention with Routed-Memory for Learnable Sparse Control

abstract: Merging multiple low-rank adapters (LoRA) provides a practical route to scaling multi-task learning and deployment more efficiently than full-model weight merging, while avoiding reliance on task-specific training data. However, most existing approaches either treat LoRA updates as dense weight deltas or depend on expensive subspace factorizations, making the merge step a primary latency bottleneck. To address this issue, this paper establishes a theoretically positive relationship between merging quality and the effective rank of the matrices being merged. Motivated by this insight, we propose CircuMerge, a sketch-based framework for low-rank model merging built on shared circulant transforms. Especially, this approach treats each adapter as a pair of low-rank matrices and applies a shared circulant transform to align all tasks in a common coordinate system. This alignment enables more efficient sampling, allowing us to generate compact sketches that effectively summarize the interactions between tasks. These compact sketches enable applying the merging rules directly to them and reconstructing a standard low-rank adapter, preserving the essential information while significantly reducing computational overhead. Across a broad multi-task LoRA benchmarks covering both vision and language settings, extensive empirical results demonstrate that CircuMerge reduces the overall merging time by at least 44% compared to the state-of-the-art approaches, with accuracy matching or exceeding the optimal level.

title: Sketch-Based Low-Rank Model Merging with Shared Circulant Transforms

abstract: With the widespread deployment of large language models (LLMs), aligning model outputs with pluralistic human values has become an important research problem. Recent approaches that train task-specific experts and merge them through parameter aggregation have shown promise for pluralistic alignment. However, these methods often overlook the intrinsic complexity of real-world value data, where multiple correlated value dimensions coexist, resulting in highly similar and entangled expert representations. Consequently, modifying the contribution of one value expert may unintentionally influence other values, limiting fine-grained controllability. To address this issue, we propose DisAlign, a model-merging framework that explicitly decomposes value representations into consensus and value-specific components using an information-geometric perspective. DisAlign first extracts a consensus anchor and subspace to capture shared structure across values, and then applies spectral decomposition to the residual representations to construct disentangled value subspaces. This design enables more precise and independent modulation of multiple values. Experiments on three datasets covering different value frameworks demonstrate that DisAlign consistently improves value disentanglement and achieves more accurate pluralistic value control compared to existing baselines. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DisAlign-7F35

However, real value data contains correlated dimensions, so the experts can learn overlapping representations. Increasing one expert’s contribution may consequently change other values, making precise control difficult.

DisAlign addresses this coupling by separating shared structure from value-specific structure. Using an information-geometric perspective, it first identifies a consensus anchor and subspace that capture what the value representations have in common. It then applies spectral decomposition to the remaining representations to construct more disentangled value subspaces. The resulting merger offers more independent ways to adjust multiple values.

These findings support the proposed separation as a useful mechanism for controlling correlated value dimensions. The claimed improvement concerns the precision of value modulation, with shared consensus explicitly represented rather than left mixed into each expert.
summary.tldr: DisAlign separates shared and value-specific representations to make merged language models’ value preferences more independently controllable.

title: Disentangling Consensus and Value-Specific Representations for Controllable Pluralistic Value Alignment in LLMs

abstract: This position paper argues one of the bottlenecks on the way towards recursively self-improving systems is the challenge of interestingness: the ability to prospectively identify which tasks or data hold the potential for future progress. We formalize interestingness as an inductive heuristic for future compression progress and investigate its predictability using tools from Kolmogorov Complexity and Algorithmic Statistics. By analyzing complexity-runtime profiles under Length, Algorithmic, and Speed priors, we demonstrate that the inductive property of interestingness—the capacity for past progress to signal future discovery—is theoretically viable and empirically supported. We prove that expected future progress depends exponentially on the recency of the last observed breakthrough. Furthermore, we show that the Algorithmic Prior is significantly more optimistic than the Length Prior, yielding a quadratic increase in expected discovery for the same observed profile. These findings are experimentally validated across three diverse universal computational paradigms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a system might identify tasks or data that are promising before further progress occurs. It formalizes interestingness as an inductive heuristic for future compression progress: observed improvements provide clues about opportunities for subsequent discovery. The authors frame this predictive ability as a bottleneck for systems that recursively improve themselves.

The analysis uses Kolmogorov complexity and algorithmic statistics to examine profiles relating complexity to runtime. It compares Length, Algorithmic, and Speed priors, which encode different assumptions in the analysis. Within this framework, the authors prove that expected future progress depends exponentially on how recently the last breakthrough occurred. They also find that the Algorithmic Prior gives a more optimistic forecast than the Length Prior, with a quadratic increase in expected discovery for the same observed profile.

Experiments across three universal computational paradigms support the theoretical findings. Together, the results support the viability of using past progress to anticipate future discovery. Their meaning is tied to the analyzed profiles and priors: the choice of assumptions materially changes how promising an identical history appears.
summary.tldr: Theoretical analysis and experiments support using past compression breakthroughs to predict future progress, with forecasts depending strongly on the prior.

title: Position: Interestingness is an Inductive Heuristic for Future Compression Progress

abstract: A cost-sensitive extension of boosting, denoted as asymmetric boosting, is presented. Unlike previous proposals, the new algorithm is derived from sound decision-theoretic principles, which exploit the statistical interpretation of boosting to determine a principled extension of the boosting loss. Similarly to AdaBoost, the cost-sensitive extension minimizes this loss by gradient descent on the functional space of convex combinations of weak learners, and produces large margin detectors. It is shown that asymmetric boosting is fully compatible with AdaBoost, in the sense that it becomes the latter when errors are weighted equally. Experimental evidence is provided to demonstrate the claims of cost-sensitivity and large margin. The algorithm is also applied to the computer vision problem of face detection, where it is shown to outperform a number of previous heuristic proposals for cost-sensitive boosting (AdaCost, CSB0, CSB1, CSB2, asymmetricAdaBoost, AdaC1, AdaC2 and AdaC3).

paragraphs: Asymmetric boosting addresses classification problems in which different kinds of mistakes carry different costs. The paper derives a cost-sensitive boosting method from decision theory and the statistical interpretation of boosting. Its central step is to incorporate those costs into a principled loss function, giving the learning objective an explicit connection to the consequences of errors.

The algorithm minimizes this loss through gradient descent over convex combinations of weak learners, following the general approach used by AdaBoost. It also produces large-margin detectors. When the costs of errors are equal, the method reduces to AdaBoost, so ordinary boosting appears as a special case of the same formulation.

Experiments provide evidence for both cost sensitivity and large margins. In face detection, the method outperforms several earlier heuristic approaches to cost-sensitive boosting. These findings support the practical value of deriving the loss from decision-theoretic principles in the evaluated setting, while the equal-cost connection explains how the method relates to an established boosting algorithm.
summary.tldr: Asymmetric boosting derives a cost-sensitive loss from decision theory, reduces to AdaBoost for equal error costs, and improves face detection in reported comparisons.

title: Asymmetric boosting

abstract: While discriminative training (e.g., CRF, structural SVM) holds much promise for machine translation, image segmentation, and clustering, the complex inference these applications require make exact training intractable. This leads to a need for approximate training methods. Unfortunately, knowledge about how to perform efficient and effective approximate training is limited. Focusing on structural SVMs, we provide and explore algorithms for two different classes of approximate training algorithms, which we call undergenerating (e.g., greedy) and overgenerating (e.g., relaxations) algorithms. We provide a theoretical and empirical analysis of both types of approximate trained structural SVMs, focusing on fully connected pairwise Markov random fields. We find that models trained with overgenerating methods have theoretic advantages over undergenerating methods, are empirically robust relative to their undergenerating brethren, and relaxed trained models favor non-fractional predictions from relaxed predictors.

paragraphs: Structured prediction applications can require inference that is too complex to perform exactly during training. This paper studies how to train structural support vector machines under that constraint. It examines two families of approximation: undergenerating methods, including greedy procedures, and overgenerating methods, including relaxations.

Undergenerating methods search a restricted collection of possibilities, while overgenerating methods expand the optimization space through a relaxation. The authors develop and analyze algorithms from both families, using theoretical arguments and empirical evaluation. Their investigation focuses on fully connected pairwise Markov random fields, providing a concrete setting for comparing the consequences of these training choices.

The authors find theoretical advantages for overgenerating methods and greater empirical robustness relative to undergenerating approaches. They also report that models trained with relaxations favor non-fractional predictions when used with relaxed predictors. This suggests that training can influence whether a relaxed prediction procedure produces a discrete result. The contribution shows that the form of approximation matters for both learning behavior and the outputs obtained at prediction time.
summary.tldr: Comparing approximate structural SVM training methods reveals theoretical and empirical advantages for overgenerating relaxations.

title: Training structural SVMs when exact inference is intractable

abstract: We consider the task of learning to accurately follow a trajectory in a vehicle such as a car or helicopter. A number of dynamic programming algorithms such as Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) and Policy Search by Dynamic Programming (PSDP), can efficiently compute non-stationary policies for these tasks --- such policies in general are well-suited to trajectory following since they can easily generate different control actions at different times in order to follow the trajectory. However, a weakness of these algorithms is that their policies are time-indexed, in that they apply different policies depending on the current time. This is problematic since 1) the current time may not correspond well to where we are along the trajectory and 2) the uncertainty over future states can prevent these algorithms from finding any good policies at all. In this paper we propose a method for space-indexed dynamic programming that overcomes both these difficulties. We begin by showing how a dynamical system can be rewritten in terms of a spatial index variable (i.e., how far along the trajectory we are) rather than as a function of time. We then use these space-indexed dynamical systems to derive space-indexed version of the DDP and PSDP algorithms. Finally, we show that these algorithms perform well on a variety of control tasks, both in simulation and on real systems.

paragraphs: A vehicle following a trajectory may reach a location earlier or later than expected. A controller that chooses its policy according to elapsed time can then select an action poorly matched to its actual progress. This paper also identifies uncertainty about future states as a reason time-indexed dynamic programming may fail to find a good policy.

The proposed solution indexes the dynamics by spatial progress along the trajectory. The authors first show how to rewrite a dynamical system using that progress variable, then derive space-indexed versions of Differential Dynamic Programming and Policy Search by Dynamic Programming. The policy can consequently vary along the route according to where the vehicle is in the trajectory.

The paper presents this reformulation as overcoming the two identified difficulties and reports good performance across several control tasks, both in simulation and on real systems. The contribution is a change in how trajectory-following problems are represented for dynamic programming, supported by working control demonstrations rather than a claim about every possible vehicle or trajectory.
summary.tldr: Space-indexed dynamic programming bases trajectory-following policies on progress along the route, addressing weaknesses of time-indexed control.

title: Space-indexed dynamic programming: learning to follow trajectories

abstract: In this paper, we present an algorithm for finding an $s$-sparse vector $x$ that minimizes the {\em square-error} $\| y - \Phi x \|^2$ where $\Phi$ satisfies the {\em restricted isometry property} (RIP). Our algorithm, called {\em {\GraDeS}} (Gradient Descent with Sparsification) starts from an arbitrary $s$-sparse $x$ and iteratively updates it as: $$x \leftarrow H_s\left(x + \frac{1}{\gamma} \cdot \Phi^\t(y - \Phi x)\right)$$ where $\gamma > 1$ is a constant and $H_s$ sets all but largest $s$ coordinates in absolute value to zero. We show that {\GraDeS}, in constant number of iterations, computes the correct $s$-sparse solution to the system $y=\Phi x$ where $\Phi$ satisfies the condition that the {\em isometric constant} $\delta_{2s} < 1/3$. This is the most general condition for which, {\em near-linear time} algorithm is known. In comparison, the best condition under which any polynomial-time algorithm is known, is $\delta_{2s} < \sqrt{2}-1$. An important contribution of the paper is to analyze how the hard-thresholding function $H_s$ acts w.r.t. the potential $\|y - \Phi x\|^2$. A special case of {\GraDeS}, corresponding to $\gamma = 1$, called {\em Iterative Hard Thresholding (IHT)}, was previously shown to converge when $\delta_{3s} < 1/\sqrt{32}$~\cite{IHT:BD08}. Our Matlab implementation of {\GraDeS} out-performs previously proposed algorithms like Subspace Pursuit, StOMP, OMP, and Lasso by an order of magnitude. Curiously, our experiments also uncovered several cases where L1-regularized regression (Lasso) fails but {\GraDeS} finds the correct solution.

paragraphs: Sparse recovery seeks a vector with only a small number of nonzero entries that explains observed measurements. The paper introduces GraDeS, which alternates a gradient step reducing squared measurement error with a sparsification step. That second step keeps only the s largest coordinates in absolute value, setting all others to zero.

Starting from any s-sparse vector, the algorithm uses a gradient step scaled by a constant gamma greater than one. Under the restricted-isometry condition δ₂s < 1/3, the authors prove recovery of the correct sparse solution to the noiseless system in a constant number of iterations. Their analysis explains how hard thresholding affects the squared-error objective, a central difficulty in combining optimization with enforced sparsity.

The abstract places this guarantee within the conditions known for near-linear and polynomial-time recovery methods. It also reports an order-of-magnitude performance advantage for a Matlab implementation over Subspace Pursuit, StOMP, OMP, and Lasso. Some experiments recover solutions that Lasso misses; these examples complement the conditional recovery theorem rather than establishing universal superiority.
summary.tldr: GraDeS alternates gradient updates with hard thresholding and proves sparse recovery under a stated restricted-isometry condition.

title: Gradient descent with sparsification: an iterative algorithm for sparse recovery with restricted isometry property

abstract: We consider the problem of embedding arbitrary objects (e.g., images, audio, documents) into Euclidean space subject to a partial order over pairwise distances. Partial order constraints arise naturally when modeling human perception of similarity. Our partial order framework enables the use of graph-theoretic tools to more efficiently produce the embedding, and exploit global structure within the constraint set. We present an embedding algorithm based on semidefinite programming, which can be parameterized by multiple kernels to yielding a unified space from heterogeneous features.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of embedding arbitrary objects (e.g., images, audio, documents) into Euclidean space subject to a partial order over pairwise distances. Partial order constraints arise naturally when modeling human perception of similarity. Our partial order framework enables the use of graph-theoretic tools to more efficiently produce the embedding, and exploit global structure within the constraint set. We present an embedding algorithm based on semidefinite programming, which can be parameterized by multiple kernels to yielding a unified space from heterogeneous features.

paragraphs: Similarity judgments need not specify exact numerical distances between objects. They can instead say that one pair should be closer than another. This paper studies embedding objects such as images, audio, and documents into Euclidean space while respecting a partial ordering of pairwise distances, a form of information that arises naturally in modeling human similarity perception.

Representing the constraints as a partial order allows the method to use graph-theoretic tools. The authors use this structure to produce embeddings more efficiently and to exploit relationships across the full constraint collection. The approach therefore treats the ordering information as a structured whole when constructing the space.

The proposed embedding algorithm is based on semidefinite programming and can be parameterized with multiple kernels. This allows heterogeneous features to contribute to a unified representation. The resulting framework links relative similarity constraints with a way to combine different descriptions of the objects, so both the supplied ordering and the available feature sources can shape the embedding.
summary.tldr: A semidefinite embedding method uses partial orders of distances and multiple kernels to combine similarity constraints with heterogeneous features.

title: Partial order embedding with multiple kernels

abstract: In this talk, I will discuss recent work by colleagues and myself on discriminative latent-variable models for object detection. Object recognition is one of the fundamental challenges of computer vision. We specifically consider the task of localizing and detecting instances of a generic object category, such as people or cars, in cluttered real-word images. Recent benchmark competitions such as the PASCAL Visual Object Challenge suggest our method is the state-of-the-art system for such tasks. This success, combined with publically-available code that runs orders of magnitude faster than comparable approaches, has turned our system into a standard baseline for contemporary research on object recognition.

paragraphs: Object detection requires identifying instances of a category and locating them within an image. The supplied abstract describes a talk about discriminative latent-variable models for this task, focusing on categories such as people and cars in cluttered real-world scenes. The setting combines recognition with localization, so success involves finding where relevant objects appear.

The work discussed uses discriminative latent-variable modeling as the basis of an object detection system. The abstract presents evidence of its standing through benchmark competitions, including the PASCAL Visual Object Challenge. Those results are described as suggesting that the system is state of the art for the detection tasks under consideration.

The abstract also emphasizes practical accessibility and speed: publicly available code runs orders of magnitude faster than comparable approaches. It attributes the system's adoption as a standard research baseline to the combination of strong benchmark performance and efficient available software. The stated contribution thus includes both the detection approach and its practical role in enabling comparisons in subsequent object-recognition research.
summary.tldr: The talk presents a discriminative latent-variable object detector whose benchmark performance and fast public implementation made it a widely used research baseline.

title: Discriminative Latent Variable Models for Object Detection

abstract: We present the first temporal-difference learning algorithm for off-policy control with unrestricted linear function approximation whose per-time-step complexity is linear in the number of features. Our algorithm, text it {Greedy-GQ}, is an extension of recent work on gradient temporal-difference learning, which has hitherto been restricted to a prediction (policy evaluation) setting, to a control setting in which the target policy is greedy with respect to a linear approximation to the optimal action-value function. A limitation of our control setting is that we require the behavior policy to be stationary. We call this setting text it {latent learning} because the optimal policy, though learned, is not manifest in behavior. Popular off-policy algorithms such as Q-learning are known to be unstable in this setting when used with linear function approximation.

Our algorithm, text it {Greedy-GQ}, is an extension of recent work on gradient temporal-difference learning, which has hitherto been restricted to a prediction (policy evaluation) setting, to a control setting in which the target policy is greedy with respect to a linear approximation to the optimal action-value function. A limitation of our control setting is that we require the behavior policy to be stationary. We call this setting text it {latent learning} because the optimal policy, though learned, is not manifest in behavior. Popular off-policy algorithms such as Q-learning are known to be unstable in this setting when used with linear function approximation.

paragraphs: Off-policy control learns a decision policy from experience generated by another policy. With linear function approximation, familiar methods such as Q-learning can be unstable in this setting. This paper introduces Greedy-GQ, a temporal-difference algorithm that extends gradient-based temporal-difference learning from evaluating a policy to learning control.

The target policy chooses actions greedily according to a linear approximation of the optimal action-value function. The authors present the method as the first off-policy temporal-difference control algorithm with unrestricted linear function approximation and per-step computation linear in the number of features. That scaling makes the cost of each update explicit as the representation grows.

The setting requires a stationary behavior policy, meaning the policy generating experience remains fixed. The authors call this latent learning because the policy being learned is not expressed in the agent's behavior during learning. This assumption defines the scope of the contribution: control learning proceeds from fixed-policy experience while the target action choices are determined by the learned value approximation.
summary.tldr: Greedy-GQ extends gradient temporal-difference learning to off-policy control with linear per-step cost, assuming a stationary behavior policy.

title: Toward Off-Policy Learning Control with Function Approximation

abstract: In this paper we propose a new framework for learning from large scale datasets based on iterative learning from small mini-batches. By adding the right amount of noise to a standard stochastic gradient optimization algorithm we show that the iterates will converge to samples from the true posterior distribution as we anneal the stepsize. This seamless transition between optimization and Bayesian posterior sampling provides an in-built protection against overfitting. We also propose a practical method for Monte Carlo estimates of posterior statistics which monitors a ``sampling threshold'' and collects samples after it has been surpassed. We apply the method to three models: a mixture of Gaussians, logistic regression and ICA with natural gradients.
originalAbstract: In this paper we propose a new framework for learning from large scale datasets based on iterative learning from small mini-batches. By adding the right amount of noise to a standard stochastic gradient optimization algorithm we show that the iterates will converge to samples from the true posterior distribution as we anneal the stepsize. This seamless transition between optimization and Bayesian posterior sampling provides an in-built protection against overfitting. We also propose a practical method for Monte Carlo estimates of posterior statistics which monitors a ``sampling threshold'' and collects samples after it has been surpassed. We apply the method to three models: a mixture of Gaussians, logistic regression and ICA with natural gradients.

paragraphs: Learning from large datasets often relies on small mini-batches rather than processing all examples at every update. This paper builds a Bayesian learning framework around that iterative workflow. It modifies standard stochastic gradient optimization by adding a carefully chosen amount of noise, connecting the process of fitting model parameters with the process of sampling their posterior distribution.

The central result concerns what happens as the step size is gradually reduced. With the appropriate noise, the iterates converge to samples from the true posterior distribution. The step-size annealing is part of that claim. The authors describe the resulting transition from optimization to posterior sampling as providing built-in protection against overfitting.

The paper also proposes a practical procedure for estimating posterior statistics by Monte Carlo. It monitors a sampling threshold and begins collecting samples after that threshold is crossed. Applications cover a Gaussian mixture model, logistic regression, and independent component analysis with natural gradients. Together, these components present a route from scalable mini-batch updates to Bayesian estimates derived from parameter samples.
summary.tldr: Adding appropriate noise to mini-batch gradient updates yields posterior samples as the step size is annealed.

title: Bayesian Learning via Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics
